constructs.name: présent de l'indicatif (verbes en -er)
aliases: présent des verbes du premier groupe
constructs.description: Present tense of regular -er verbs: one stem plus the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

card.formation: Remove -er from the infinitive and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. The forms in -e, -es and -ent are pronounced the same.
card.use: This is the present-tense pattern of the largest verb group, which covers most French verbs and nearly all new ones. Once learned, it lets you conjugate thousands of verbs.
pitfalls: The -ent ending of the ils/elles form is silent: ils parlent sounds like il parle.
Verbs in -cer write ç before -ons (nous commençons) and verbs in -ger keep an e (nous mangeons).
Some verbs change their stem before a silent ending: j'achète, j'appelle, je préfère, but nous achetons, nous appelons, nous préférons.
Je becomes j' before a vowel or mute h: j'aime, j'habite.
Aller ends in -er but is irregular (je vais, ils vont).

contrasts.note: Second-group -ir verbs have different endings (-is, -is, -it) and add -iss- in the plural.
Irregular verbs change their stem and often end in -s, -s, -t in the singular.
That entry is about what the present means, not how its forms are built.

examples.sentence: Je parle français avec mes amis.
examples.translation: I speak French with my friends.

examples.sentence: Nous mangeons à midi.
examples.translation: We eat at noon.

examples.sentence: Ils habitent à Lyon.
examples.translation: They live in Lyon.

constructs.name: présent de l'indicatif (verbes en -ir à deux radicaux)
aliases: présent des verbes du deuxième groupe
constructs.description: Present tense of second-group -ir verbs, which insert -iss- in the plural.

card.formation: Remove -ir and add -is, -is, -it in the singular; in the plural add -iss- before -ons, -ez, -ent (nous finissons, ils finissent).
card.use: This is the present tense of the regular second group, verbs like finir, choisir, réussir, grandir and many verbs made from adjectives (rougir, vieillir).
pitfalls: Not every verb in -ir follows this pattern: partir, dormir, sortir, venir and ouvrir are irregular (nous partons, not nous partissons).
Je finis, tu finis and il finit all sound the same.
The -iss- stem also appears in the imparfait, the subjonctif and the participe présent (finissait, finisse, finissant).

contrasts.note: Irregular -ir verbs such as partir drop a consonant in the singular (je pars) and never add -iss-.
-er verbs end in -e, -es, -e and have a single stem.
The imparfait is built on the plural stem, so these verbs keep -iss- there too: je finissais.

examples.sentence: Le film finit à dix heures.
examples.translation: The film ends at ten o'clock.

examples.sentence: Nous choisissons un dessert.
examples.translation: We are choosing a dessert.

examples.sentence: Les enfants grandissent vite.
examples.translation: Children grow up fast.

constructs.name: présent de l'indicatif (verbes irréguliers)
aliases: présent des verbes du troisième groupe
constructs.description: Present tense of irregular and third-group verbs, with changing stems in the singular and plural.

card.formation: Most irregular verbs end in -s, -s, -t (or -d, -x) in the singular and -ons, -ez, -ent in the plural, but their stem changes: often one stem for je/tu/il, another for nous/vous, and sometimes a third for ils (venir: viens, venons, viennent). Être, avoir, aller and faire are irregular throughout.
card.use: These forms cover the most frequent verbs of the language (être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir, prendre, venir), so they appear in almost every sentence.
pitfalls: The vous forms of faire, dire and être are vous faites, vous dites, vous êtes, not *faisez or *disez.
Ils sont, ils ont, ils vont and ils font are easily mixed up.
Pouvoir and vouloir end in -x: je peux, tu veux.
Verbs in -dre have no -t in the il form: il prend, il attend.
Prendre and venir double the n in the ils form: ils prennent, ils viennent.

contrasts.note: Regular -er verbs keep one stem and end in -e, -es, -e.
Regular -ir verbs add -iss- in the plural instead of changing their stem.
The subjunctive is built on the ils stem of these verbs (ils viennent, que je vienne), so knowing it helps there.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes en retard.
examples.translation: We are late.

examples.sentence: Ils vont au cinéma ce soir.
examples.translation: They are going to the cinema tonight.

examples.sentence: Vous faites du sport ?
examples.translation: Do you do any sport?

examples.sentence: Elle prend le bus.
examples.translation: She takes the bus.

constructs.name: présent de l'indicatif (emplois)
constructs.description: Uses of the present: current facts, habits, general truths and near future.

card.formation: The ordinary present-tense forms; the meaning comes from context and time expressions, not from a different form.
card.use: The present describes what is happening now, habits, general truths and timeless facts. With a time expression it can refer to the near future (je pars demain), and with depuis to an action that started in the past and is still going on.
pitfalls: French has no separate progressive form: 'I am eating' and 'I eat' are both je mange.
For an action that started in the past and continues, use depuis with the present: j'habite ici depuis deux ans, not *j'ai habité.
After quand with a future meaning, French uses the future, not the present: quand je serai là.
After si expressing a condition, French uses the present, not the future: s'il pleut, je reste.

contrasts.note: Être en train de stresses that the action is in progress right now; the simple present is neutral.
Aller + infinitive marks the future explicitly; the present needs a time word to point to the future.
Depuis + present expresses ongoing duration, where English uses the present perfect.
The passé composé describes completed actions, not ones still going on.

examples.sentence: Je travaille le lundi.
examples.translation: I work on Mondays.

examples.sentence: L'eau bout à cent degrés.
examples.translation: Water boils at a hundred degrees.

examples.sentence: J'habite ici depuis deux ans.
examples.translation: I have been living here for two years.

examples.sentence: Je pars demain matin.
examples.translation: I'm leaving tomorrow morning.

constructs.name: présent progressif (être en train de + infinitif)
constructs.description: Expresses an action in progress at a given moment.

card.formation: Conjugated être + en train de + infinitive; de becomes d' before a vowel. With être in the imparfait it describes an action in progress in the past.
card.use: It stresses that an action is under way at a particular moment, often to explain why someone is busy or to set up an interruption. It is optional: the simple present usually says the same thing.
pitfalls: Do not use it for every English -ing form; the simple present is the normal choice.
It is not used with state verbs such as savoir, avoir or aimer.
It does not express future plans: 'I'm leaving tomorrow' is je pars demain.
Object pronouns go before the infinitive: je suis en train de le lire.

contrasts.note: The simple present can also describe an ongoing action, without the emphasis.
The imparfait alone can describe an action in progress in the past; j'étais en train de stresses it.
En + participe présent expresses simultaneity or manner, not an action in progress.
Aller + infinitive points to the future, être en train de to the present moment.

examples.sentence: Je suis en train de cuisiner.
examples.translation: I'm cooking right now.

examples.sentence: Chut, le bébé est en train de dormir.
examples.translation: Shh, the baby is sleeping.

examples.sentence: On était en train de manger.
examples.translation: We were in the middle of eating.

constructs.name: futur proche (aller + infinitif)
constructs.description: Expresses a future action seen as near or already planned.

card.formation: Aller in the present (je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont) + infinitive, with no preposition in between.
card.use: It expresses a future action that is close, planned or already certain from the present situation. In everyday speech it is often used instead of the futur simple.
pitfalls: No preposition goes between aller and the infinitive: je vais manger, not *je vais à manger.
The negation surrounds aller: je ne vais pas partir.
Object pronouns go before the infinitive: je vais le faire.
Aller + infinitive can also mean real movement: je vais chercher le pain (I'm going to get the bread).

contrasts.note: The futur simple is more neutral or formal and is used for predictions, promises and more distant plans.
Venir de + infinitive is its mirror image: an action that has just happened.
With aller in the imparfait, the same structure expresses what was about to happen in the past.
The present with a time word (je pars demain) can also express a near future.

examples.sentence: Je vais appeler ma mère.
examples.translation: I'm going to call my mother.

examples.sentence: Regarde le ciel, il va pleuvoir.
examples.translation: Look at the sky, it's going to rain.

examples.sentence: Nous allons partir en vacances.
examples.translation: We are going to go on holiday.

examples.sentence: Elle ne va pas venir.
examples.translation: She isn't going to come.

constructs.name: passé récent (venir de + infinitif)
constructs.description: Expresses an action that has just happened.

card.formation: Venir in the present (je viens, il vient, nous venons, ils viennent) + de + infinitive; de becomes d' before a vowel. With venir in the imparfait it means 'had just'.
card.use: It expresses an action that happened a very short time ago, like English 'have just done'.
pitfalls: Venir de + noun means 'come from': je viens de Paris; only venir de + infinitive means 'have just'.
Do not put venir in the passé composé: 'I have just eaten' is je viens de manger, not *je suis venu de manger.
Object pronouns go before the infinitive: je viens de le voir.
'Had just' uses the imparfait: je venais de partir.

contrasts.note: The passé composé states a completed action without saying it was very recent.
Aller + infinitive is the forward-looking counterpart: something about to happen.
Venir in the imparfait + de + infinitive is a close, more immediate alternative to the plus-que-parfait.

examples.sentence: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.
examples.translation: I've just finished my homework.

examples.sentence: Le train vient d'arriver.
examples.translation: The train has just arrived.

examples.sentence: Nous venions de manger.
examples.translation: We had just eaten.

constructs.name: passé composé avec avoir
constructs.description: Compound past formed with avoir in the present plus the past participle.

card.formation: Avoir in the present + past participle (j'ai parlé, tu as fini, il a pris). -er verbs make their participle in -é, regular -ir verbs in -i, and many common verbs have irregular participles (fait, pris, vu, eu, été, dit, mis).
card.use: Avoir is the auxiliary of the passé composé for most verbs, including avoir and être themselves. It is used for all transitive verbs and for most intransitive ones.
pitfalls: Être takes avoir: 'I have been' is j'ai été, not *je suis été.
The negation surrounds the auxiliary: je n'ai pas mangé, not *je n'ai mangé pas.
Short adverbs usually go between the auxiliary and the participle: j'ai bien dormi, il a déjà fini.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, but it agrees with a direct object placed before it: les fleurs que j'ai achetées.
Object pronouns go before the auxiliary: je l'ai vu.

contrasts.note: Verbs of movement and change of state and all pronominal verbs use être instead.
That entry explains when the passé composé is used rather than how it is built.
Covers the agreement with a preceding direct object in detail.
Covers how past participles, including the irregular ones, are formed.
Same structure, but with avoir in the imparfait, for an action before another past one.

examples.sentence: J'ai mangé une pomme.
examples.translation: I ate an apple.

examples.sentence: Nous avons fini le travail.
examples.translation: We have finished the work.

examples.sentence: Elle a pris le train.
examples.translation: She took the train.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai pas vu ce film.
examples.translation: I haven't seen this film.

constructs.name: passé composé avec être
constructs.description: Compound past formed with être for a set of intransitive verbs of movement and change of state, with the participle agreeing with the subject.

card.formation: Être in the present + past participle, which agrees with the subject in gender and number (elle est allée, ils sont partis). It is used with a closed list of intransitive verbs of movement or change of state (aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, rester, tomber, retourner, passer, and their compounds such as revenir, rentrer, devenir).
card.use: It forms the passé composé of these verbs, with the same meaning as the passé composé with avoir.
pitfalls: The participle must agree with the subject: elle est partie, nous sommes allés.
Learners often use avoir with these verbs: *j'ai allé instead of je suis allé.
Verbs of movement that are not on the list take avoir: j'ai marché, j'ai couru, j'ai voyagé.
Être + participle also forms the passive, which has a different meaning: la porte est fermée.
Several of these verbs take avoir when they have a direct object: j'ai monté les valises.

contrasts.note: Avoir is the auxiliary for all other verbs and has no agreement with the subject.
Monter, sortir, passer and others switch to avoir when they take a direct object.
Covers the agreement rule in detail.
Pronominal verbs also take être in compound tenses (je me suis levé), but follow their own agreement rules.
The passive also uses être + participle, but the subject undergoes the action.

examples.sentence: Elle est partie à huit heures.
examples.translation: She left at eight o'clock.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes allés au marché.
examples.translation: We went to the market.

examples.sentence: Mon grand-père est mort l'an dernier.
examples.translation: My grandfather died last year.

examples.sentence: Ils sont nés en 2010.
examples.translation: They were born in 2010.

constructs.name: passé composé (emplois)
constructs.description: Uses of the passé composé for completed past events, successions of actions and results.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the present + past participle; see the formation entries for the choice of auxiliary.
card.use: The passé composé presents past actions as completed: single events, a series of events that follow each other, and actions whose result matters now. It is the normal past tense of speech and everyday writing, covering both 'I did' and 'I have done'.
pitfalls: An action that started in the past and is still going on takes the present with depuis, not the passé composé.
Past habits, descriptions and backgrounds take the imparfait, not the passé composé.
A limited, closed duration still takes the passé composé: il a plu toute la journée.
It translates both the English simple past and the present perfect.

contrasts.note: Covers how passé composé and imparfait share the work in a story.
The imparfait describes backgrounds, states and habits rather than completed events.
The passé simple plays the same role in literary narrative.
Depuis + present is used for actions still going on, where English uses the present perfect.
Venir de + infinitive stresses that the action is very recent.

examples.sentence: Hier, j'ai vu Paul au café.
examples.translation: Yesterday I saw Paul at the café.

examples.sentence: Elle a ouvert la porte et elle est sortie.
examples.form: a ouvert la porte et elle est sortie
examples.translation: She opened the door and went out.

examples.sentence: J'ai habité trois ans à Rome.
examples.translation: I lived in Rome for three years.

examples.sentence: Oh non, j'ai perdu mes clés !
examples.translation: Oh no, I've lost my keys!

constructs.name: verbes à double auxiliaire (avoir ou être)
constructs.description: Verbs like monter or sortir that take être when intransitive and avoir when they have a direct object.

card.formation: A few verbs of the être group (monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, passer, retourner) take être when they have no direct object and avoir when they have one. With avoir, the participle follows the avoir agreement rules.
card.use: Without an object they describe the subject's own movement; with a direct object their meaning changes, e.g. sortir le chien (take the dog out), monter les valises (carry the cases up), passer une semaine (spend a week).
pitfalls: Elle est sortie means she went out; elle a sorti la poubelle means she took the bin out.
Passer with a time expression takes avoir: j'ai passé une semaine à Nice.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject: elle a monté les valises.
Retourner with an object means 'turn over' or 'send back' and takes avoir: j'ai retourné la crêpe.

contrasts.note: These verbs belong to the être group when they have no direct object.
With a direct object they follow the avoir pattern.
With avoir, agreement is only with a direct object placed before the verb: les valises que j'ai montées.

examples.sentence: Elle est sortie ce soir.
examples.translation: She went out tonight.

examples.sentence: Elle a sorti la poubelle.
examples.translation: She took the bin out.

examples.sentence: J'ai monté les valises.
examples.translation: I carried the suitcases up.

examples.sentence: Nous avons passé une semaine à Nice.
examples.translation: We spent a week in Nice.

constructs.name: imparfait (formation)
constructs.description: Imperfect tense built on the nous stem of the present plus -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

card.formation: Take the nous form of the present, remove -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient (nous finissons → je finissais). The only exception is être, whose stem is ét- (j'étais).
card.use: This is how the imparfait is built for all verbs; its uses are covered separately.
pitfalls: Être is the only irregular stem: j'étais, not *j'essais.
Verbs in -cer and -ger keep their spelling before a: je commençais, je mangeais.
Verbs whose stem ends in -i have a double i with nous and vous: nous étudiions, vous oubliiez.
The -ais, -ait and -aient endings all sound the same.
The nous and vous forms often look like the present subjunctive: que nous parlions.

contrasts.note: Covers what the imparfait expresses rather than its forms.
The conditional uses the same endings, but on the future stem: je parlerais vs je parlais.
The nous and vous forms of the subjunctive are often identical to those of the imparfait.

examples.sentence: Nous habitions à Lille.
examples.translation: We used to live in Lille.

examples.sentence: Il faisait beau.
examples.translation: The weather was nice.

examples.sentence: J'étais fatigué.
examples.translation: I was tired.

examples.sentence: Vous mangiez ensemble ?
examples.translation: Did you use to eat together?

constructs.name: imparfait (description et habitude)
constructs.description: Use of the imperfect for background, descriptions, states and repeated actions in the past.

card.formation: The imparfait forms: nous stem of the present + -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
card.use: The imparfait describes the past without marking a beginning or an end: settings, people, states, feelings, and actions in progress. It also expresses repeated actions and habits, like English 'used to' or 'would'.
pitfalls: Do not use it for a single completed event: hier, j'ai mangé, not *je mangeais, when telling what happened.
English 'would' for a past habit is the imparfait, not the conditional: nous allions à la plage.
English 'was -ing' usually corresponds to the imparfait.
A state that changes at a precise moment takes the passé composé: tout à coup, j'ai eu peur.

contrasts.note: Covers how the imparfait and the passé composé combine in a story.
The passé composé presents actions as completed events.
The plus-que-parfait places an action before another past moment.
After si, the imparfait expresses an imagined present, not the past.
J'étais en train de stresses an action in progress more strongly than the imparfait alone.

examples.sentence: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais au foot.
examples.translation: When I was little, I used to play football.

examples.sentence: Il faisait froid et il neigeait.
examples.translation: It was cold and it was snowing.

examples.sentence: Le samedi, nous allions au marché.
examples.translation: On Saturdays we would go to the market.

examples.sentence: Elle avait les cheveux longs.
examples.translation: She had long hair.

constructs.name: alternance passé composé et imparfait
aliases: temps du passé dans le récit
constructs.description: Choosing between passé composé for events and imparfait for background when telling a story.

card.formation: A story mixes the two tenses: passé composé for the events, imparfait for the circumstances around them. A typical pattern is an imparfait action in progress interrupted by a passé composé event, often linked by quand.
card.use: The passé composé moves the story forward (what happened next); the imparfait paints the background (what things were like, what was going on). The choice depends on the role of the action in the story, not on how long it lasted.
pitfalls: Do not choose by length of time: il a vécu dix ans à Paris is a completed period and takes the passé composé.
Words like soudain, tout à coup and un jour usually go with the passé composé; d'habitude, souvent and tous les jours with the imparfait.
Pendant que is normally followed by the imparfait.
Some verbs change meaning: je savais (I knew) vs j'ai su (I found out).
Il y avait describes a situation; il y a eu reports an event.

contrasts.note: Covers the uses of the passé composé on its own.
Covers the uses of the imparfait on its own.
Adds a third layer: events that happened before the story's time.
In literary narrative the passé simple takes the role of the passé composé alongside the imparfait.

examples.sentence: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.form: dormais quand le téléphone a sonné
examples.translation: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

examples.sentence: Il pleuvait, alors nous sommes restés à la maison.
examples.translation: It was raining, so we stayed at home.

examples.sentence: Pendant que je lisais, il est arrivé.
examples.translation: While I was reading, he arrived.

constructs.name: futur simple (formation)
constructs.description: Simple future formed on the infinitive (or an irregular stem) plus -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.

card.formation: Add -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive; verbs in -re drop their final e (prendre → je prendrai). Common irregular stems: être → ser-, avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, venir → viendr-, voir → verr-, pouvoir → pourr-, vouloir → voudr-, devoir → devr-, savoir → saur-, falloir → faudr-.
card.use: This is how the simple future is built; the stem always ends in r. Its uses are covered separately.
pitfalls: Je ferai (future) and je ferais (conditional) are pronounced almost the same but are different tenses.
Verbs in -re lose their final e: je prendrai, not *je prendrerai.
Some -er verbs change their stem: j'achèterai, j'appellerai, j'essaierai.
Pouvoir, voir, envoyer, mourir and courir have a double r: je pourrai, je verrai.
Irregular stems must be learned: j'irai, je serai, j'aurai, je ferai.

contrasts.note: Covers when the futur simple is used.
The conditional uses the same stems with imparfait endings: je parlerai vs je parlerais.
The near future is built with aller + infinitive instead of endings.

examples.sentence: Je parlerai au directeur.
examples.translation: I will speak to the manager.

examples.sentence: Nous serons là à midi.
examples.translation: We will be there at noon.

examples.sentence: Tu pourras venir demain ?
examples.translation: Will you be able to come tomorrow?

examples.sentence: Ils prendront le train.
examples.translation: They will take the train.

constructs.name: futur simple (emplois)
constructs.description: Use of the simple future for predictions, promises, plans and instructions.

card.formation: The futur simple forms: infinitive (or irregular stem) + -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.
card.use: The futur simple expresses predictions, promises, plans and future facts, often more distant or less certain than with aller + infinitive. It is also used for polite instructions (vous prendrez la deuxième rue) and after quand, dès que or lorsque when the action is in the future.
pitfalls: After quand, dès que and lorsque with a future meaning, use the future, not the present: quand je serai grand.
Never use the future after si expressing a condition: s'il pleut, not *s'il pleuvra.
In speech, plans for the near future are usually expressed with aller + infinitive.
'Will you…?' as a request is usually translated with vouloir: tu veux bien m'aider ?

contrasts.note: Aller + infinitive is more spoken and presents the future as close or already decided.
In si-sentences the future goes in the main clause, the present after si.
The futur antérieur marks a future action that will be completed before another.
When the reference point is in the past, the conditional replaces the future.
The present with a time word can also refer to a planned future.

examples.sentence: Demain, il fera beau.
examples.translation: Tomorrow the weather will be nice.

examples.sentence: Je t'appellerai ce soir, promis.
examples.translation: I'll call you tonight, I promise.

examples.sentence: Quand je serai grand, je serai pilote.
examples.translation: When I grow up, I'll be a pilot.

examples.sentence: Vous prendrez la deuxième rue à droite.
examples.translation: Take the second street on the right.

constructs.name: plus-que-parfait
constructs.description: Compound tense (imparfait of avoir or être plus past participle) for an action before another past action.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the imparfait + past participle (j'avais fini, elle était partie). The choice of auxiliary and the agreement rules are the same as in the passé composé.
card.use: It expresses an action completed before another past action or moment: the 'past of the past'. It is also used in reported speech after a past verb, in si-clauses about an unreal past, and in regrets with si seulement.
pitfalls: English often uses the simple past where French needs the plus-que-parfait: il a dit qu'il avait perdu ses clés.
With être the participle agrees with the subject: elle était partie.
Do not use it for events that follow each other in order; those take the passé composé.
An ongoing past state with depuis takes the imparfait, not the plus-que-parfait: il habitait là depuis un an.

contrasts.note: The passé composé places an action in the past without relating it to an earlier one.
The literary passé antérieur also marks anteriority, but only right before a passé simple action.
In reported speech after a past verb, a passé composé becomes a plus-que-parfait.
After si, it expresses a condition that was not fulfilled in the past.
The imparfait describes a situation at the same time as the past events, not before them.

examples.sentence: J'avais déjà mangé quand il est arrivé.
examples.translation: I had already eaten when he arrived.

examples.sentence: Elle était partie avant midi.
examples.translation: She had left before noon.

examples.sentence: Il a dit qu'il avait perdu ses clés.
examples.translation: He said he had lost his keys.

constructs.name: futur dans le passé
aliases: conditionnel à valeur de futur dans le passé
constructs.description: Conditional used to express a later event seen from a past point of view.

card.formation: The present conditional (future stem + -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) in a sentence whose reference point is in the past, usually after a main verb in a past tense.
card.use: It expresses an action that was still to come at a past moment, mainly in reported speech and in narrative: il a dit qu'il viendrait (he said he would come). It carries no idea of condition.
pitfalls: After a past verb of saying or thinking, the futur simple normally becomes the conditional: il a dit qu'il viendrait.
Do not read it as a hypothesis: there is no condition, only a later time.
Viendrait (conditional) and viendra (future) differ only by their ending, which matters for meaning.

contrasts.note: The futur simple looks forward from the present moment, not from a past one.
The future in the past is part of the tense shift in reported speech.
Aller in the imparfait + infinitive is the near-future equivalent: il a dit qu'il allait partir.
The same forms express wishes, advice and imagined situations, which is a different use.

examples.sentence: Il a dit qu'il viendrait.
examples.translation: He said he would come.

examples.sentence: Je savais qu'elle réussirait.
examples.translation: I knew she would succeed.

examples.sentence: On pensait qu'il ferait beau.
examples.translation: We thought the weather would be nice.

constructs.name: futur proche dans le passé (aller à l'imparfait + infinitif)
constructs.description: Aller in the imperfect plus infinitive for an action that was about to happen in the past.

card.formation: Aller in the imparfait (j'allais, il allait, nous allions) + infinitive.
card.use: It expresses that something was about to happen at a past moment, often because it was then interrupted or did not happen. It is also the past form of aller + infinitive in reported speech.
pitfalls: Use the imparfait of aller, not the passé composé: j'allais partir, not *je suis allé partir.
J'allais au marché (with a place) is ordinary movement: I was going or used to go to the market.
It often implies that the action did not take place: j'allais t'appeler (I was going to call you).

contrasts.note: With aller in the present, the action is about to happen now.
The conditional expresses a later action from a past point of view, without the idea of imminence.
The imparfait of aller with a place describes movement or habit, not an upcoming action.
In reported speech after a past verb, je vais partir becomes il allait partir.

examples.sentence: J'allais partir quand tu as appelé.
examples.translation: I was about to leave when you called.

examples.sentence: Il a dit qu'il allait pleuvoir.
examples.translation: He said it was going to rain.

examples.sentence: Nous allions sortir, mais il a neigé.
examples.translation: We were going to go out, but it snowed.

constructs.name: futur antérieur
constructs.description: Compound future (future of avoir or être plus past participle) for an action completed before a future point.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the futur simple + past participle (j'aurai fini, elle sera partie). Auxiliary and agreement follow the passé composé rules.
card.use: It expresses an action that will be completed before another future action or a future moment, often after quand, dès que, lorsque, une fois que or après que. It can also express a guess about the past: il aura oublié (he must have forgotten).
pitfalls: After quand or dès que, French uses the futur antérieur where English uses the present perfect: quand j'aurai fini (when I have finished).
With être the participle agrees with the subject: elle sera partie.
The guessing use (il aura oublié) refers to the past and is easy to misread as future.
J'aurai fini (futur antérieur) and j'aurais fini (conditionnel passé) sound almost the same.

contrasts.note: The futur simple states a future action without marking it as completed before another.
The plus-que-parfait does the same job in the past: completed before another past action.
The conditionnel passé is built with the conditional of the auxiliary and has a different meaning.
Après que with a future meaning is followed by the futur antérieur.

examples.sentence: Je t'appellerai quand j'aurai fini.
examples.translation: I'll call you when I've finished.

examples.sentence: Dès qu'elle sera arrivée, on mangera.
examples.translation: As soon as she has arrived, we'll eat.

examples.sentence: Il est en retard, il aura oublié.
examples.translation: He's late, he must have forgotten.

examples.sentence: À midi, nous serons partis.
examples.translation: By noon we will have left.

constructs.name: passé simple
constructs.description: Simple past of written narrative, history and biography, replacing the passé composé in literary texts.

card.formation: -er verbs take -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent; -ir verbs and most -re verbs take -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent; many others take -us, -us, -ut, -ûmes, -ûtes, -urent. Frequent irregular forms include il fut (être), il eut (avoir), il fit (faire), il vint (venir) and il naquit (naître).
card.use: The passé simple narrates completed past events in literature, tales, history and biography, where speech uses the passé composé. It is used together with the imparfait for the background, and appears mostly in the third person.
pitfalls: Il finit can be present or passé simple; only the context tells.
Il fut (être) and il fit (faire) are easily confused.
Il parla (passé simple) differs from il parlait (imparfait) by a single letter but has a different role.
It belongs to written narrative; do not use it in conversation or ordinary letters.
Many irregular forms are hard to recognise: il naquit, il vécut, il mourut, ils eurent.

contrasts.note: The passé composé is the spoken equivalent for completed past events.
The passé simple shares the narrative work with the imparfait in the same way.
The passé antérieur is its compound form, for an action just before a passé simple action.
The imparfait gives the background, the passé simple the events.
The imparfait du subjonctif is built on the passé simple and is distinguished by a circumflex: il fut vs qu'il fût.

examples.sentence: Elle entra dans la cuisine.
examples.translation: She went into the kitchen.

examples.sentence: Victor Hugo naquit en 1802.
examples.translation: Victor Hugo was born in 1802.

examples.sentence: Ils furent très surpris.
examples.translation: They were very surprised.

examples.sentence: Le roi eut trois enfants.
examples.translation: The king had three children.

constructs.name: passé antérieur
constructs.description: Literary compound tense (passé simple of avoir or être plus past participle) for an action just before another in the passé simple.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the passé simple + past participle (il eut fini, elle fut partie). Auxiliary and agreement follow the passé composé rules.
card.use: A literary tense for an action completed just before another action in the passé simple, usually after quand, lorsque, dès que, après que or à peine. It is found in written narrative only.
pitfalls: Do not confuse il eut fini (passé antérieur) with il eût fini (plus-que-parfait du subjonctif, with a circumflex).
It is used only alongside the passé simple; with other past tenses the plus-que-parfait is used.
It is a reading tense: in speech the plus-que-parfait or a passé composé is used instead.

contrasts.note: The plus-que-parfait expresses anteriority in general, in speech and writing.
The passé simple narrates the main event that the passé antérieur precedes.
Looks almost identical but has a circumflex on the auxiliary (eût, fût) and is a subjunctive.
The futur antérieur does the same job for the future.

examples.sentence: Quand il eut fini, il sortit.
examples.translation: When he had finished, he went out.

examples.sentence: Dès qu'elle fut partie, il pleura.
examples.translation: As soon as she had left, he cried.

examples.sentence: Après qu'ils eurent mangé, ils dormirent.
examples.translation: After they had eaten, they slept.

constructs.name: impératif (formation)
constructs.description: Imperative forms (tu, nous, vous) without a subject pronoun, to give orders, advice or instructions.

card.formation: Use the tu, nous and vous forms of the present without the subject pronoun. -er verbs (and verbs like ouvrir) drop the -s of the tu form (mange, va), except before y and en (vas-y). Être (sois, soyons, soyez), avoir (aie, ayons, ayez), savoir (sache) and vouloir (veuillez) are irregular.
card.use: The imperative gives orders, instructions, advice and invitations. The nous form means 'let's', and the vous form is used for several people or politely for one.
pitfalls: Do not write -s on the tu form of -er verbs: mange, not *manges.
Être and avoir have special forms: sois sage, n'aie pas peur.
Object pronouns come after the verb with a hyphen, and me becomes moi: donne-le-moi.
Pronominal verbs keep their pronoun after the verb: lève-toi, asseyez-vous.

contrasts.note: In the negative, pronouns go back before the verb: ne le mange pas.
Covers the order of pronouns after an affirmative imperative.
Recipes and signs often use the infinitive instead of the imperative.
The tu imperative of -er verbs is the present form minus its -s.

examples.sentence: Ferme la fenêtre, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Close the window, please.

examples.sentence: Allons au parc !
examples.translation: Let's go to the park!

examples.sentence: Soyez patients.
examples.translation: Be patient.

examples.sentence: Lève-toi, il est tard.
examples.translation: Get up, it's late.

constructs.name: impératif négatif
constructs.description: Negative imperative, with ne before and pas after the verb, to forbid or warn.

card.formation: Ne + imperative + pas (or another negative word); object pronouns go before the verb in their usual form and order (ne le mange pas, ne te lève pas).
card.use: It forbids something, warns or advises against it.
pitfalls: Pronouns go before the verb in the negative: ne le prends pas, not *ne prends-le pas.
Moi and toi become me and te: ne me regarde pas, ne te lève pas.
Ne becomes n' before a vowel: n'oublie pas.
In casual speech ne is often dropped (touche pas !), but it is required in writing.

contrasts.note: In the affirmative, pronouns follow the verb with a hyphen.
Covers pronoun position in affirmative and negative imperatives.
Written instructions often use ne pas + infinitive instead: ne pas toucher.
The negation works as with other verbs, around the conjugated form.

examples.sentence: Ne touche pas, c'est chaud !
examples.translation: Don't touch, it's hot!

examples.sentence: N'oubliez pas vos clés.
examples.translation: Don't forget your keys.

examples.sentence: Ne te lève pas.
examples.translation: Don't get up.

examples.sentence: Ne le mange pas !
examples.translation: Don't eat it!

constructs.name: conditionnel de politesse
constructs.description: Conditional of a few verbs used as fixed polite forms to ask for something.

card.formation: Conditional forms of a few verbs learned as set phrases: je voudrais, j'aimerais, vous pourriez / pourriez-vous, tu pourrais. They are followed by a noun or an infinitive.
card.use: It softens requests and questions so they sound polite, for example in shops, restaurants or when asking for help.
pitfalls: Je veux sounds blunt in a request; je voudrais is the polite choice.
Je voudrais (conditional) and je voudrai (future) look and sound alike.
No preposition follows these verbs before an infinitive: pourriez-vous m'aider ?
Accepting an offer is je veux bien, not je voudrais.

contrasts.note: The general uses of the conditional (wishes, advice, suggestions) build on these polite forms.
Explains how all conditional forms are built.
The future has nearly identical forms (je voudrai) but a different meaning.
Je voulais can also soften a request, but it is less common than je voudrais.

examples.sentence: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.translation: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.sentence: Pourriez-vous m'aider ?
examples.translation: Could you help me?

examples.sentence: J'aimerais réserver une table.
examples.translation: I would like to book a table.

constructs.name: conditionnel présent (formation)
constructs.description: Present conditional formed on the future stem plus the imperfect endings.

card.formation: Add the imparfait endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient to the future stem (parler → je parlerais, prendre → je prendrais). Irregular verbs use the same stems as in the future: ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, pourr-, voudr-, devr-, saur-, viendr-, verr-.
card.use: This is how the present conditional is built for all verbs; its uses are covered separately.
pitfalls: -rais (conditional) and -rai (future) sound almost the same but are different tenses.
Do not confuse il parlerait (conditional) with il parlait (imparfait); the conditional always has the r of the future stem.
Pouvoir, voir, envoyer, mourir and courir keep a double r: je pourrais, je verrais.
Il serait (être) and il saurait (savoir) are easily mixed up.

contrasts.note: Same stem, but with the future endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.
Same endings, but on the nous stem of the present instead of the future stem.
The past conditional is a compound form: conditional of avoir or être + participle.
Covers what the present conditional expresses.

examples.sentence: Nous aimerions partir.
examples.translation: We would like to leave.

examples.sentence: Tu pourrais m'aider ?
examples.translation: Could you help me?

examples.sentence: Ils seraient contents.
examples.translation: They would be happy.

examples.sentence: Elle viendrait avec plaisir.
examples.translation: She would gladly come.

constructs.name: conditionnel présent (souhait, conseil, suggestion)
constructs.description: Present conditional to express wishes, advice, suggestions and imagined situations.

card.formation: The present conditional forms: future stem + -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
card.use: The present conditional expresses wishes (j'aimerais), advice (tu devrais, à ta place je…), suggestions (on pourrait) and imagined situations. It is also the verb of the main clause after si + imparfait.
pitfalls: Never use the conditional after si: si j'avais le temps, not *si j'aurais le temps.
'Should' as advice is devoir in the conditional: tu devrais.
'Could' as a suggestion is pouvoir in the conditional: on pourrait.
English 'would' for a past habit is the imparfait, not the conditional.

contrasts.note: Si + imparfait sets the condition; the conditional gives the imagined result.
The polite conditional is a fixed use of a few verbs for requests.
Si + imparfait on its own (si on allait au cinéma ?) also makes a suggestion.
The same forms can present information as unconfirmed, which is a different use.
The same forms can express a future seen from the past.

examples.sentence: Tu devrais dormir plus.
examples.translation: You should sleep more.

examples.sentence: On pourrait aller au cinéma.
examples.translation: We could go to the cinema.

examples.sentence: J'aimerais vivre au bord de la mer.
examples.translation: I would like to live by the sea.

examples.sentence: À ta place, je partirais.
examples.translation: If I were you, I would leave.

constructs.name: conditionnel (information non confirmée)
constructs.description: Conditional used to report information that is not confirmed, typical of the press.

card.formation: The present conditional for present or future facts, the past conditional for past events, often together with selon or d'après.
card.use: It presents information as reported but not confirmed, so the speaker does not vouch for it. It is typical of news reports.
pitfalls: Do not translate it as 'would': it means 'reportedly', 'apparently' or 'is said to'.
There is no condition involved; it marks distance from the source.
Past events take the past conditional: le voleur aurait fui.

contrasts.note: The same forms express wishes or imagined situations, not reported facts.
Used for unconfirmed information about the past.
The same forms can express a later event from a past point of view.

examples.sentence: Le ministre serait malade.
examples.translation: The minister is reportedly ill.

examples.sentence: Selon la police, il y aurait trois blessés.
examples.translation: According to the police, there are said to be three injured.

examples.sentence: Le voleur aurait fui en voiture.
examples.translation: The thief apparently fled by car.

constructs.name: conditionnel passé (formation)
constructs.description: Past conditional formed with avoir or être in the conditional plus the past participle.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the present conditional + past participle (j'aurais fini, elle serait partie). Auxiliary and agreement follow the passé composé rules.
card.use: This is how the past conditional is built; its uses are covered separately.
pitfalls: 'Could have' is j'aurais pu + infinitive and 'should have' is j'aurais dû + infinitive.
Choose the auxiliary as in the passé composé: elle serait venue, not *elle aurait venu.
With être the participle agrees with the subject.
J'aurais fini (conditional) and j'aurai fini (futur antérieur) sound almost the same.

contrasts.note: Covers what the past conditional expresses.
Built with the future of the auxiliary instead of the conditional.
The simple form, for the present or future.
Built with the imparfait of the auxiliary; it is the tense used after si for the unreal past.

examples.sentence: J'aurais aimé venir.
examples.translation: I would have liked to come.

examples.sentence: Elle serait partie plus tôt.
examples.translation: She would have left earlier.

examples.sentence: Nous aurions pris le train.
examples.translation: We would have taken the train.

constructs.name: conditionnel passé (regret, reproche)
aliases: past conditional for regret and reproach
constructs.description: Past conditional to express regret, reproach or an unrealised possibility in the past.

card.formation: The past conditional: avoir or être in the conditional + past participle, often with aimer, devoir or pouvoir + infinitive.
card.use: It expresses regret (j'aurais aimé), reproach (tu aurais dû, vous auriez pu) and what would have happened in the past if things had been different, as the result of si + plus-que-parfait.
pitfalls: 'Should have' is aurait dû + infinitive: tu aurais dû me le dire.
'Could have' is aurait pu + infinitive: on aurait pu gagner.
Never use it in the si-clause: si j'avais su, not *si j'aurais su.
J'aurais aimé que is followed by the subjunctive: j'aurais aimé que tu viennes.

contrasts.note: Si + plus-que-parfait states the unreal past condition; the past conditional gives its result.
The present conditional gives advice or wishes for now or the future.
The same forms can report an unconfirmed past event.
In literary texts it can replace the past conditional: on eût dit = on aurait dit.

examples.sentence: Tu aurais dû me prévenir.
examples.translation: You should have warned me.

examples.sentence: J'aurais aimé te voir.
examples.translation: I would have liked to see you.

examples.sentence: On aurait pu gagner.
examples.translation: We could have won.

examples.sentence: Vous auriez pu appeler !
examples.translation: You could have called!

constructs.name: subjonctif présent (formation)
constructs.description: Present subjunctive built on the ils stem of the present plus -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent, with irregular verbs.

card.formation: Take the ils form of the present, remove -ent, and add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent (ils finissent → que je finisse). Verbs with two stems use the nous stem for nous and vous (que je vienne, que nous venions). Être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir and falloir are irregular (que je sois, que j'aie, que j'aille, que je fasse, que je puisse, que je sache).
card.use: This is how the present subjunctive is built. It almost always appears in a clause introduced by que, after a verb, expression or conjunction that requires it.
pitfalls: For -er verbs the singular forms look the same as the present indicative: que je parle.
Two-stem verbs change in nous and vous: que je boive but que nous buvions.
Être and avoir are fully irregular: que je sois, qu'il soit, que nous soyons; que j'aie, qu'il ait.
Que nous soyons and que vous ayez have no i after y.
The nous and vous forms often look like the imparfait: que nous parlions.

contrasts.note: The past subjunctive is a compound form for actions completed before the main verb.
The subjunctive stem comes from the ils form of the present indicative.
The nous and vous forms of both often coincide.
Il faut que is the most common trigger, usually the first context learners meet.

examples.sentence: Il faut que tu viennes.
examples.translation: You have to come.

examples.sentence: Je veux qu'il fasse ses devoirs.
examples.translation: I want him to do his homework.

examples.sentence: Il faut que nous soyons prêts.
examples.translation: We need to be ready.

examples.sentence: Il faut que je parte.
examples.translation: I have to leave.

constructs.name: subjonctif après expressions d'obligation
constructs.description: Subjunctive after expressions of obligation and necessity.

card.formation: An expression of necessity (il faut, il est nécessaire, il est indispensable, il est obligatoire) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: It says that a specific person must do something. Il faut que + subjunctive is the most frequent subjunctive construction in French.
pitfalls: For a general obligation or one that applies to the speaker, il faut + infinitive is often enough: il faut partir.
Il ne faut pas que means 'must not', not 'doesn't have to': il ne faut pas que tu le dises.
Avoir besoin que is also followed by the subjunctive.
Devoir + infinitive is a common alternative: tu dois partir.

contrasts.note: Il faut + infinitive expresses a general obligation without naming a person.
Il est important que and similar expressions judge rather than oblige, but also take the subjunctive.
Vouloir que expresses someone's wish rather than a necessity.
Covers the forms of the subjunctive itself.

examples.sentence: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.
examples.translation: You have to leave now.

examples.sentence: Il est nécessaire que vous signiez ici.
examples.translation: You need to sign here.

examples.sentence: Il ne faut pas qu'il le sache.
examples.form: ne faut pas qu'il le sache
examples.translation: He mustn't find out.

constructs.name: subjonctif après expressions de volonté
constructs.description: Subjunctive after verbs and expressions of will, wish, order or permission.

card.formation: A verb of will, wish, order or permission (vouloir, souhaiter, désirer, préférer, aimer, exiger, demander, permettre, refuser, accepter) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: It expresses what someone wants, prefers, demands or allows another person to do. The subjunctive marks the action as desired, not as a fact.
pitfalls: With the same subject, use the infinitive: je veux partir, not *je veux que je parte.
'I want you to come' cannot be built with an infinitive: je veux que tu viennes.
Espérer takes the indicative: j'espère que tu viendras.
Asking someone to do something is more often demander à quelqu'un de + infinitive.
Vouloir and aimer are often in the conditional: j'aimerais que tu restes.

contrasts.note: Same subject in both clauses means infinitive instead of que + subjunctive.
Espérer looks like a verb of wish but takes the indicative.
Il faut que expresses necessity rather than a person's will.
Verbs of feeling react to a situation rather than ask for it.
Tenir à and veiller à also express will, but introduce the clause with à ce que.

examples.sentence: Je veux que tu viennes.
examples.translation: I want you to come.

examples.sentence: Elle préfère que nous restions ici.
examples.translation: She prefers us to stay here.

examples.sentence: J'aimerais que tu m'appelles.
examples.translation: I'd like you to call me.

examples.sentence: Le prof exige que vous soyez à l'heure.
examples.translation: The teacher demands that you be on time.

constructs.name: subjonctif après expressions de sentiment
constructs.description: Subjunctive after verbs, adjectives and nouns expressing feelings such as joy, fear or regret.

card.formation: A verb, adjective or noun of feeling (être content, heureux, triste, désolé, surpris que; avoir peur que; regretter que; craindre que) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: It expresses a feeling or reaction about another person's action or a situation, such as joy, sadness, surprise, fear or regret.
pitfalls: With the same subject, use de + infinitive: je suis content de te voir.
After avoir peur que and craindre que, formal French may add a ne that is not a negation: j'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve.
Parce que after a feeling takes the indicative: je suis content parce que tu es là.
For a completed action, use the past subjunctive: je suis content que tu sois venu.

contrasts.note: Same subject in both clauses means de + infinitive instead of que + subjunctive.
The ne after verbs of fear is expletive and does not make the sentence negative.
Used when the feeling is about something already done.
C'est dommage que and similar impersonal phrases express an evaluation rather than a personal feeling.
Content de + infinitive is the same-subject construction.

examples.sentence: Je suis content que tu sois là.
examples.translation: I'm glad you're here.

examples.sentence: J'ai peur qu'il pleuve demain.
examples.translation: I'm afraid it will rain tomorrow.

examples.sentence: Elle regrette que vous partiez.
examples.translation: She's sorry you're leaving.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes surpris qu'il ne vienne pas.
examples.translation: We're surprised he isn't coming.

constructs.name: subjonctif ou indicatif après verbes d'opinion
constructs.description: Choice of mood after verbs of opinion, hope and certainty, which take the indicative when affirmative.

card.formation: Affirmative verbs and expressions of opinion, hope and certainty (penser, croire, trouver, espérer, être sûr, il me semble, il est évident, il est probable) + que + indicative.
card.use: Because the speaker presents the content as true or likely, these verbs take the indicative when affirmative. When they are negative or inverted in a question, the subjunctive becomes usual.
pitfalls: Espérer takes the indicative, often the future: j'espère que tu viendras, not *que tu viennes.
Je pense que takes the indicative: je pense qu'il a raison.
Il est probable que takes the indicative, but il est possible que takes the subjunctive.
Il me semble que takes the indicative, but il semble que often takes the subjunctive to show doubt.

contrasts.note: Negative or inverted forms of the same verbs usually take the subjunctive.
Doubt and possibility take the subjunctive, unlike certainty and probability.
The general rule: que-clauses after verbs of saying and thinking take the indicative.
Verbs of wish take the subjunctive, except espérer.

examples.sentence: Je pense qu'il a raison.
examples.translation: I think he's right.

examples.sentence: J'espère que tu viendras.
examples.translation: I hope you'll come.

examples.sentence: Je ne crois pas qu'il vienne.
examples.translation: I don't think he's coming.

examples.sentence: Il est sûr que nous gagnerons.
examples.translation: He's sure we'll win.

constructs.name: subjonctif ou infinitif
constructs.description: Use of the infinitive instead of the subjunctive when both clauses have the same subject.

card.formation: If both clauses have the same subject, use an infinitive (with de after many verbs and adjectives, and pour, avant de, sans, afin de instead of the conjunctions). If the subjects differ, use que + subjunctive.
card.use: French avoids que + subjunctive when the person who wants, feels or acts is the same in both parts of the sentence: je veux partir but je veux que tu partes.
pitfalls: Never say *je veux que je parte; say je veux partir.
The preposition depends on the expression: content de partir, avant de partir, pour partir, sans partir.
Bien que has no infinitive counterpart, so it keeps the subjunctive even with the same subject.
Il faut + infinitive is general; il faut que + subjunctive names the person.

contrasts.note: The volonté verbs show the switch most often: vouloir + infinitive vs vouloir que.
Feelings switch to de + infinitive with the same subject.
Pour que becomes pour + infinitive with the same subject.
Avant que becomes avant de + infinitive with the same subject.
Covers verbs followed directly by an infinitive, like vouloir and préférer.

examples.sentence: Je veux partir tôt.
examples.translation: I want to leave early.

examples.sentence: Je veux que tu partes tôt.
examples.translation: I want you to leave early.

examples.sentence: Elle est triste de partir.
examples.translation: She is sad to be leaving.

examples.sentence: Appelle-moi avant de partir.
examples.translation: Call me before you leave.

constructs.name: subjonctif après conjonctions de but
constructs.description: Subjunctive after conjunctions expressing purpose.

card.formation: A conjunction of purpose (pour que, afin que, de sorte que, de façon que, de manière que) + subjunctive.
card.use: It states the aim of an action, what someone does it for.
pitfalls: With the same subject, use pour or afin de + infinitive: je travaille pour réussir.
De sorte que + indicative expresses a result, not a purpose.
Do not confuse 'so that' (pour que) with 'so' (donc, alors).
Negation goes inside the clause: pour qu'il ne parte pas.

contrasts.note: Pour + infinitive or noun expresses purpose without a second subject.
Si bien que and de sorte que + indicative state a result that happened.
De peur que expresses a purpose to avoid something.
Same subject switches pour que to pour + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Je parle lentement pour que tu comprennes.
examples.translation: I speak slowly so that you understand.

examples.sentence: Ferme la porte afin que le chat ne sorte pas.
examples.form: afin que le chat ne sorte pas
examples.translation: Close the door so the cat doesn't get out.

examples.sentence: Je t'explique pour que tu saches.
examples.translation: I'm explaining so that you know.

constructs.name: subjonctif après conjonctions de concession
constructs.description: Subjunctive after conjunctions expressing concession.

card.formation: A conjunction of concession (bien que, quoique, and in formal style encore que) + subjunctive.
card.use: It states a fact that might be expected to prevent the main action but does not, like English 'although'.
pitfalls: Même si means 'even if' and takes the indicative: même s'il pleut.
Bien que keeps the subjunctive even when both clauses share a subject: bien qu'il soit fatigué, il travaille.
Malgré que in the sense of bien que is common in speech, but careful usage avoids it; use bien que.
Quoique (although, one word) is not quoi que (whatever, two words).
With the same subject, bien que can be shortened before an adjective or participle: bien que fatigué.

contrasts.note: Même si + indicative expresses a hypothetical or real concession.
Malgré + noun expresses concession without a clause.
Pourtant and cependant link two independent sentences.
Quoi que and qui que mean whatever and whoever, not although.
Alors que and tandis que contrast two facts and take the indicative.

examples.sentence: Bien qu'il pleuve, nous sortons.
examples.translation: Although it's raining, we're going out.

examples.sentence: Elle travaille bien qu'elle soit malade.
examples.translation: She works although she is ill.

examples.sentence: Quoiqu'il soit riche, il vit simplement.
examples.translation: Although he is rich, he lives simply.

constructs.name: subjonctif après expressions de doute et de possibilité
constructs.description: Subjunctive after verbs and impersonal expressions of doubt, possibility and uncertainty.

card.formation: A verb or impersonal expression of doubt, possibility or uncertainty (douter que, il est possible que, il se peut que, il est peu probable que, il semble que, ce n'est pas sûr que) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: The subjunctive marks the content as uncertain: the speaker does not claim it is true.
pitfalls: Il est probable que takes the indicative; il est possible que takes the subjunctive.
Douter que (doubt) takes the subjunctive, but se douter que (suspect) takes the indicative.
Peut-être que takes the indicative: peut-être qu'il viendra.
Il semble que often takes the subjunctive when there is doubt, but il me semble que takes the indicative.

contrasts.note: Certainty and probability take the indicative.
A negated opinion also signals doubt and takes the subjunctive.
Il est important que and similar expressions judge rather than doubt.

examples.sentence: Je doute qu'il vienne.
examples.translation: I doubt he'll come.

examples.sentence: Il est possible qu'elle soit malade.
examples.translation: She may be ill.

examples.sentence: Il se peut qu'il pleuve ce soir.
examples.translation: It might rain tonight.

constructs.name: subjonctif après verbes d'opinion à la forme négative ou interrogative
aliases: je ne pense pas que + subjonctif
constructs.description: Subjunctive after verbs of opinion when they are negative or inverted in a question.

card.formation: A verb of opinion in the negative (je ne pense pas que, je ne crois pas que, je ne suis pas sûr que) or in an inverted question (penses-tu que, croyez-vous que) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: Negating or questioning an opinion makes its content uncertain, so the subjunctive is used. The indicative remains possible when the speaker wants to stress that the fact is real.
pitfalls: The affirmative takes the indicative: je pense qu'il a raison, but je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.
Questions without inversion, asked by intonation, usually keep the indicative in everyday French: tu crois qu'il viendra ?
Inversion questions in formal style take the subjunctive: crois-tu qu'il vienne ?

contrasts.note: In the affirmative, the same verbs take the indicative.
Douter que expresses the same uncertainty directly.
Covers the inverted question form that triggers the subjunctive here.

examples.sentence: Je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.
examples.form: ne pense pas qu'il ait raison
examples.translation: I don't think he's right.

examples.sentence: Crois-tu qu'elle puisse venir ?
examples.translation: Do you think she can come?

examples.sentence: Je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit vrai.
examples.form: ne suis pas sûr que ce soit vrai
examples.translation: I'm not sure it's true.

constructs.name: subjonctif après expressions impersonnelles de jugement
constructs.description: Subjunctive after impersonal expressions of judgement or appreciation.

card.formation: An impersonal expression of judgement (il est important, normal, essentiel, préférable, dommage, temps que; c'est dommage que; il vaut mieux que) + que + subjunctive.
card.use: It gives an evaluation or appreciation of an action or situation: whether it is important, normal, regrettable or better.
pitfalls: For a general statement without a specific person, use de + infinitive: il est important de dormir.
Expressions of certainty take the indicative: il est évident, certain, clair, vrai que.
Il vaut mieux que takes the subjunctive; il vaut mieux + infinitive is the general form.
In speech, c'est replaces il est: c'est normal que tu sois fatigué.

contrasts.note: Il faut que expresses necessity rather than evaluation.
Il est possible que expresses uncertainty rather than judgement.
Il est évident or il est probable que take the indicative.
Il est + adjective + de + infinitive is the general form without a specific subject.
Covers impersonal il constructions in general.

examples.sentence: Il est important que tu dormes bien.
examples.translation: It's important that you sleep well.

examples.sentence: C'est dommage qu'il ne vienne pas.
examples.translation: It's a pity he isn't coming.

examples.sentence: Il vaut mieux que nous partions.
examples.translation: We'd better leave.

constructs.name: subjonctif après conjonctions de temps
constructs.description: Subjunctive after conjunctions of time that point to a later or expected event.

card.formation: A conjunction of time pointing to a later or expected event (avant que, jusqu'à ce que, en attendant que) + subjunctive.
card.use: The subjunctive is used because the event in the clause has not happened yet at the time of the main action.
pitfalls: Après que takes the indicative in standard French: après qu'il est parti.
With the same subject, use avant de + infinitive: mange avant de partir.
In formal style avant que may be followed by a ne that is not a negation: avant qu'il ne parte.
Quand, lorsque, dès que and pendant que take the indicative.

contrasts.note: Après que refers to something that has happened and takes the indicative.
Most time conjunctions take the indicative.
The optional ne after avant que does not negate.
Same subject switches avant que to avant de + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Rentre avant qu'il fasse nuit.
examples.translation: Come home before it gets dark.

examples.sentence: Attends ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
examples.translation: Wait here until I come back.

examples.sentence: Range ta chambre avant que maman arrive.
examples.translation: Tidy your room before Mum arrives.

constructs.name: subjonctif après conjonctions de condition
constructs.description: Subjunctive after conjunctions that state a condition or a restriction.

card.formation: A conjunction of condition or restriction (à condition que, pourvu que, à moins que, en admettant que, en supposant que, pour peu que) + subjunctive.
card.use: It states a condition that must be met (à condition que, pourvu que), an exception (à moins que, 'unless') or an assumption (en supposant que).
pitfalls: Si takes the indicative, not the subjunctive: s'il fait beau.
With the same subject, use à condition de or à moins de + infinitive.
In formal style à moins que may be followed by a ne that is not a negation: à moins qu'il ne pleuve.
Pourvu que at the start of an exclamation means 'let's hope that': pourvu qu'il fasse beau !

contrasts.note: Si + present is the basic condition and takes the indicative.
Covers other ways to express a hypothesis, some with the conditional.
The optional ne after à moins que does not negate.
Same subject switches to à condition de or à moins de + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Je viendrai à condition que tu m'invites.
examples.translation: I'll come on condition that you invite me.

examples.sentence: Tu peux sortir pourvu que tu rentres tôt.
examples.translation: You can go out as long as you come back early.

examples.sentence: On sortira, à moins qu'il pleuve.
examples.translation: We'll go out, unless it rains.

examples.sentence: Pourvu qu'il fasse beau demain !
examples.translation: Let's hope the weather is nice tomorrow!

constructs.name: subjonctif après sans que
constructs.description: Subjunctive after sans que ('without') for something that does not happen alongside the main action; with the same subject, sans + infinitive is used instead.

card.formation: Sans que + subjunctive, used when the two clauses have different subjects.
card.use: It says that the main action happens without another thing happening or without someone doing something, like English 'without someone doing'.
pitfalls: With the same subject, use sans + infinitive: il est parti sans dire au revoir.
Do not add pas: sans que je le sache, not *sans que je ne le sache pas.
Careful usage avoids adding ne after sans que in an affirmative sentence: sans qu'il le voie, not sans qu'il ne le voie.
English 'without me knowing' becomes sans que je le sache.

contrasts.note: Same subject switches sans que to sans + infinitive.
Sans + infinitive is the same-subject construction.
Bien que concedes a fact rather than excluding an action.
A ne sometimes added after sans que does not negate, and careful usage leaves it out in affirmative sentences.

examples.sentence: Il est parti sans que je le voie.
examples.translation: He left without me seeing him.

examples.sentence: Elle entre sans qu'on l'entende.
examples.translation: She comes in without anyone hearing her.

examples.sentence: Ils ont décidé sans que nous le sachions.
examples.translation: They decided without our knowing.

constructs.name: subjonctif passé
constructs.description: Past subjunctive (subjunctive of avoir or être plus past participle) for an action completed before the main one.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the present subjunctive + past participle (que j'aie fini, qu'elle soit partie). Auxiliary and agreement follow the passé composé rules.
card.use: It is used where the subjunctive is required and the action is completed before the main verb or before a given future moment.
pitfalls: Choose between présent and passé by when the action happens relative to the main verb, not by the tense of the main verb.
The auxiliary is subjunctive: que j'aie fini, not *que j'ai fini.
With être the participle agrees with the subject: qu'elle soit partie.
It can refer to the future: il faut que tu aies fini avant midi.

contrasts.note: The present subjunctive is used for actions at the same time as or after the main verb.
Same structure, but with the auxiliary in the indicative.
Its literary counterpart after a main verb in the past.
With the same subject, an infinitif passé replaces it: je suis content d'avoir fini.

examples.sentence: Je suis contente que tu sois venu.
examples.translation: I'm glad you came.

examples.sentence: Je doute qu'il ait compris.
examples.translation: I doubt he understood.

examples.sentence: Il faut que tu aies fini avant midi.
examples.translation: You must have finished before noon.

examples.sentence: C'est dommage qu'elle soit partie.
examples.translation: It's a pity she left.

constructs.name: subjonctif dans les relatives
constructs.description: Subjunctive in relative clauses after a superlative or 'the only', or describing something sought or uncertain.

card.formation: A relative clause (qui, que, où…) in the subjunctive, after a superlative or le seul, le premier, le dernier, l'unique; after a negative or indefinite antecedent (personne qui, rien que); or after something sought whose existence is uncertain.
card.use: The subjunctive shows that the speaker is giving a subjective judgement or that the thing described may not exist. With the indicative, the same sentence refers to something real and known.
pitfalls: If the person or thing exists and is known, use the indicative: je connais quelqu'un qui parle chinois.
The mood can change the meaning: je cherche un hôtel qui est calme (a specific one) vs qui soit calme (any such one).
After a superlative or le seul, the subjunctive is the norm, but the indicative is used to state a plain fact: c'est le seul film qu'il a vu cette année.

contrasts.note: Ordinary relative clauses take the indicative.
Ordinary relative clauses with que take the indicative.
A superlative before the relative is one of the triggers of the subjunctive.
Covers the forms of the subjunctive.

examples.sentence: C'est le meilleur film que j'aie vu.
examples.translation: It's the best film I've ever seen.

examples.sentence: Je cherche un appartement qui soit calme.
examples.translation: I'm looking for a flat that is quiet.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a personne qui puisse m'aider.
examples.translation: There's nobody who can help me.

examples.sentence: C'est la seule personne qui me comprenne.
examples.translation: She's the only person who understands me.

constructs.name: subjonctif dans une proposition indépendante (ordre, souhait)
constructs.description: A que + subjunctive sentence standing on its own, giving an order to a third person or expressing a wish (also with pourvu que); it does not depend on a following main clause.

card.formation: Que + subject + subjunctive, as a complete sentence with no main clause (Qu'il entre !). Wishes can also start with pourvu que, and a few set phrases and literary wishes drop que (Vive la France !, Puissiez-vous réussir).
card.use: It gives an order or instruction to a third person, since the imperative has no il/elle/ils forms, or expresses a wish or hope. It can also express indignation (Moi, que je lui demande pardon !).
pitfalls: This is a full sentence: do not look for a missing main clause.
Orders with que work only in the third person; for tu, nous and vous use the imperative.
Pourvu que on its own means 'let's hope that', not 'provided that'.
A negative order follows the normal negation: que personne ne sorte, qu'il ne parte pas.

contrasts.note: The imperative gives orders to tu, nous and vous; que + subjunctive does it for il, elle and ils.
There the que-clause is the subject or an alternative and the sentence continues with a main clause.
Inside a sentence, pourvu que means 'provided that' and sets a condition.
With a verb of will the wish is stated by a main clause: je veux qu'il entre.

examples.sentence: Qu'il entre !
examples.translation: Let him come in!

examples.sentence: Que personne ne sorte avant midi.
examples.translation: Nobody is to leave before noon.

examples.sentence: Pourvu qu'il fasse beau demain !
examples.translation: Let's hope the weather is nice tomorrow!

examples.sentence: Qu'ils attendent un peu, je suis occupé.
examples.translation: They can wait a bit, I'm busy.

constructs.name: subjonctif après conjonctions de crainte
constructs.description: Subjunctive after conjunctions expressing fear or a purpose to avoid.

card.formation: A conjunction of fear (de peur que, de crainte que) + subjunctive, often with an expletive ne in formal style.
card.use: It gives the reason for an action as the wish to avoid something feared, like English 'for fear that' or 'in case'.
pitfalls: The ne that may follow is not a negation: de peur qu'il ne pleuve means 'for fear it rains'.
With the same subject, use de peur de or de crainte de + infinitive.
Avoir peur que is a verb of feeling, not this conjunction, though it also takes the subjunctive.

contrasts.note: Avoir peur que and craindre que express the feeling itself rather than the reason for an action.
Pour que gives a purpose to reach, de peur que one to avoid.
The ne often found after these conjunctions does not negate.
Same subject switches to de peur de + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Je parle bas de peur qu'il ne se réveille.
examples.form: de peur qu'il ne se réveille
examples.translation: I speak quietly for fear he'll wake up.

examples.sentence: Prends un parapluie de peur qu'il pleuve.
examples.translation: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

examples.sentence: Il se tait de peur qu'on se moque de lui.
examples.translation: He stays quiet for fear people will laugh at him.

examples.sentence: Elle part tôt de crainte qu'il y ait des bouchons.
examples.form: de crainte qu'il y ait des bouchons
examples.translation: She leaves early for fear there will be traffic jams.

constructs.name: subjonctif après verbe + à ce que
constructs.description: Subjunctive after verbs built with à, which introduce the clause with à ce que.

card.formation: A verb or expression built with à (tenir à, s'attendre à, veiller à, consentir à, s'opposer à, être habitué à) + à ce que + subjunctive.
card.use: When a verb that takes à introduces a clause, à ce que replaces plain que, and the clause is in the subjunctive.
pitfalls: Do not drop à ce: je tiens à ce que tu viennes, not *je tiens que tu viennes.
With the same subject, use à + infinitive: je tiens à venir.
Aimer à ce que is non-standard; use aimer que.

contrasts.note: Verbs like vouloir take plain que + subjunctive.
Same subject switches to à + infinitive.
Covers verbs followed by à + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Je tiens à ce que tu viennes.
examples.translation: I really want you to come.

examples.sentence: Il ne s'attendait pas à ce qu'elle parte.
examples.translation: He didn't expect her to leave.

examples.sentence: Veille à ce que la porte soit fermée.
examples.form: à ce que la porte soit fermée
examples.translation: Make sure the door is closed.

constructs.name: subjonctif après relatifs indéfinis de concession
constructs.description: Subjunctive after indefinite concessive expressions meaning whoever, whatever or wherever.

card.formation: Qui que, quoi que, où que, or quel que (agreeing with the noun, usually before être) + subjunctive; in literary style also quelque + noun or adjective + que.
card.use: It means whoever, whatever, wherever or whatever … may be: no matter who, what or where, the main statement stays true.
pitfalls: Quoi que (whatever, two words) is not quoique (although, one word).
Quel que agrees with the subject that follows: quelle que soit la raison, quels que soient les risques.
These expressions always take the subjunctive.
Do not confuse quel que (+ être) with quelque (+ noun or adjective).

contrasts.note: Bien que and quoique mean although and concede one fact.
Même si + indicative concedes one possibility rather than all of them.
N'importe qui, quoi or où express 'anyone, anything, anywhere' without a clause.
Quelqu'un and quelque chose are ordinary indefinites with no concessive meaning.

examples.sentence: Quoi que tu fasses, je t'aime.
examples.translation: Whatever you do, I love you.

examples.sentence: Où que tu ailles, appelle-moi.
examples.translation: Wherever you go, call me.

examples.sentence: Quel que soit le prix, je l'achète.
examples.translation: Whatever the price, I'll buy it.

examples.sentence: Qui que vous soyez, entrez.
examples.translation: Whoever you are, come in.

constructs.name: subjonctif après cause rejetée
constructs.description: Subjunctive after expressions that reject a possible cause.

card.formation: An expression that rejects a cause (non que, non pas que, ce n'est pas que) + subjunctive; the real cause usually follows with mais + indicative.
card.use: It rules out a possible explanation before giving the real one: 'not that …, but …'.
pitfalls: Ce n'est pas parce que … que … takes the indicative: ce n'est pas parce qu'il est riche qu'il est heureux.
The real cause after mais is in the indicative.
Non que is formal; ce n'est pas que is the everyday form.

contrasts.note: Parce que and puisque give a real cause and take the indicative.
Covers other ways of justifying, all with the indicative.
Bien que admits a fact that does not prevent the result, rather than rejecting a cause.

examples.sentence: Ce n'est pas que je sois fatigué, mais j'ai froid.
examples.form: Ce n'est pas que je sois fatigué
examples.translation: It's not that I'm tired, but I'm cold.

examples.sentence: Je refuse, non que ce soit difficile.
examples.translation: I refuse, not that it's difficult.

examples.sentence: Non pas qu'il soit méchant, mais il est distrait.
examples.translation: Not that he's mean, but he's absent-minded.

constructs.name: que + subjonctif en tête de phrase
constructs.description: A que-clause in the subjunctive placed first, as subject or to express an alternative.

card.formation: A clause que + subjunctive placed at the start of the sentence, either as its subject (Qu'il soit en retard m'étonne) or in a pair que … ou que … / que … ou non expressing an alternative.
card.use: As a fronted subject, the clause takes the subjunctive even when it states a fact. In the alternative pattern, it means 'whether … or …': the main statement holds in either case.
pitfalls: A fronted que-clause takes the subjunctive even for a fact: qu'il soit parti est certain, but il est certain qu'il est parti.
In the alternative pattern, repeat que before the second verb: qu'il pleuve ou qu'il neige.
