Do not confuse it with si … ou non in indirect questions, which takes the indicative: je ne sais pas s'il vient ou non.

contrasts.note: Quoi que and où que also say 'no matter', but about any thing or place, not two alternatives.
The same judgement can be expressed with the clause after the expression: il est étonnant qu'il soit en retard.
Si … ou non introduces an indirect question in the indicative.

examples.sentence: Qu'il pleuve ou qu'il neige, je sortirai.
examples.translation: Whether it rains or snows, I'll go out.

examples.sentence: Que tu le veuilles ou non, on part.
examples.form: Que tu le veuilles ou non
examples.translation: Whether you like it or not, we're leaving.

examples.sentence: Qu'elle soit en retard ne m'étonne pas.
examples.translation: That she is late doesn't surprise me.

constructs.name: imparfait du subjonctif
constructs.description: Literary subjunctive tense built on the passé simple, found in older and literary narrative.

card.formation: Take the tu form of the passé simple, remove the final -s, and add -sse, -sses, -^t, -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent (tu parlas → que je parlasse, qu'il parlât). The third person singular has a circumflex: qu'il fût, qu'il eût, qu'il finît, qu'il vînt.
card.use: A literary tense used where the subjunctive is required after a main verb in the past, mainly in older and literary texts. In modern French the present subjunctive replaces it, so it is mostly recognised rather than used, and mostly in the third person singular.
pitfalls: Qu'il fût and qu'il eût (subjunctive) differ from il fut and il eut (passé simple) only by the circumflex.
Do not use it in speech or ordinary writing; use the present subjunctive.
Its meaning is that of an ordinary subjunctive; it does not add a past meaning by itself.

contrasts.note: Modern French uses the present subjunctive in the same contexts.
It is built on the passé simple and looks like it, except for the circumflex and the -ss- endings.
Its compound form, for an action completed before the main verb.

examples.sentence: Il fallait qu'il partît.
examples.translation: He had to leave.

examples.sentence: Je voulais qu'elle vînt.
examples.translation: I wanted her to come.

examples.sentence: Bien qu'il fût malade, il travaillait.
examples.translation: Although he was ill, he kept working.

constructs.name: plus-que-parfait du subjonctif
constructs.description: Literary compound subjunctive, also used in literature as a past conditional.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the imparfait du subjonctif + past participle (qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie).
card.use: A literary tense for a completed action in a subjunctive context after a past main verb. Literature also uses it instead of the past conditional or the plus-que-parfait in unreal past hypotheses: s'il l'eût su, il fût venu (if he had known, he would have come).
pitfalls: Il eût fini (subjunctive) differs from il eut fini (passé antérieur) only by the circumflex.
In hypotheses it means 'would have' or 'had': on eût dit = on aurait dit.
It is a reading tense; modern French uses the past subjunctive or the past conditional instead.

contrasts.note: Modern French uses the past subjunctive in the same contexts.
Its simple form, for an action not completed before the main verb.
Looks almost identical but has no circumflex (il eut fini) and is an indicative tense.
In literary hypotheses it replaces the past conditional.
The modern construction for an unreal past is si + plus-que-parfait with the past conditional.

examples.sentence: Je regrettais qu'il fût parti.
examples.translation: I regretted that he had left.

examples.sentence: Bien qu'elle eût fini, elle restait.
examples.translation: Although she had finished, she stayed.

examples.sentence: On eût dit un enfant.
examples.translation: You would have thought he was a child.

constructs.name: participe passé (formation)
constructs.description: Regular and irregular forms of the past participle, used in compound tenses and the passive.

card.formation: Verbs in -er take -é (parlé), regular -ir verbs take -i (fini), and many -re verbs take -u (vendu). Many common verbs are irregular and must be learned: eu, été, fait, pris, mis, dit, écrit, vu, venu, ouvert, mort, né.
card.use: The past participle is the second part of every compound tense (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur) and of the passive. It can also stand alone as an adjective.
pitfalls: Writing the infinitive instead of the participle, since -er and -é sound alike: j'ai mangé, not j'ai manger.
Regularising irregular verbs, e.g. prendu instead of pris or ouvri instead of ouvert.
Forgetting the silent final consonant that appears in the feminine: prise, faite, écrite.
Confusing a participle with a different word that sounds the same, e.g. dû (from devoir) with du.

contrasts.note: The participle is one part; the passé composé is the tense built from an auxiliary plus the participle.
Same form, but used without an auxiliary to describe a noun.
The -ant form expresses an ongoing action, not a completed one.
Covers when the participle adds -e or -s; formation only covers the basic form.

examples.sentence: J'ai fini mes devoirs.
examples.translation: I finished my homework.

examples.sentence: Nous avons vendu la voiture.
examples.translation: We sold the car.

examples.sentence: Tu as pris ton parapluie ?
examples.translation: Did you take your umbrella?

examples.sentence: Il a ouvert la fenêtre.
examples.translation: He opened the window.

constructs.name: verbe + infinitif (sans préposition)
constructs.description: Verbs such as the modals or verbs of liking followed directly by an infinitive.

card.formation: A conjugated verb is followed directly by an infinitive, with no preposition in between. Typical verbs are the modals (pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir), verbs of liking (aimer, adorer, détester, préférer), and aller, venir, espérer, compter.
card.use: It expresses ability, wish, obligation, preference or intention with respect to another action. Object pronouns belonging to the infinitive go directly before it.
pitfalls: Adding a preposition by analogy with English 'to': je veux partir, not je veux de partir.
Conjugating both verbs: je peux venir, not je peux viens.
Placing the object pronoun before the conjugated verb: je veux le voir, not je le veux voir.
Putting ne ... pas around the infinitive instead of the conjugated verb: je ne peux pas venir.

contrasts.note: Those verbs need à before the infinitive (commencer à, apprendre à).
Those verbs need de before the infinitive (décider de, essayer de).
Aller + infinitive is a specific case of this pattern, expressing the near future.
Il faut is impersonal; devoir + infinitive is conjugated for the person.
There the infinitive has its own subject, different from the subject of the main verb.

examples.sentence: Je peux t'aider ce soir.
examples.translation: I can help you tonight.

examples.sentence: Elle aime lire le soir.
examples.translation: She likes reading in the evening.

examples.sentence: Nous devons partir à huit heures.
examples.translation: We have to leave at eight.

examples.sentence: Tu veux venir avec nous ?
examples.translation: Do you want to come with us?

constructs.name: il faut + infinitif
constructs.description: Impersonal expression of obligation or prohibition followed by an infinitive.

card.formation: Impersonal il + faut (in any tense: il fallait, il faudra) + infinitive. Il never changes, and the negative is il ne faut pas + infinitive.
card.use: It states a general obligation or necessity, without naming who must act. In the negative it expresses a prohibition (one must not), not an absence of obligation.
pitfalls: Reading il ne faut pas as 'you don't have to'; it means 'you must not'. For 'no need' use ce n'est pas la peine de or pas besoin de.
Replacing il with another subject: je faut is impossible; use je dois.
Adding a preposition: il faut partir, not il faut de partir.
Using il faut + infinitive when a specific person is meant and the subjunctive is needed: il faut que tu partes.

contrasts.note: Il faut que + subjunctive names the person who must act; il faut + infinitive stays general.
Devoir + infinitive has a personal subject: je dois partir.
Falloir is one of the impersonal verbs; this entry covers its use with an infinitive.
A bare infinitive gives an instruction directly, without il faut.

examples.sentence: Il faut acheter du pain.
examples.translation: We need to buy bread.

examples.sentence: Il ne faut pas toucher ce bouton.
examples.translation: You must not touch this button.

examples.sentence: Il faudra partir tôt demain.
examples.translation: We will have to leave early tomorrow.

constructs.name: verbe + à + infinitif
constructs.description: Verbs whose infinitive complement is introduced by à.

card.formation: Conjugated verb + à + infinitive. Common verbs: apprendre à, commencer à, continuer à, réussir à, hésiter à, chercher à, s'habituer à, aider quelqu'un à, inviter quelqu'un à.
card.use: The preposition is fixed by the verb, so each verb must be learned with it. Many of these verbs express effort, beginning or progress toward a result.
pitfalls: Leaving out à: j'apprends à nager, not j'apprends nager.
Using de with verbs that take à, or the reverse: il a réussi à, but il a essayé de.
Not knowing that commencer and continuer accept both à and de, while finir only takes de.
Contracting à: à is never contracted before an infinitive (à le faire, not au faire).

contrasts.note: Same structure with de; the verb decides which preposition is used.
Modals and verbs of liking take no preposition.
The same verbs can take à + a noun; there à contracts with le and les.
There the preposition depends on an adjective, not a verb (prêt à, content de).
When the subject changes, some à-verbs take à ce que + subjunctive instead.

examples.sentence: Mon fils apprend à nager.
examples.translation: My son is learning to swim.

examples.sentence: Il commence à pleuvoir.
examples.translation: It is starting to rain.

examples.sentence: J'ai réussi à ouvrir la porte.
examples.translation: I managed to open the door.

examples.sentence: Tu m'aides à porter ce sac ?
examples.translation: Will you help me carry this bag?

constructs.name: verbe + de + infinitif
constructs.description: Verbs whose infinitive complement is introduced by de.

card.formation: Conjugated verb + de (d' before a vowel) + infinitive. Common verbs: décider de, essayer de, oublier de, arrêter de, finir de, refuser de, accepter de, choisir de, and verbs of saying or asking with a person: demander à quelqu'un de, dire à quelqu'un de, conseiller à quelqu'un de.
card.use: The preposition is fixed by the verb and must be learned with it. With verbs like demander or dire, the person is introduced by à and the action by de.
pitfalls: Leaving out de: j'ai oublié de fermer, not j'ai oublié fermer.
Translating 'to' as à: il a décidé de partir, not à partir.
Swapping the prepositions with dire or demander: je demande à Paul de venir.
Forgetting the elision before a vowel: essayer d'ouvrir, not de ouvrir.
Contracting de before an infinitive: de le faire, not du faire.

contrasts.note: Same structure with à; each verb takes one or the other.
Modals and verbs of liking take the infinitive directly.
With a different subject, many de-verbs switch to que + subjunctive.
Venir de + infinitive is a fixed tense form meaning 'have just'.
After some de-verbs (regretter de, remercier de), a past infinitive shows an earlier action.

examples.sentence: J'ai oublié de fermer la porte.
examples.translation: I forgot to close the door.

examples.sentence: Elle a décidé de partir.
examples.translation: She decided to leave.

examples.sentence: Arrête de crier, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Stop shouting, please.

examples.sentence: Je vais essayer d'arriver tôt.
examples.translation: I'll try to arrive early.

constructs.name: adjectif + préposition + infinitif
constructs.description: Adjectives followed by de or à and an infinitive.

card.formation: Être (or another linking verb) + adjective + de or à + infinitive. Adjectives of feeling and certainty usually take de (content de, heureux de, sûr de, désolé de); others take à (prêt à, seul à, le premier à).
card.use: It says how someone feels about an action or how ready or able they are for it. After an adjective like facile or difficile, à gives the thing a passive sense (c'est facile à faire), while il est ... de introduces the action as the real subject (il est facile de faire ça).
pitfalls: Using à after adjectives of feeling: je suis content de te voir, not à te voir.
Mixing up c'est facile à comprendre (the thing is easy to understand) and il est facile de comprendre (it is easy to understand that).
Leaving out the preposition by analogy with English: prêt à partir, not prêt partir.
Forgetting that the adjective agrees with the subject: elle est prête à partir.

contrasts.note: The same adjectives can take a noun after the preposition (content de ton travail).
There the preposition depends on a verb rather than an adjective.
Il est + adjective + de + infinitive is the impersonal form with no personal subject.
With a different subject, content de becomes content que + subjunctive.

examples.sentence: Je suis content de te voir.
examples.translation: I'm happy to see you.

examples.sentence: Tu es prête à partir ?
examples.translation: Are you ready to leave?

examples.sentence: Ce livre est facile à lire.
examples.translation: This book is easy to read.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes désolés d'arriver en retard.
examples.translation: We're sorry for arriving late.

constructs.name: préposition + infinitif
constructs.description: Prepositions other than those of purpose followed by an infinitive.

card.formation: Preposition + infinitive, e.g. sans, avant de, au lieu de, à force de, de peur de. After après, the past infinitive is required (après avoir mangé).
card.use: It links a second action to the main verb when both have the same subject. Where English uses an -ing form after a preposition, French uses the infinitive; only en takes the present participle (gérondif).
pitfalls: Using the -ant form after a preposition, copying English: sans parler, not sans parlant.
Forgetting de in avant de: avant de partir, not avant partir.
Using the simple infinitive after après: après avoir mangé, not après manger.
Using this structure when the subjects differ; then a conjunction is needed (avant que tu partes).

contrasts.note: Pour and afin de + infinitive express purpose and are a separate entry.
En is the one preposition followed by the -ant form, not the infinitive.
Après and sans can take the past infinitive for an earlier, completed action.
When the subjects differ, avant de becomes avant que + subjunctive.
When the infinitive is negated, ne pas goes together before it (au lieu de ne pas répondre).

examples.sentence: Il est parti sans dire au revoir.
examples.translation: He left without saying goodbye.

examples.sentence: Lave-toi les mains avant de manger.
examples.translation: Wash your hands before eating.

examples.sentence: Il regarde la télé au lieu de travailler.
examples.translation: He watches TV instead of working.

constructs.name: infinitif à valeur d'impératif
constructs.description: Infinitive used instead of the imperative in instructions, notices and recipes.

card.formation: A bare infinitive stands alone as the verb of the sentence, with no subject. In the negative, ne pas goes together before the infinitive (ne pas fumer).
card.use: It gives instructions to no one in particular: recipes, user manuals, signs, forms and exam questions. It sounds neutral and impersonal compared with the imperative.
pitfalls: Splitting the negation around the infinitive: ne pas toucher, never ne toucher pas.
Taking it for an incomplete sentence or a mistake; it is a normal written style.
Using it to address a specific person in conversation, where the imperative is expected.
Placing a pronoun after the infinitive: le mélanger, not mélanger-le.

contrasts.note: The imperative addresses someone directly (mélangez); the infinitive is impersonal.
Explains why both parts of the negation come before the infinitive.
Il faut + infinitive also gives a general instruction, but as a full sentence.
Signs can also use a noun alone (sortie, entrée interdite) instead of a verb.

examples.sentence: Ne pas fumer.
examples.translation: No smoking.

examples.sentence: Mélanger la farine et le sucre.
examples.translation: Mix the flour and the sugar.

examples.sentence: Cocher la bonne réponse.
examples.translation: Tick the right answer.

constructs.name: participe passé employé comme adjectif
aliases: past participle used as an adjective
constructs.description: Past participle used without an auxiliary to describe a noun, agreeing with it like an adjective.

card.formation: The past participle is used without an auxiliary, after a noun or after être and similar verbs (sembler, rester), and agrees in gender and number with the noun like any adjective.
card.use: It describes a state that results from an action: une porte fermée, un plat préparé. With être, it describes the state rather than the event.
pitfalls: Forgetting agreement: les fenêtres sont ouvertes, une lettre écrite.
Putting the participle before the noun as in English: une porte fermée, not une fermée porte.
Confusing a state (la porte est fermée, 'is closed') with a passive event (la porte a été fermée, 'was closed').
Taking être + participle for a passé composé: elle est fatiguée describes her state now.

contrasts.note: The passive presents an action done to the subject; the adjectival participle presents a state.
Elle est partie is a past event; elle est fatiguée is a present state.
Verbal adjectives come from present participles (-ant) and describe active properties.
A participial clause uses the participle with its own subject to express time or cause.

examples.sentence: La porte est fermée.
examples.translation: The door is closed.

examples.sentence: J'ai acheté une table cassée.
examples.translation: I bought a broken table.

examples.sentence: Les enfants semblent fatigués.
examples.translation: The children seem tired.

constructs.name: gérondif
constructs.description: En plus the present participle, expressing simultaneity, manner, means, cause or condition with the same subject.

card.formation: En + present participle: take the nous form of the present, drop -ons and add -ant (en parlant, en finissant). Three irregular forms: en ayant, en étant, en sachant.
card.use: It describes an action done by the same subject as the main verb, expressing simultaneity (while), manner or means (by), and sometimes cause or condition. Tout en stresses simultaneity or a contrast.
pitfalls: Using it when the subject differs: the gérondif always refers to the subject of the main verb.
Leaving out en, which turns it into a participe présent with a different use.
Making the form agree; the gérondif is invariable.
Translating every English -ing with a gérondif; after other prepositions French uses the infinitive.

contrasts.note: Without en, the -ant form describes a noun or gives a cause, mostly in writing.
A verbal adjective agrees with its noun and describes a property, not an action.
Prepositions other than en take the infinitive (sans parler).
Être en train de stresses an ongoing action as the main verb, not a background action.
A gérondif can replace a si-clause to express a condition.

examples.sentence: Je chante en prenant ma douche.
examples.translation: I sing while taking a shower.

examples.sentence: Il a appris l'anglais en regardant des films.
examples.translation: He learned English by watching films.

examples.sentence: Elle est tombée en courant.
examples.translation: She fell while running.

constructs.name: infinitif passé
constructs.description: Avoir or être in the infinitive plus past participle, for an action completed before the main one.

card.formation: Avoir or être in the infinitive + past participle (avoir mangé, être parti). With être, the participle agrees with the subject; in the negative, ne pas usually goes before the auxiliary (ne pas avoir compris).
card.use: It expresses an action completed before the action of the main verb, with the same subject. It is required after après and common after sans, regretter de, remercier de, être content de.
pitfalls: Using the simple infinitive after après: après avoir fini, not après finir.
Choosing the wrong auxiliary; it follows the passé composé rules (être arrivé, s'être levé).
Forgetting agreement with être: après être arrivées, elles ont dîné.
Placing the negation around the auxiliary as in a conjugated verb; the usual order is ne pas avoir fait.

contrasts.note: The simple infinitive after a preposition shows an action at the same time or later.
Après que + indicative is used when the subjects differ.
Ayant fini also marks an earlier action, but as a participle in formal writing.
With a different subject, regretter d'avoir fait becomes regretter que tu aies fait.

examples.sentence: Après avoir mangé, on est sortis.
examples.translation: After eating, we went out.

examples.sentence: Merci d'être venu.
examples.translation: Thank you for coming.

examples.sentence: Il est parti sans avoir payé.
examples.translation: He left without having paid.

examples.sentence: Je regrette de ne pas avoir appelé.
examples.translation: I regret not having called.

constructs.name: proposition infinitive (verbe de perception + infinitif)
aliases: infinitive clause after verbs of perception
constructs.description: A verb of perception followed by an infinitive that has its own subject, the person or thing perceived.

card.formation: Verb of perception (voir, regarder, entendre, écouter, sentir) + noun + infinitive, or verb + infinitive + noun when the infinitive has no object. As a pronoun, the person or thing perceived goes before the perception verb (je les entends chanter).
card.use: It reports what someone sees, hears or feels another person or thing doing. The noun is the subject of the infinitive but the object of the perception verb.
pitfalls: Using the -ant form as in English: j'entends les enfants rire, not riant.
Using a subject pronoun: je les vois partir, not je vois ils partir.
Putting the pronoun before the infinitive instead of before the perception verb: je l'entends chanter.
Placing a noun after an infinitive that has its own object, which makes the sentence ambiguous.

In compound tenses, the participle agrees with a preceding direct object only if it performs the infinitive's action: les chanteuses que j'ai entendues chanter, but les chansons que j'ai entendu chanter.

contrasts.note: Faire + infinitive means causing the action, not perceiving it, and the noun must follow the infinitive.
Laisser has the same word order options but means allowing the action.
There the subject of both verbs is the same.
Je vois Paul qui arrive is a close alternative with a relative clause.

examples.sentence: J'entends les oiseaux chanter.
examples.translation: I hear the birds singing.

examples.sentence: Je l'ai vu partir ce matin.
examples.translation: I saw him leave this morning.

examples.sentence: On regarde passer les trains.
examples.translation: We watch the trains go by.

constructs.name: participe présent
constructs.description: Invariable -ant form used mainly in writing, replacing a relative clause or expressing cause.

card.formation: Take the nous form of the present tense, drop -ons and add -ant (nous finissons → finissant). Irregular: ayant, étant, sachant. It is invariable.
card.use: It is mostly written and formal. It replaces a relative clause with qui (les personnes habitant ici) or gives a cause or circumstance at the start of a sentence (ne sachant pas quoi faire, ...).
pitfalls: Making it agree; as a verb form it never takes -e or -s.
Using it in everyday speech, where a relative clause or parce que sounds more natural.
Confusing it with the gérondif, which needs en and refers to the subject of the main verb.
Mixing it up with the verbal adjective, which can be spelled differently (fatiguant vs fatigant).

contrasts.note: En + -ant describes how or when the subject acts; the bare participle usually describes a noun or a cause.
The verbal adjective agrees and expresses a lasting quality; the participle is an action and invariable.
A qui-clause is the everyday equivalent of a present participle after a noun.
Ayant or étant + past participle marks an earlier, completed action.
A participle with its own subject forms a participial clause.

examples.sentence: On cherche un vendeur parlant anglais.
examples.translation: We are looking for a salesperson who speaks English.

examples.sentence: Étant malade, elle est restée chez elle.
examples.translation: Being ill, she stayed at home.

examples.sentence: Les élèves voulant participer doivent s'inscrire.
examples.translation: Students wishing to take part must sign up.

constructs.name: adjectif verbal
constructs.description: Adjective derived from a present participle, which agrees with its noun and may differ in spelling.

card.formation: An adjective in -ant derived from a present participle, which agrees with its noun (des films amusants). Some differ in spelling: verbs in -guer and -quer drop the u in the adjective (fatiguant → fatigant, convainquant → convaincant), and some adjectives end in -ent (précédant → précédent, négligeant → négligent, équivalant → équivalent).
card.use: It describes a quality or state of a noun rather than an action. Test: if the word agrees, can take très or can be replaced by another adjective, it is a verbal adjective; if it has an object or complement, or is negated with ne, it is a participle and stays invariable.
pitfalls: Leaving it invariable like the participle: des rues glissantes.
Using the participle spelling for the adjective: un travail fatigant, but en se fatiguant.
Writing -ant for adjectives that end in -ent: un salaire équivalent, but un salaire équivalant au mien.
Treating every -ant word after a noun as an adjective; if it has an object, it is a participle (des enfants obéissant à leurs parents).

contrasts.note: The participle expresses an action, is invariable and keeps the verb's spelling.
The gérondif is preceded by en and modifies the verb, not a noun.
A past participle adjective describes a state undergone (fatigué), the verbal adjective an effect produced (fatigant).
Verbal adjectives follow the normal agreement rules of adjectives.

examples.sentence: C'est un travail très fatigant.
examples.translation: It is very tiring work.

examples.sentence: Elle raconte des histoires amusantes.
examples.translation: She tells funny stories.

examples.sentence: Attention, la route est glissante.
examples.translation: Careful, the road is slippery.

constructs.name: participe présent (forme composée)
constructs.description: Compound participle (ayant or étant plus past participle) for a completed action, often expressing cause.

card.formation: Ayant or étant (the present participle of the auxiliary) + past participle: ayant fini, étant arrivé. With étant, the past participle agrees with the subject it refers to.
card.use: It presents an action completed before the main action, often as its cause, in formal written French. It usually opens the sentence and shares the main verb's subject.
pitfalls: Choosing the wrong auxiliary; use étant with verbs that take être in the passé composé.
Forgetting agreement with étant: étant arrivées en retard, elles ...
Using it in conversation, where puisque or comme + plus-que-parfait or passé composé is more natural.
Letting it refer to someone other than the subject of the main clause.

contrasts.note: The simple form marks an action at the same time as the main verb.
Après avoir fini also marks an earlier action, but with a preposition and in all registers.
The gérondif expresses simultaneous actions, never a completed earlier one.
A participial clause has its own subject, different from the main clause.

examples.sentence: Ayant raté le train, il a pris un taxi.
examples.translation: Having missed the train, he took a taxi.

examples.sentence: Étant arrivée tôt, elle a attendu.
examples.translation: Having arrived early, she waited.

examples.sentence: Ayant fini ses devoirs, Léa est sortie.
examples.translation: Having finished her homework, Léa went out.

constructs.name: verbes pronominaux (présent)
constructs.description: Verbs conjugated with a reflexive pronoun of the same person as the subject.

card.formation: The verb is preceded by a reflexive pronoun of the same person as the subject: je me, tu te, il/elle/on se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se. Me, te and se become m', t', s' before a vowel or silent h.
card.use: Many everyday routines use pronominal verbs (se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher), as do verbs whose action the subject does to itself. Some verbs exist only in pronominal form (se souvenir, s'en aller).
pitfalls: Forgetting the pronoun or using the wrong person: je me lève, not je lève or je se lève.
Dropping the pronoun after another verb: je vais me coucher, not je vais coucher.
Using a possessive with body parts: je me lave les mains, not je lave mes mains.
Putting ne ... pas around the verb only: je ne me lève pas, with ne before the pronoun.

contrasts.note: In compound tenses these verbs always take être.
With a plural subject, se can mean 'each other' rather than 'oneself'.
With a thing as subject, se can give a passive meaning (ça se vend bien).
The reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject; an object pronoun refers to someone else.

examples.sentence: Je me lève à sept heures.
examples.translation: I get up at seven.

examples.sentence: Tu t'appelles comment ?
examples.translation: What's your name?

examples.sentence: Nous nous couchons tard le samedi.
examples.translation: We go to bed late on Saturdays.

constructs.name: verbes impersonnels
constructs.description: Verbs used only with the impersonal subject il, such as weather verbs and the verb of necessity.

card.formation: The verb is used only in the third person singular with il, which refers to nothing. Typical cases are weather verbs (il pleut, il neige), il fait + adjective for weather, and falloir (il faut).
card.use: These verbs describe weather, time and necessity, where there is no real agent. They exist in all tenses, always with il.
pitfalls: Conjugating them with another person: je faut, nous pleuvons are impossible.
Using être for weather: il fait froid, not il est froid.
Interpreting il as 'he'; in these verbs it means nothing.

contrasts.note: Ordinary verbs can also be used with impersonal il (il manque deux chaises); these verbs are always impersonal.
Covers falloir followed by an infinitive in detail.
Il y a is another fixed impersonal expression, for existence and location.
Personal il refers to a masculine noun or person; impersonal il refers to nothing.

examples.sentence: Il pleut depuis ce matin.
examples.translation: It has been raining since this morning.

examples.sentence: En hiver, il neige souvent ici.
examples.translation: In winter, it often snows here.

examples.sentence: Il fait très chaud aujourd'hui.
examples.translation: It's very hot today.

constructs.name: verbes pronominaux aux temps composés
constructs.description: Pronominal verbs in compound tenses, always with the auxiliary être.

card.formation: Reflexive pronoun + être in the required tense + past participle: je me suis levé, elle s'était trompée. In the negative, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the auxiliary (je ne me suis pas levé).
card.use: All pronominal verbs form their compound tenses with être. The participle usually agrees with the subject, unless the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object or a direct object follows the verb.
pitfalls: Using avoir: je me suis lavé, not je m'ai lavé.
Forgetting agreement in the common case: elle s'est levée.
Making the participle agree when a direct object follows: elle s'est lavé les mains.
Making it agree when se is indirect: ils se sont parlé, ils se sont téléphoné.
Placing pas before the auxiliary: je ne me suis pas réveillé.

contrasts.note: In the present the pronoun goes directly before the conjugated verb, with no auxiliary.
Verbs of movement also take être, but have no reflexive pronoun.
Gives the detailed agreement rules for these participles.
The same verb used without the pronoun takes avoir (elle a lavé la voiture).

examples.sentence: Elle s'est levée tôt ce matin.
examples.translation: She got up early this morning.

examples.sentence: Nous nous sommes bien amusés.
examples.translation: We had a great time.

examples.sentence: Je ne me suis pas réveillé à temps.
examples.translation: I didn't wake up in time.

constructs.name: voix passive (formation)
constructs.description: Être in the required tense plus the past participle, which agrees with the subject.

card.formation: Être in the tense of the active verb + past participle, which agrees with the subject: la maison est vendue, elle a été invitée, ils seront payés. Only verbs with a direct object can be made passive.
card.use: It puts the person or thing undergoing the action in subject position, when that is the topic or when the doer is unknown or unimportant. It is more common in writing; speech often prefers on.
pitfalls: Getting the tense wrong: the tense is carried by être (la lettre a été écrite = was written; la lettre est écrite = is written).
Confusing the passive with a passé composé with être: elle est partie is active.
Forgetting agreement: les maisons ont été construites.
Making verbs with à passive, as in English: on m'a dit, not j'ai été dit.

contrasts.note: Covers how the doer is added with par or de.
On + active verb is the everyday alternative when the doer is unspecified.
Se + verb gives a passive meaning for general facts, with no agent.
Être + participle can also describe a state rather than an action.
Verbs like partir use être in the active passé composé, not as a passive.

examples.sentence: Le courrier est distribué le matin.
examples.translation: The mail is delivered in the morning.

examples.sentence: Ma voiture a été volée hier.
examples.translation: My car was stolen yesterday.

examples.sentence: Les résultats seront publiés demain.
examples.translation: The results will be published tomorrow.

constructs.name: complément d'agent
constructs.description: Introducing the agent of a passive verb with par or, for verbs of feeling and states, with de.

card.formation: The doer of a passive action is usually introduced by par (le livre a été écrit par Hugo). After participles of description or position (couvert, entouré, rempli, accompagné) and many verbs of feeling (aimer, respecter, admirer), de is common instead.
card.use: It names who or what performs the action when that information matters, and is often left out when the doer is obvious or unknown. With verbs of feeling, par is also possible, especially for a single concrete action.
pitfalls: Translating 'by' with de in all cases; par is the default, and de belongs to description and feeling (couvert de neige, aimé de tous).
Keeping des or du after de: entouré d'arbres, couvert de neige, not de des arbres.
Adding an agent to a pronominal passive, which does not allow one.
Overusing par phrases where an active sentence would be more natural.

contrasts.note: Covers how the passive verb itself is built.
The pronominal passive cannot name an agent.
Se faire + infinitive also introduces the doer with par.
In the causative, par introduces the person made to act, not a passive agent.

examples.sentence: Ce tableau a été peint par Monet.
examples.translation: This painting was painted by Monet.

examples.sentence: Cette chanteuse est aimée de tous.
examples.translation: This singer is loved by everyone.

examples.sentence: Le jardin est entouré d'un mur.
examples.translation: The garden is surrounded by a wall.

constructs.name: verbes pronominaux réciproques
constructs.description: Plural pronominal verbs expressing a mutual action.

card.formation: A plural subject (nous, vous, ils, elles, or on meaning nous) with the pronoun nous, vous or se + verb: ils se parlent. L'un l'autre or entre eux can be added to remove ambiguity.
card.use: It expresses an action that two or more people do to each other: s'aimer, se téléphoner, se rencontrer, se dire bonjour.
pitfalls: Using a singular subject; the reciprocal meaning needs at least two people.
Leaving out the pronoun: on se voit demain, not on voit demain.
Making the participle agree when se is indirect: elles se sont téléphoné, se sont parlé.
Missing the ambiguity of ils se regardent, which can mean 'each other' or 'themselves'.

contrasts.note: Reflexive meaning: the subject acts on itself, not on another.
There se gives a passive meaning, with a thing as subject.
Agreement depends on whether se is a direct or indirect object.
On se voit uses on for nous, with a reciprocal meaning.

examples.sentence: On se voit demain ?
examples.translation: Shall we see each other tomorrow?

examples.sentence: Ils s'aiment depuis dix ans.
examples.translation: They have loved each other for ten years.

examples.sentence: Nous nous téléphonons tous les soirs.
examples.translation: We phone each other every evening.

examples.sentence: Elles se sont rencontrées à Lyon.
examples.translation: They met in Lyon.

constructs.name: verbes pronominaux à sens passif
constructs.description: Pronominal construction with a non-human subject, used with a passive meaning.

card.formation: Se + verb in the third person, with a thing (not a person) as subject: ce vin se boit frais, ces livres se vendent bien. No agent can be added.
card.use: It states general facts, habits and norms about how something is done or happens. Ça ne se fait pas means 'that isn't done'.
pitfalls: Adding an agent with par, which this construction does not allow.
Using it with a person as subject, where the meaning becomes reflexive.
Reading it as reflexive: le français se parle au Québec does not mean French speaks itself.
Forgetting plural agreement of the verb: ces chaussures se vendent bien.

contrasts.note: The être passive can name an agent and describe a single event.
On + active verb expresses the same idea with a human subject (on boit ce vin frais).
With a person as subject, se has a reflexive meaning.
Se faire + infinitive is a passive with a person as subject, usually for one event.

examples.sentence: Ce vin se boit frais.
examples.translation: This wine is drunk chilled.

examples.sentence: Le français se parle aussi au Canada.
examples.translation: French is also spoken in Canada.

examples.sentence: Ça ne se fait pas.
examples.translation: That isn't done.

constructs.name: construction impersonnelle
constructs.description: Ordinary verbs used with impersonal il, placing the real subject after the verb.

card.formation: Impersonal il + a verb that normally has a real subject, with the real subject placed after the verb: il manque deux chaises, il reste du pain, il est arrivé un accident. Il est + adjective + de + infinitive (or que + clause) follows the same idea.
card.use: It introduces new information or a judgement while keeping the subject position empty. It is common with verbs of existence, appearance, lack and occurrence, and with judgements such as il est important de.
pitfalls: Making the verb plural: il manque deux élèves, not il manquent.
Using c'est instead of il est before de + infinitive in formal writing: il est interdit de fumer.
Interpreting il as 'he'; it refers to nothing.
Using a definite noun as real subject; it is usually indefinite (il est arrivé un accident).

contrasts.note: Those verbs are always impersonal; here ordinary verbs are used impersonally.
Il y a is the most common fixed impersonal expression of existence.
Il est + adjective + que often needs the subjunctive.
With a personal subject the adjective may take à (c'est facile à faire).
C'est is the informal presentative; il est is the impersonal form in writing.

examples.sentence: Il manque deux chaises.
examples.translation: Two chairs are missing.

examples.sentence: Il reste du gâteau dans le frigo.
examples.translation: There is some cake left in the fridge.

examples.sentence: Il est interdit de fumer ici.
examples.translation: Smoking is forbidden here.

constructs.name: faire causatif (faire + infinitif)
constructs.description: Faire plus infinitive, meaning to make someone do something or have something done.

card.formation: Faire (conjugated) + infinitive + the person or thing affected: je fais réparer ma voiture. The person who does the action follows the infinitive, introduced by à or par when the infinitive already has an object; object pronouns go before faire (je la fais réparer).
card.use: It means making someone do something, or having something done by someone else. The subject causes the action but does not perform it.
pitfalls: Putting the noun between faire and the infinitive: je fais venir le médecin, not je fais le médecin venir.
Placing the pronoun before the infinitive: je le fais réparer, not je fais le réparer.
Making fait agree in compound tenses; before an infinitive it stays invariable (elle les a fait venir).
Using faire alone when the result is meant: je fais couper mes cheveux means I have someone cut them.

contrasts.note: Se faire + infinitive presents the subject as the one affected.
Laisser means allowing an action, not causing it.
Perception verbs take a similar structure but report what is perceived.
The passive also hides the doer, but with no one causing the action.

examples.sentence: Je fais réparer ma voiture.
examples.translation: I'm having my car repaired.

examples.sentence: Ce film m'a fait rire.
examples.translation: This film made me laugh.

examples.sentence: Elle fait venir le médecin.
examples.translation: She sends for the doctor.

constructs.name: se faire + infinitif
aliases: to get something done to oneself
constructs.description: Se faire plus infinitive, presenting the subject as undergoing an action or having it done.

card.formation: Reflexive pronoun + faire + infinitive, with être in compound tenses: il s'est fait voler son vélo. The participle fait stays invariable, and the doer can be introduced by par.
card.use: It presents the subject as undergoing an action, either something unpleasant that happens to them (se faire voler, se faire renverser) or a service they arrange (se faire couper les cheveux).
pitfalls: Making fait agree: elle s'est fait opérer, not faite.
Using a possessive for body parts: je me suis fait couper les cheveux, not mes cheveux.
Using avoir in compound tenses: je me suis fait, not je m'ai fait.
Missing whether the action was wanted or not; context decides.

contrasts.note: Without se, the subject causes the action to someone or something else.
The être passive is neutral; se faire stresses the subject's involvement.
Has a thing as subject and states a general fact.
Se laisser + infinitive means letting oneself be affected.

examples.sentence: Je me suis fait couper les cheveux.
examples.translation: I had my hair cut.

examples.sentence: Il s'est fait voler son vélo.
examples.translation: He had his bike stolen.

examples.sentence: Elle s'est fait renverser par une voiture.
examples.translation: She was hit by a car.

constructs.name: laisser + infinitif
constructs.description: Laisser plus infinitive, meaning to let or allow something to happen.

card.formation: Laisser (conjugated) + infinitive; the person or thing allowed can come before or after the infinitive (il laisse les enfants jouer, il laisse jouer les enfants). Object pronouns go before laisser, and se laisser + infinitive means letting oneself be affected.
card.use: It means allowing or not preventing an action. Se laisser often describes giving in (se laisser convaincre, se laisser aller).
pitfalls: Putting the pronoun before the infinitive: laisse-moi parler, je le laisse partir.
Translating 'let's' with laisser; 'let's go' is the imperative allons-y.

Agreement of laissé: traditionally it agrees with a preceding direct object that performs the infinitive's action (je les ai laissés partir); the 1990 spelling rectifications allow it to stay invariable (je les ai laissé partir), and both spellings are correct.
Confusing laisser + infinitive with faire + infinitive, which means causing, not allowing.

contrasts.note: Faire causes the action; laisser only allows it, and allows more flexible word order.
Se faire presents an action done to the subject; se laisser stresses that they do not resist.
Same word order options, but the verb reports a perception.
Laisse-moi + infinitive is a common imperative use of laisser.

examples.sentence: Laisse-moi parler, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Let me speak, please.

examples.sentence: Il laisse les enfants jouer dehors.
examples.translation: He lets the children play outside.

examples.sentence: Elle s'est laissé convaincre.
examples.translation: She let herself be persuaded.

constructs.name: pronoms personnels sujets
constructs.description: Subject pronouns, including the choice between tu and vous.

card.formation: je (j' before a vowel), tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. Ils is used for a group with at least one masculine member.
card.use: A subject pronoun is needed before every conjugated verb, since French verbs cannot stand without one. Tu is informal and singular; vous is plural, or polite singular.
pitfalls: Leaving out the subject as in some languages: je parle, not parle.
Using tu with strangers or superiors where vous is expected.
Using elles for a mixed group; ils is required if one member is masculine.
Referring to things with ça instead of il or elle by grammatical gender: la table ? Elle est cassée.

contrasts.note: Stressed forms (moi, toi, lui, eux) are used alone, after prepositions and for emphasis.
On takes a third-person singular verb but often means 'we'.
Impersonal il refers to nothing (il pleut).
Object forms (le, la, les) replace the object, not the subject.

examples.sentence: Tu habites à Paris ?
examples.translation: Do you live in Paris?

examples.sentence: Nous travaillons ensemble.
examples.translation: We work together.

examples.sentence: Vous êtes Madame Martin ?
examples.translation: Are you Mrs Martin?

examples.sentence: J'aime ce restaurant.
examples.translation: I like this restaurant.

constructs.name: pronoms toniques
constructs.description: Stressed pronoun forms used alone, after prepositions, after c'est and for emphasis.

card.formation: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles, and soi for an indefinite subject. They never elide and can be followed by -même.
card.use: They are used alone (moi aussi), after prepositions (avec toi, chez eux), after c'est (c'est lui), in comparisons (plus grand que moi), for emphasis (moi, je ...) and in compound subjects (toi et moi).
pitfalls: Using subject forms after a preposition or c'est: avec moi, c'est moi, not avec je or c'est je.
Writing eux for a group of women; the feminine is elles.
Using lui before the verb with verbs like penser à, which keep à + stressed pronoun: je pense à lui, not je lui pense.
Forgetting the subject pronoun after emphasis: moi, je pense que ..., not moi pense.

contrasts.note: Subject pronouns stand directly before the verb and cannot stand alone.
Lui and leur before the verb replace à + person with most verbs; toniques follow the preposition with a few verbs.
C'est à moi expresses possession like c'est le mien.
C'est + tonique + qui is used to highlight the subject.
For people, de or à + tonique is used where en or y would replace a thing.

examples.sentence: Tu viens avec moi ?
examples.translation: Are you coming with me?

examples.sentence: Moi, je préfère le thé.
examples.translation: I prefer tea.

examples.sentence: Ce soir, on mange chez eux.
examples.translation: Tonight we're eating at their place.

examples.sentence: C'est lui, mon frère.
examples.translation: That's him, my brother.

constructs.name: pronoms démonstratifs neutres
constructs.description: Invariable demonstratives referring to things, ideas or situations.

card.formation: ça (spoken), cela (written), ceci (formal, often for what comes next or what is close). They are invariable and have no gender or number.
card.use: They refer to a thing that is pointed at but not named, or to an idea, a situation or something just said. Ça is used in many everyday expressions (ça va, ça coûte combien, j'aime ça).
pitfalls: Writing ça est; with être use c'est.
Confusing ça with çà (an adverb) or forgetting the cedilla.
Using ça for a person in a neutral sentence; it sounds dismissive.
Using ceci and cela in speech where ça is normal.

contrasts.note: Celui, celle, ceux replace a specific noun and agree with it.
Ce (c') is the neutral demonstrative used with être.
Le can also replace an idea, but goes before the verb as an object pronoun.
Ce, cet, cette, ces stand before a noun instead of replacing it.

examples.sentence: Ça coûte combien ?
examples.translation: How much does it cost?

examples.sentence: J'adore ça !
examples.translation: I love that!

examples.sentence: Cela n'a aucune importance.
examples.translation: That doesn't matter at all.

constructs.name: pronom on
constructs.description: On used for 'we', for people in general or for an unspecified someone.

card.formation: On always takes a third-person singular verb. Its reflexive pronoun is se; its stressed form is nous when it means 'we' and soi when it means 'people'.
card.use: In everyday speech on usually means 'we'. It also means people in general (en France, on mange tard) or an unspecified someone (on a sonné).
pitfalls: Using a plural verb: on va, not on vont or on allons.
Missing that adjectives and participles may agree with the real meaning when on means 'we': on est contents, on est parties.
Mixing nous and on in one sentence without care: nous, on part, is fine, but not on partons.
Translating on always as 'one'; usually 'we', 'people' or a passive is better.

contrasts.note: Nous takes a first-person plural verb and is more formal.
On + active verb is the everyday equivalent of a passive without agent.
Another way to state a general rule without naming who acts.
Quelqu'un names an unknown person; on leaves the doer completely vague.

examples.sentence: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
examples.translation: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

examples.sentence: En France, on mange tard.
examples.translation: In France, people eat late.

examples.sentence: On m'a volé mon sac.
examples.translation: My bag was stolen.

constructs.name: pronoms compléments d'objet direct
constructs.description: Pronouns replacing a direct object, placed before the conjugated verb.

card.formation: me (m'), te (t'), le, la (both l' before a vowel), nous, vous, les. They go before the conjugated verb, before the auxiliary in compound tenses, and before the infinitive in verb + infinitive.
card.use: They replace a direct object, a person or thing linked to the verb without a preposition, usually a noun with a definite article, possessive or demonstrative.
pitfalls: Placing the pronoun after the verb as in English: je le vois, not je vois le.
Using lui instead of le for verbs with a direct object: je l'aide, je l'appelle.
Forgetting that écouter, regarder, chercher, attendre take a direct object: je l'attends.
Forgetting agreement of the participle with a preceding direct object: je les ai vues.
Using le, la, les for a noun with an indefinite or partitive article; that needs en.

contrasts.note: Lui and leur replace à + person; le, la, les replace a direct object.
En replaces a noun with un, des, du or a quantity.
Le can also replace an adjective or a whole idea, and then never agrees.
Gives the placement rules in detail, including with infinitives.
A direct object pronoun before avoir makes the participle agree.

examples.sentence: Ce film ? Je l'ai déjà vu.
examples.translation: That film? I've already seen it.

examples.sentence: Tu m'appelles demain ?
examples.translation: Will you call me tomorrow?

examples.sentence: Je vais les acheter ce soir.
examples.translation: I'm going to buy them tonight.

examples.sentence: Je t'attends devant la gare.
examples.translation: I'll wait for you in front of the station.

constructs.name: pronoms compléments d'objet indirect
constructs.description: Pronouns replacing a person introduced by à, placed before the verb.

card.formation: me (m'), te (t'), lui, nous, vous, leur. They go before the conjugated verb, like direct object pronouns; lui and leur are used for both genders.
card.use: They replace a person introduced by à after verbs of communication and giving, such as parler à, téléphoner à, dire à, donner à, écrire à, répondre à, demander à.
pitfalls: Adding -s to the pronoun leur: je leur parle, not je leurs parle.
Using le or la for verbs with à: je lui téléphone, not je le téléphone.
Using lui with verbs like penser à or s'intéresser à, which take à + stressed pronoun: je pense à elle.
Using lui or leur for things; à + thing is replaced by y.
Making the participle agree with an indirect object: je leur ai parlé.

contrasts.note: Le, la, les replace an object without preposition.
A few verbs keep à + stressed pronoun instead (penser à lui).
Y replaces à + thing or idea, not a person.
Leur before a noun is a possessive and takes -s in the plural (leurs amis).
With a direct object pronoun as well, lui and leur come second (je le lui donne).

examples.sentence: Je lui téléphone ce soir.
examples.translation: I'm phoning him tonight.

examples.sentence: Tu leur as dit la vérité ?
examples.translation: Did you tell them the truth?

examples.sentence: Elle m'écrit chaque semaine.
examples.translation: She writes to me every week.

constructs.name: pronom en (quantité)
constructs.description: En replacing a noun with a partitive, indefinite article or expression of quantity.

card.formation: En goes before the verb (or before the infinitive or auxiliary) and replaces de + noun, a partitive, or a noun with un, des or a number. A number or expression of quantity is repeated after the verb: j'en ai deux, j'en veux un kilo.
card.use: It replaces an amount of something already mentioned, answering questions about how much or how many.
pitfalls: Leaving out the number: j'en ai un, not j'en ai when the answer is 'one'.
Using le, la, les for a noun with an indefinite or partitive article: du pain ? J'en veux.
Repeating the noun after en: j'en ai trois, not j'en ai trois pommes.
Getting the negative wrong: je n'en ai pas, with en directly before the verb.

contrasts.note: Le, la, les replace a definite noun, the whole thing rather than an amount.
En also replaces de + noun after verbs like parler de.
Y replaces a place; en can replace a place you come from (j'en viens).
Beaucoup de pommes becomes j'en ai beaucoup.
Nouns with du, de la, des are replaced by en.

examples.sentence: Du café ? Oui, j'en veux bien.
examples.translation: Coffee? Yes, I'd like some.

examples.sentence: Des enfants ? J'en ai deux.
examples.translation: Children? I have two.

examples.sentence: Je n'en ai plus.
examples.translation: I don't have any left.

constructs.name: pronom y (lieu)
constructs.description: Y replacing a place introduced by à, en, dans or chez.

card.formation: Y goes before the verb (or the auxiliary or the infinitive) and replaces a place introduced by à, en, dans, chez, sur or sous. In the affirmative imperative it follows the verb: vas-y, allons-y.
card.use: It refers back to a place already mentioned, meaning 'there'.
pitfalls: Keeping y before the future and conditional of aller; to avoid the clash of sounds, French says j'irai rather than j'y irai.
Using y for a place introduced by de: je viens de Paris becomes j'en viens.
Forgetting the -s in vas-y.
Leaving out y where English omits 'there': tu vas à la plage ? Oui, j'y vais.

contrasts.note: Y also replaces à + thing after verbs like penser à.
En replaces de + noun, including a place one comes from.
Où links a clause to a place; y refers back to it in a new sentence.
Il y a contains y as a fixed part, not referring to a specific place.

examples.sentence: Tu vas à Lyon ? Oui, j'y vais demain.
examples.translation: Are you going to Lyon? Yes, I'm going there tomorrow.

examples.sentence: On y va ?
examples.translation: Shall we go?

examples.sentence: J'y habite depuis cinq ans.
examples.translation: I've lived there for five years.

constructs.name: pronoms démonstratifs variables
constructs.description: Demonstrative pronouns agreeing with the noun they replace, often with -ci or -là.

card.formation: celui (m. sg.), celle (f. sg.), ceux (m. pl.), celles (f. pl.), followed here by -ci or -là. They agree with the noun they replace.
card.use: They replace a noun just mentioned to point out one item among others: celui-ci (this one), celui-là (that one). In speech, -là is often used for both.
pitfalls: Using celui alone; it needs -ci, -là, de or a relative clause.
Writing ceux with an -s or celles with one l.
Choosing the gender of the owner instead of the replaced noun: la voiture → celle-ci.
Using ça for a specific noun that has a gender: ce pull ? Je préfère celui-là.

contrasts.note: Ça and cela have no gender and refer to things not named.
Ce, cet, cette, ces stand before a noun (ce livre-ci).
Celui qui, celle de: the same pronouns completed by a clause or de.
Le mien replaces a noun by its owner, not by pointing.

examples.sentence: Je préfère celui-ci.
examples.translation: I prefer this one.

examples.sentence: Quelles chaussures ? Celles-là, en noir.
examples.translation: Which shoes? Those ones, in black.

examples.sentence: Ces gâteaux sont bons, mais ceux-ci sont meilleurs.
examples.translation: These cakes are good, but these ones are better.

constructs.name: pronoms possessifs
constructs.description: Pronouns replacing a possessive determiner plus noun.

card.formation: le mien, la mienne, les miens, les miennes; likewise le tien, le sien; le nôtre, la nôtre, les nôtres; le vôtre; le leur, la leur, les leurs. The article contracts with à and de (au mien, du sien).
card.use: They replace a possessive determiner + noun to avoid repeating the noun: ton vélo et le mien. They agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner.
pitfalls: Agreeing with the owner: le sien can mean his or hers, depending only on the noun.
Forgetting the article: c'est le mien, not c'est mien.
Missing the circumflex: le nôtre (pronoun) vs notre (determiner).
Forgetting contraction: je pense au mien, not à le mien.

contrasts.note: Mon, ma, mes stand before a noun; le mien replaces it.
C'est à moi is a common alternative to c'est le mien.
Celui de Paul names the owner with a noun.
Au mien and du sien follow the usual contraction rules.

examples.sentence: Ce n'est pas ton sac, c'est le mien.
examples.translation: It's not your bag, it's mine.

examples.sentence: Ma voiture est vieille, la leur est neuve.
examples.translation: My car is old, theirs is new.

examples.sentence: Tes enfants jouent avec les nôtres.
examples.translation: Your children are playing with ours.

constructs.name: pronoms indéfinis de personne et de chose
constructs.description: Indefinite pronouns for an unspecified person or thing, and tout.

card.formation: quelqu'un (someone), quelque chose (something), tout (everything), and combinations like quelqu'un d'autre, autre chose. An adjective after them is introduced by de and stays masculine singular (quelqu'un de gentil).
card.use: They refer to a person or thing that is not identified, or with tout to everything. Their negative counterparts are personne and rien.
pitfalls: Leaving out de before an adjective: quelque chose de bon, not quelque chose bon.
Making the adjective feminine: quelque chose d'important, even though chose is feminine.
Writing quelque chose in one word or quelqu'un without the apostrophe.
Placing tout after the participle: j'ai tout compris, not j'ai compris tout.

contrasts.note: Rien and personne are the negative equivalents, used with ne.
Plusieurs, certains, chacun refer to part of a known group.
Tout before a noun is a determiner and agrees (toute la journée).
N'importe qui and n'importe quoi mean anyone and anything at all.
On leaves the person completely vague, while quelqu'un names one unknown person.

examples.sentence: Quelqu'un a sonné à la porte.
examples.translation: Someone rang the doorbell.

examples.sentence: Tout est prêt pour la fête.
examples.translation: Everything is ready for the party.

examples.sentence: J'ai quelque chose pour toi.
examples.translation: I have something for you.

examples.sentence: Tu connais quelqu'un de sympa ici ?
examples.translation: Do you know anyone nice here?

constructs.name: pronom relatif qui
constructs.description: Qui introducing a relative clause in which it is the subject.

card.formation: Noun (the antecedent) + qui + verb. Qui never elides, and the verb agrees with the antecedent (c'est moi qui suis là).
card.use: It introduces a relative clause in which it is the subject, for people and things alike. It also follows prepositions when referring to people (l'ami avec qui je pars).
pitfalls: Choosing qui for people and que for things; the choice depends on the function in the clause.
Writing qu' before a vowel: l'homme qui arrive, never qu'arrive.
Making the verb agree with il: c'est nous qui avons gagné.
Confusing qui with qu'il, which sound alike in speech.

contrasts.note: Que is the object of the relative clause, followed by a subject.
Ce qui has no noun antecedent and means 'what'.
After a preposition, qui is used for people and lequel for things.
Interrogative qui asks 'who?'; relative qui links to a noun.
C'est ... qui uses relative qui to highlight the subject.

examples.sentence: J'ai un ami qui habite à Nice.
examples.translation: I have a friend who lives in Nice.

examples.sentence: C'est le bus qui va à la gare.
examples.translation: That's the bus that goes to the station.

examples.sentence: Prends la veste qui est sur la chaise.
examples.translation: Take the jacket that's on the chair.

constructs.name: pronom relatif que
constructs.description: Que introducing a relative clause in which it is the direct object.

card.formation: Noun + que (qu' before a vowel) + subject + verb. In compound tenses with avoir, the participle agrees with the antecedent (les photos que j'ai prises).
card.use: It introduces a relative clause in which it is the direct object, for people and things. Unlike English 'that' or 'which', que can never be left out.
pitfalls: Leaving it out as in English: le livre que je lis, not le livre je lis.
Using qui because the antecedent is a thing: la robe que tu portes.
Forgetting participle agreement: la lettre que j'ai écrite.
Confusing relative que with the conjunction que after verbs like penser.

contrasts.note: Qui is the subject of the relative clause and is followed directly by the verb.
Dont replaces a complement with de, not a direct object.
Ce que has no noun antecedent and means 'what'.
The conjunction que follows a verb, not a noun, and has no function in its clause.
Que before avoir makes the past participle agree.

examples.sentence: C'est le livre que je lis.
examples.translation: It's the book I'm reading.

examples.sentence: La fille que tu vois est ma sœur.
examples.translation: The girl you see is my sister.

examples.sentence: Voici le gâteau qu'elle a fait.
examples.translation: Here is the cake she made.

constructs.name: pronom relatif où
aliases: où relatif de lieu et de temps
constructs.description: Où introducing a relative clause of place or time.

card.formation: Noun of place or time + où + subject + verb. It can be combined with de and par (d'où, par où).
card.use: It introduces a relative clause giving a place (la ville où j'habite) or a moment (le jour où je suis né). For time, it translates English 'when'.
pitfalls: Using quand after a noun of time: le jour où, not le jour quand.
Forgetting the accent: où (where) vs ou (or).
Using que after a noun of place: la maison où j'habite, not que j'habite.
Using où for a thing that is not a place; then a preposition + lequel is needed.

contrasts.note: Y refers back to a place in a separate sentence; où links a clause to a noun.
Dans lequel can replace où for places, and is needed with other prepositions.
Que is the object of the relative clause, not a place or time.
Interrogative où asks 'where?'.

examples.sentence: C'est la ville où je suis né.
examples.translation: It's the town where I was born.

examples.sentence: Je me souviens du jour où on s'est rencontrés.
examples.translation: I remember the day we met.

examples.sentence: Voici le restaurant où on mange souvent.
examples.translation: Here is the restaurant where we often eat.

constructs.name: pronom relatif dont
constructs.description: Dont replacing a complement introduced by de, including possession.

card.formation: Noun + dont + subject + verb, where dont replaces de + noun. It is used with verbs and adjectives built with de (parler de, avoir besoin de, fier de) and for possession (l'homme dont la fille ...).
card.use: It links a clause to a noun that would be introduced by de in that clause: the meaning is 'of which', 'about which' or 'whose'.
pitfalls: Adding a possessive after dont: l'ami dont le père est médecin, not dont son père.
Using que with verbs built with de: le livre dont j'ai besoin, not que j'ai besoin.
Changing word order after dont: l'auteur dont j'ai lu le livre, not dont le livre j'ai lu.
Using dont after a compound preposition like près de; then duquel or de qui is needed.

contrasts.note: Que replaces a direct object without preposition.
After près de, à côté de and similar, use duquel or de qui.
Ce dont is used without a noun antecedent.
En also replaces de + noun, but in a separate sentence.

examples.sentence: C'est le livre dont je t'ai parlé.
examples.translation: It's the book I told you about.

examples.sentence: Voici l'outil dont tu as besoin.
examples.translation: Here's the tool you need.

examples.sentence: J'ai une amie dont le frère est pilote.
examples.translation: I have a friend whose brother is a pilot.

constructs.name: pronoms relatifs composés
constructs.description: Relative pronouns after a preposition, with lequel and its contracted forms or qui for people.

card.formation: Preposition + lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles, agreeing with the antecedent. With à they contract to auquel, auxquels, auxquelles (but à laquelle), with de to duquel, desquels, desquelles (but de laquelle). For people, preposition + qui is usual.
card.use: They introduce a relative clause when the antecedent is the complement of a preposition other than simple de: la raison pour laquelle, l'ami avec qui, le parc près duquel.
pitfalls: Forgetting the contraction: le projet auquel je pense, not à lequel.
Choosing the gender of the subject instead of the antecedent: la table sur laquelle.
Using que after a preposition: la personne avec qui je travaille, not avec que.
Using qui after parmi or entre, which require lesquels or lesquelles.
Using dont after a compound preposition: près duquel, not près dont.

contrasts.note: Dont replaces simple de + noun; duquel is for compound prepositions ending in de.
Où can replace dans lequel for places and times.
Qui alone is the subject; after a preposition it refers to people only.
The same forms in questions mean 'which one?'.

examples.sentence: C'est la raison pour laquelle je suis parti.
examples.translation: That's the reason why I left.

examples.sentence: Voici l'ami avec qui je voyage.
examples.translation: Here is the friend I travel with.

examples.sentence: C'est un sujet auquel je pense souvent.
examples.translation: It's a subject I often think about.

constructs.name: pronoms relatifs neutres (ce qui, ce que, ce dont)
aliases: tout ce qui, tout ce que
constructs.description: Relative pronouns with the antecedent ce, meaning 'what' or 'the thing that'.

card.formation: Ce + qui (subject), ce + que (object), ce + dont (complement with de). Tout can precede them: tout ce qui, tout ce que.
card.use: They mean 'what' or 'the thing that' when there is no noun antecedent. They also replace qu'est-ce que and qu'est-ce qui in indirect questions (dis-moi ce que tu veux).
pitfalls: Using qu'est-ce que in an indirect question: je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.
Leaving out ce: ce que je veux, c'est dormir, not que je veux.
Choosing by meaning rather than function: ce qui me plaît (subject), ce que j'aime (object).
Using ce que with verbs built with de: ce dont j'ai besoin.

contrasts.note: Qui and que alone need a noun antecedent.
Dont refers to a noun; ce dont refers to a thing not named.
Ce qui and ce que are the indirect-question forms of qu'est-ce qui and qu'est-ce que.
Ce qui ..., c'est ... uses them to highlight part of the sentence.

examples.sentence: Dis-moi ce que tu veux.
examples.translation: Tell me what you want.

examples.sentence: Ce qui me plaît, c'est le calme.
examples.translation: What I like is the quiet.

examples.sentence: C'est exactement ce dont j'ai besoin.
examples.translation: It's exactly what I need.

examples.sentence: Merci pour tout ce que tu fais.
examples.translation: Thanks for everything you do.

constructs.name: pronoms en et y (compléments de verbes prépositionnels)
constructs.description: En and y replacing a complement of a verb built with de or à.

card.formation: En replaces de + thing, idea or infinitive after verbs built with de (parler de, avoir besoin de, avoir envie de, se souvenir de); y replaces à + thing, idea or infinitive after verbs built with à (penser à, s'attendre à, se préparer à). Both go before the verb.
card.use: They avoid repeating a prepositional complement that is a thing, an idea or an action. For people, French keeps the preposition + stressed pronoun (je parle de lui, je pense à eux).
pitfalls: Using le instead of en or y: je m'en souviens, j'y pense, not je le souviens.
Using y or en for people in careful language: je pense à elle, je parle de lui.
Using y for à + person after verbs like parler or téléphoner, which take lui.
Forgetting en in fixed expressions like j'en ai besoin or je m'en occupe.

contrasts.note: En also replaces an amount of something (j'en ai deux).
Y also replaces a place.
Lui and leur replace à + person with most verbs.
For people, de or à + moi, lui, eux is used.
Le replaces an idea after verbs with a direct object (je le sais).

examples.sentence: Ton examen ? J'y pense tous les jours.
examples.translation: Your exam? I think about it every day.

examples.sentence: Ce voyage, je m'en souviens bien.
examples.translation: That trip, I remember it well.

examples.sentence: La voiture ? Oui, j'en ai besoin.
examples.translation: The car? Yes, I need it.

constructs.name: double pronominalisation
constructs.description: Two object pronouns together before the verb, in a fixed order.

card.formation: Before the verb the order is fixed: me, te, se, nous, vous → le, la, les → lui, leur → y → en. In the affirmative imperative, the direct object comes first: donne-le-moi, donne-m'en.
card.use: It replaces two complements of the same verb at once, for example a thing and a person: je donne le livre à Paul becomes je le lui donne.
pitfalls: Swapping le and lui: je le lui donne, not je lui le donne.
Putting en before y: il y en a, not il en y a.
Using moi instead of m' before en in the imperative: donne-m'en.
Combining me or te with lui or leur; then à + stressed pronoun is used (je me présente à lui).

contrasts.note: Covers the position of a single pronoun relative to the verb.
The affirmative imperative uses a different order and hyphens.
One of the two pronouns is usually a direct object.
Lui and leur come after le, la, les but me, te, nous, vous come before them.

examples.sentence: Je te le prête demain.
examples.translation: I'll lend it to you tomorrow.

examples.sentence: Elle le lui a dit.
examples.translation: She told him so.

examples.sentence: Il y en a beaucoup.
examples.translation: There are a lot of them.

examples.sentence: Donne-le-moi, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Give it to me, please.

constructs.name: pronoms indéfinis de quantité
constructs.description: Indefinite pronouns expressing an imprecise quantity or each member of a group.

card.formation: plusieurs (invariable), certains/certaines, quelques-uns/quelques-unes, chacun/chacune, la plupart, d'autres. When they refer to a noun already mentioned as an object, en is placed before the verb (j'en ai lu plusieurs).
card.use: They stand for an imprecise number of people or things, or for each member of a group taken one by one.
pitfalls: Using a plural verb with chacun: chacun a sa chambre.
Forgetting en when they are objects: j'en connais quelques-uns, not je connais quelques-uns.
Writing quelques-uns without the hyphen or as quelques-un.
Using chaque or quelques as pronouns; they are determiners and need a noun.

contrasts.note: Chaque, quelques, plusieurs + noun are the determiner forms.
En accompanies these pronouns when they are objects.
Quelqu'un and quelque chose refer to one unidentified person or thing.
Aucun is the negative counterpart, used with ne.
Tous as a pronoun means everyone, and its final s is pronounced.

examples.sentence: Chacun apporte quelque chose à boire.
examples.translation: Everyone brings something to drink.

examples.sentence: Des films ? J'en ai vu plusieurs.
examples.translation: Films? I've seen several.

examples.sentence: Certains préfèrent rester à la maison.
examples.translation: Some prefer to stay at home.

examples.sentence: Ses amis ? J'en connais quelques-uns.
examples.translation: Her friends? I know a few of them.

constructs.name: pronoms démonstratifs suivis d'une relative ou de de
constructs.description: Demonstrative pronouns followed by a relative clause or a de-complement instead of -ci/-là.

card.formation: celui, celle, ceux, celles + a relative clause (celui qui, celle que, ceux dont) or + de + noun (celle de ma sœur).
card.use: They replace a noun that is identified by what follows, to avoid repeating it. Ceux qui and celui qui also refer to people in general (ceux qui veulent venir).
pitfalls: Adding an article: celui que je veux, not le celui.
Using a possessive structure with à: celui de Paul, not celui à Paul.
Choosing the wrong form for the replaced noun: la maison → celle que j'aime.
Using ce qui when a noun is being replaced: celui qui, not ce qui, for a specific masculine noun.

contrasts.note: Celui-ci, celui-là point to an item without further description.
Ce qui, ce que refer to a thing not named, without gender.
Le mien expresses possession by a person pronoun; celui de uses a noun.
The relative clause after celui follows the normal qui/que/dont rules.

examples.sentence: Je prends celui qui est le moins cher.
examples.translation: I'll take the one that's the cheapest.

examples.sentence: Ce n'est pas ma voiture, c'est celle de Paul.
examples.translation: It's not my car, it's Paul's.

examples.sentence: Ceux qui veulent venir sont les bienvenus.
examples.translation: Those who want to come are welcome.

constructs.name: pronom neutre le
constructs.description: Le replacing an adjective, an infinitive or a whole clause.

card.formation: Le (l' before a vowel) goes before the verb like an object pronoun but never agrees. It replaces an adjective (or a participle used as one), an infinitive, a clause or a whole sentence.
card.use: It refers back to an idea or a quality rather than a noun: tu es fatiguée ? Oui, je le suis; je le savais; comme je l'ai dit.
pitfalls: Making it agree: elles sont prêtes ? Oui, elles le sont, not elles la sont.
Leaving it out with être and an adjective: oui, je le suis, not oui, je suis.
Using le for an idea after verbs built with de or à, which take en or y instead: j'en ai envie, j'y pense.

contrasts.note: Personal le replaces a masculine noun and the participle may agree with it.
En and y replace ideas after verbs built with de and à.
Ça and cela can also refer to an idea, but stand in noun position.
Le often stands for a que-clause already mentioned.

examples.sentence: Tu es prête ? Oui, je le suis.
examples.translation: Are you ready? Yes, I am.

examples.sentence: Il va pleuvoir, je le sais.
examples.translation: It's going to rain, I know.

examples.sentence: Comme je l'ai dit, c'est fermé.
examples.translation: As I said, it's closed.

constructs.name: article défini
constructs.description: Definite articles, used for specific or known things and for general statements.

card.formation: le (m.), la (f.), l' (before a vowel or silent h), les (plural). It agrees in gender and number with the noun.
card.use: It marks something specific or already known, and also things in general (j'aime le chocolat, les chats sont curieux). It is also used with languages, countries, days for habits (le lundi) and parts of the body.
pitfalls: Leaving out the article in general statements as in English: la vie est belle, j'aime la musique.
Using a partitive after verbs of liking: j'aime le café, not du café.
Eliding before an aspirated h: le héros, la honte, but l'homme.
Confusing le lundi (every Monday) with lundi (this coming Monday).

contrasts.note: Un, une, des introduce something not yet identified.
Du, de la express an unspecified amount; le, la the thing in general.
Le and les contract with à and de (au, du, aux, des).
With body parts, French uses the definite article where English uses a possessive.
Some contexts take no article at all.

examples.sentence: J'aime beaucoup le chocolat.
examples.translation: I really like chocolate.

examples.sentence: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Close the door, please.

examples.sentence: Les enfants sont à l'école.
examples.translation: The children are at school.

constructs.name: article indéfini
constructs.description: Indefinite articles, introducing countable things not yet identified.

card.formation: un (m.), une (f.), des (plural for both genders). In the plural, des becomes de before an adjective placed before the noun in careful language (de beaux jours).
card.use: It introduces a countable person or thing that is new to the conversation or not identified. The plural des is needed where English uses 'some' or no article.
pitfalls: Leaving out des in the plural: j'ai des amis à Paris, not j'ai amis.
Keeping un, une, des after a negation: je n'ai pas de voiture.
Using un with professions after être: il est médecin, but c'est un médecin.
Confusing indefinite des with des = de + les.

contrasts.note: Le, la, les mark something specific or general.
Du, de la are used for uncountable amounts, un, une for single countable items.
After pas, un, une, des become de.
Professions after être take no article.
Contracted des means 'of the', not 'some'.

examples.sentence: J'ai un chien et une chatte.
examples.translation: I have a dog and a cat.

examples.sentence: Il y a des fleurs sur la table.
examples.translation: There are flowers on the table.

examples.sentence: C'est une bonne idée.
examples.translation: That's a good idea.

constructs.name: article contracté
constructs.description: Contraction of à and de with the definite articles le and les.

card.formation: à + le = au, à + les = aux, de + le = du, de + les = des. À la, à l', de la and de l' do not contract.
card.use: Contraction is required whenever the preposition à or de meets the articles le or les, for example after aller à, parler de, or in noun complements.
pitfalls: Writing à le or de les: je vais au cinéma, le livre des enfants.
