Contracting before l': à l'hôtel, de l'école, not au hôtel.
Contracting with la: à la plage, de la gare.
Contracting with the object pronoun le: je commence à le faire, not au faire.

contrasts.note: The contracted forms are the definite article merged with à or de.
Partitive du means 'some', contracted du means 'of the' or 'from the'.
Indefinite des means 'some', contracted des means 'of the'.
Masculine countries take au and aux (au Japon, aux États-Unis).
Lequel contracts the same way (auquel, duquel).

examples.sentence: Ce soir, on va au cinéma.
examples.translation: Tonight we're going to the cinema.

examples.sentence: Je reviens du marché.
examples.translation: I'm coming back from the market.

examples.sentence: Elle parle aux enfants.
examples.translation: She is talking to the children.

constructs.name: article partitif
constructs.description: Partitive article for an unspecified amount of something uncountable.

card.formation: du (m.), de la (f.), de l' (before a vowel or silent h). After a negation or an expression of quantity, it becomes de or d'.
card.use: It expresses an unspecified amount of something uncountable: food and drink (du pain, de l'eau), materials, abstract qualities (du courage) and activities with faire (faire du sport).
pitfalls: Leaving out the article as English does with 'some': je bois de l'eau, not je bois eau.
Using the partitive after verbs of liking: j'aime le fromage, but je mange du fromage.
Keeping du after a negation: je ne mange pas de viande.
Keeping du after a quantity: beaucoup de pain, not beaucoup du pain.

contrasts.note: Le, la refer to the thing in general or a specific portion.
Un, une count single items; du, de la measure an amount.
After pas, du and de la become de.
After a quantity word, only de remains.
A noun with a partitive is replaced by en.

examples.sentence: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
examples.translation: I'd like some bread, please.

examples.sentence: Tu veux de l'eau ?
examples.translation: Do you want some water?

examples.sentence: Elle fait de la natation le mardi.
examples.translation: She goes swimming on Tuesdays.

constructs.name: article après une négation
constructs.description: Indefinite and partitive articles becoming de after a negation.

card.formation: After a negation (ne ... pas, plus, jamais), un, une, des, du, de la and de l' become de (d' before a vowel). The definite article le, la, les does not change.
card.use: It expresses the absence of something: there is none, not any. It does not apply after être (ce n'est pas un problème) or when contrasting (ce n'est pas du vin, c'est du jus).
pitfalls: Keeping the article: je n'ai pas de voiture, not pas une voiture.
Changing le, la, les: je n'aime pas le café stays as it is.
Applying the rule after être: ce n'est pas une erreur.
Forgetting elision: il n'y a pas d'eau.

contrasts.note: The partitive is the affirmative form that becomes de after a negation.
Un, une, des also become de after a negation.
The definite article stays unchanged after a negation.
Ne ... aucun is a stronger way to say 'not a single'.
Covers the negation itself, not the change of article.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai pas de voiture.
examples.translation: I don't have a car.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a plus de lait.
examples.translation: There's no milk left.

examples.sentence: Elle ne boit jamais d'alcool.
examples.translation: She never drinks alcohol.

constructs.name: absence d'article
constructs.description: Cases where no article is used, such as after some prepositions, in lists or before professions.

card.formation: The noun is used with no article in specific contexts: after être or devenir with professions, nationalities and religions; after en and often after sans, avec + abstract noun or par; in noun complements of type or purpose (une tasse à café); in lists, headlines and signs.
card.use: Leaving out the article gives the noun a general or classifying meaning rather than referring to a specific thing.
pitfalls: Adding un with professions after être: elle est avocate, not elle est une avocate.
Leaving out the article when an adjective is added: c'est un bon avocat.
Adding an article after en: en voiture, en été, not en la voiture.
Leaving out articles in ordinary sentences where English has none; omission is limited to these cases.

contrasts.note: C'est un médecin uses the article; il est médecin does not.
After quantity words, de stands alone without an article.
After a negation, only de remains.
Noun complements like un sac de sport often have no article.
Headlines and signs often drop articles.

examples.sentence: Mon père est médecin.
examples.translation: My father is a doctor.

examples.sentence: On part en voiture.
examples.translation: We're leaving by car.

examples.sentence: Il a répondu avec patience.
examples.translation: He answered patiently.

constructs.name: expressions de quantité + de
constructs.description: Adverbs and nouns of quantity followed by de and a noun without article.

card.formation: Adverb or noun of quantity + de (d') + noun without article: beaucoup de, peu de, trop de, assez de, un peu de, un kilo de, une bouteille de. Exceptions: la plupart des, bien des, and des when the noun is specific (beaucoup des amis de Paul).
card.use: It expresses a precise or imprecise amount of something.
pitfalls: Keeping the article: beaucoup de gens, not beaucoup des gens.
Forgetting that la plupart takes des: la plupart des élèves.
Using un peu de with countable nouns; use quelques: quelques amis.
Forgetting elision: beaucoup d'amis.

contrasts.note: Without a quantity word, du or de la expresses the amount.
Pas de follows the same pattern of de without article.
En replaces the noun and the quantity stays: j'en ai beaucoup.
Beaucoup and trop also modify verbs, without de.
Quelques and plusieurs are determiners and take no de.

examples.sentence: Il y a beaucoup de monde ici.
examples.translation: There are a lot of people here.

examples.sentence: Je voudrais un kilo de tomates.
examples.translation: I'd like a kilo of tomatoes.

examples.sentence: Tu as assez d'argent ?
examples.translation: Do you have enough money?

constructs.name: adjectifs possessifs
constructs.description: Possessive determiners agreeing with the thing possessed, not the possessor.

card.formation: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs. They agree with the thing possessed; mon, ton, son replace ma, ta, sa before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or silent h (mon amie).
card.use: They show who something belongs to or is related to. Son, sa, ses can mean his, her or its; the gender comes from the noun, not the owner.
pitfalls: Agreeing with the owner: sa mère is his or her mother.
Using ma before a vowel: mon école, not ma école.
Confusing leur (one thing per owner group) and leurs (several things).
Using a possessive with body parts after a pronominal verb: je me brosse les dents.

contrasts.note: Le mien, la tienne replace the noun instead of preceding it.
Body parts often take the definite article instead.
Leur before a verb is a pronoun and never takes -s.
Ce, cette, ces point to something instead of naming its owner.

examples.sentence: Voici mon frère et ma sœur.
examples.translation: This is my brother and my sister.

examples.sentence: Paul cherche sa clé.
examples.translation: Paul is looking for his key.

examples.sentence: Les voisins promènent leurs chiens.
examples.translation: The neighbours are walking their dogs.

constructs.name: adjectifs démonstratifs
constructs.description: Demonstrative determiners pointing to a thing or a time.

card.formation: ce (m.), cet (m. before a vowel or silent h), cette (f.), ces (plural). -ci or -là can be added to the noun to contrast near and far (ce livre-ci).
card.use: They point to a specific person or thing in the situation or in the text. With time words they refer to the current period (ce matin, cette semaine); with -là to a period in the past (ce jour-là).
pitfalls: Using ce before a vowel: cet homme, cet arbre.
Confusing the homophones ces, ses and c'est.
Using ce matin-ci instead of ce matin for 'this morning'.
Missing that ce soir-là means 'that evening' in the past, not tonight.

contrasts.note: Celui, celle replace the noun instead of preceding it.
Le, la identify without pointing.
Ça stands alone and has no gender.
Ses (his, her) sounds like ces (these).

examples.sentence: Cette robe est très jolie.
examples.translation: This dress is very pretty.

examples.sentence: Tu connais cet homme ?
examples.translation: Do you know that man?

examples.sentence: Je suis fatigué ce matin.
examples.translation: I'm tired this morning.

constructs.name: adjectif indéfini tout
constructs.description: Tout as a determiner meaning all or every, agreeing with the noun.

card.formation: tout (m. sg.), toute (f. sg.), tous (m. pl.), toutes (f. pl.), usually followed by an article, possessive or demonstrative: tout le temps, toute la nuit, tous les jours, toutes mes amies. As a determiner, the final s of tous is silent.
card.use: In the singular with an article it means 'the whole' (toute la journée); in the plural it means 'all' or 'every' (tous les matins). Without an article in the singular it means 'any' or 'every' in formal style (tout passager).
pitfalls: Writing touts; the masculine plural is tous.
Forgetting agreement: toute la semaine, toutes les filles.
Translating 'every day' with chaque jour only; tous les jours is more common.
Pronouncing the s of tous as a determiner; it is pronounced only when tous is a pronoun.

contrasts.note: Chaque + singular noun focuses on each item individually.
Tous and toutes can stand alone as pronouns (ils sont tous là).
Tout alone as a pronoun means 'everything'.
Tout before an adjective is an adverb meaning 'quite, very'.

examples.sentence: J'ai travaillé toute la journée.
examples.translation: I worked all day.

examples.sentence: Il pleut tous les jours.
examples.translation: It rains every day.

examples.sentence: Tous mes amis sont venus.
examples.translation: All my friends came.

constructs.name: déterminants indéfinis
constructs.description: Determiners expressing an imprecise quantity or each element of a set.

card.formation: chaque (singular), quelques (plural), plusieurs (plural, invariable), certains/certaines (plural), divers, différents. They replace the article before the noun.
card.use: They express an imprecise quantity (quelques, plusieurs, certains) or each element of a set considered individually (chaque).
pitfalls: Putting chaque in the plural: chaque jour, never chaques jours.
Giving plusieurs a feminine form; it is the same for both genders.
Adding an article: quelques amis, not des quelques amis.
Confusing quelques (a few) with quelque chose or with the pronoun quelques-uns.

contrasts.note: Chacun, quelques-uns, plusieurs stand alone as pronouns.
Tous les + noun means every, viewing the set as a whole.
Des is neutral about quantity; quelques says the number is small.
Aucun is the negative determiner.
Beaucoup de and peu de need de; these determiners do not.

examples.sentence: Je fais du sport chaque matin.
examples.translation: I exercise every morning.

examples.sentence: J'ai invité quelques amis.
examples.translation: I invited a few friends.

examples.sentence: Il a appelé plusieurs fois.
examples.translation: He called several times.

constructs.name: indéfinis avec n'importe
constructs.description: N'importe plus a determiner, pronoun or adverb, meaning any at all.

card.formation: N'importe + qui, quoi, où, quand, comment, lequel, or + quel/quelle/quels/quelles + noun. Quel and lequel agree with the noun.
card.use: They mean any person, thing, place, time or way at all, without choosing. Some uses are critical: dire n'importe quoi (to talk nonsense), faire n'importe comment (to do carelessly).
pitfalls: Forgetting agreement: n'importe quelle couleur.
Confusing n'importe with peu importe, which means 'it doesn't matter'.
Missing the negative tone of n'importe quoi or n'importe comment in many contexts.
Writing n'importe without the apostrophe or with a hyphen.

contrasts.note: Quelqu'un means one particular unknown person; n'importe qui means anyone at all.
Chaque and quelques have no idea of free choice.
Pas n'importe qui means 'not just anyone', not 'no one'.
Qui que, quoi que + subjunctive mean 'whoever, whatever' in a concessive clause.

examples.sentence: Tu peux m'appeler n'importe quand.
examples.translation: You can call me any time.

examples.sentence: Il dit vraiment n'importe quoi.
examples.translation: He's really talking nonsense.

examples.sentence: Prends n'importe quelle chaise.
examples.translation: Take any chair.

constructs.name: genre des noms
constructs.description: Grammatical gender of nouns and the feminine of nouns for people.

card.formation: Every French noun is either masculine or feminine, shown by its article or determiner (le/un for masculine, la/une for feminine). Some endings hint at the gender: -tion, -sion, -té and -ure are mostly feminine, -ment, -age and -isme mostly masculine. Many nouns for people form a feminine by changing the ending: -e added (ami/amie), -er/-ère, -eur/-euse, -teur/-trice, -ien/-ienne.
card.use: The gender of a noun decides the form of every article, adjective, pronoun and past participle that refers to it. For things the gender is arbitrary and must be learned with the noun; for people and many animals it usually follows the sex.
pitfalls: Learning a noun without its article, so its gender is unknown later.
Assuming every noun ending in -e is feminine: le problème, le musée, le livre are masculine.
Exceptions to ending rules, such as la plage, la page and l'image, which are feminine despite -age.
Elided l' hides the gender: l'hôtel is masculine, l'eau is feminine.
A few nouns change meaning with gender, such as le tour (tour) and la tour (tower).

contrasts.note: The feminine of adjectives follows the noun's gender; the noun itself has a fixed gender and does not change for agreement.
The plural marks number; gender stays the same in the plural, though les hides it.
The article is where gender is most visible; it is the marker, not the gender itself.
Possessives agree with the noun owned, not the owner, and use mon/ton/son before a feminine noun starting with a vowel (mon amie).

examples.sentence: La voiture de mon père est rouge.
examples.translation: My father's car is red.

examples.sentence: Le problème est simple.
examples.translation: The problem is simple.

examples.sentence: Mon voisin est boulanger et sa femme est boulangère.
examples.translation: My neighbour is a baker and his wife is a baker.

examples.sentence: C'est une très bonne actrice.
examples.translation: She is a very good actress.

constructs.name: pluriel des noms
constructs.description: Plural of nouns in -s and in -x, and spoken vs written plural marks.

card.formation: Most nouns add -s in the plural, and nouns already ending in -s, -x or -z do not change. Nouns in -eau, -au and -eu add -x, most nouns in -al become -aux, and seven nouns in -ou (bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou) add -x. A few are irregular, such as œil/yeux and monsieur/messieurs.
card.use: The plural is used for more than one item. In speech the final -s or -x is usually silent, so the plural is mostly heard on the article or determiner (le/les, un/des) and in liaison.
pitfalls: Writing -s after -eau or -al endings: des bateaux, des journaux, not bateaus or journals.
Forgetting exceptions such as des pneus, des bleus, des festivals and des bals, which take -s.
Adding an ending to nouns already in -s, -x or -z: un prix, des prix.
Pronouncing the silent plural -s.
Forgetting irregular plurals such as un œil, des yeux.

contrasts.note: Adjectives follow almost the same spelling rules but agree with a noun; a few adjectives in -al take -als (finals, banals).
Gender is fixed for a noun; number changes with how many things there are.
Des is the plural of un/une and often the only spoken sign of the plural.

examples.sentence: J'ai acheté deux livres.
examples.translation: I bought two books.

examples.sentence: Il y a trois bateaux sur le lac.
examples.translation: There are three boats on the lake.

examples.sentence: Je lis les journaux le matin.
examples.translation: I read the newspapers in the morning.

examples.sentence: Elle a les yeux bleus.
examples.translation: She has blue eyes.

constructs.name: féminin des adjectifs
constructs.description: Feminine forms of adjectives, regular and irregular.

card.formation: Most adjectives add -e for the feminine (grand/grande), and those already ending in -e do not change (rouge). Common patterns change the ending: -er/-ère, -eux/-euse, -if/-ive, and doubling of the final consonant in -el, -en, -on, -et (cruelle, ancienne, bonne, muette). Some are irregular: blanc/blanche, long/longue, doux/douce, frais/fraîche, beau/belle, nouveau/nouvelle, vieux/vieille.
card.use: An adjective takes the feminine form when it describes a feminine noun or pronoun, whether it stands next to the noun or after a verb such as être. Adding -e often makes a silent final consonant heard (petit/petite).
pitfalls: Forgetting the feminine after être: elle est contente, not content.
Adding -e to adjectives already ending in -e: une table rouge, not rougee.
Missing the doubled consonant: bonne, italienne, not bone or italiene.
Using beau, nouveau, vieux before a masculine noun starting with a vowel instead of bel, nouvel, vieil.
Adding an extra -e to irregular feminines such as blanche or longue.

contrasts.note: The plural adds -s (or -x) to the masculine or feminine form; both can combine (grandes).
The noun has a fixed gender; the adjective changes form to match it.
Placement decides where the adjective goes; agreement happens in either position.
Past participles with être agree like adjectives, but they are verb forms in a compound tense.

examples.sentence: Ma sœur est très grande.
examples.translation: My sister is very tall.

examples.sentence: Elle porte une robe blanche.
examples.translation: She is wearing a white dress.

examples.sentence: C'est une bonne idée.
examples.translation: It's a good idea.

examples.sentence: Ma grand-mère est très heureuse.
examples.translation: My grandmother is very happy.

constructs.name: pluriel des adjectifs
constructs.description: Plural forms of adjectives and their agreement with the noun.

card.formation: Adjectives add -s in the plural, to the masculine or the feminine form (petits, petites). Those ending in -s or -x do not change, -eau becomes -eaux, and most adjectives in -al become -aux in the masculine plural (normaux), though the feminine stays regular (normales).
card.use: An adjective is plural when it describes a plural noun or pronoun. If it describes nouns of both genders together, it takes the masculine plural.
pitfalls: Forgetting the plural -s in writing, since it is usually silent.
Using the feminine plural for a mixed group: Paul et Marie sont contents, not contentes.
Changing adjectives in -s or -x: des fruits frais, des hommes heureux.
Writing -aux in the feminine: des lois normales, not normaux.
Forgetting that banal, final and fatal take -als.

contrasts.note: The feminine marks gender; the plural marks number, and the two endings combine (-es).
Nouns follow the same spelling patterns but choose their own number; adjectives copy it from the noun.
Participles after être take the same -s, -e, -es endings as adjectives.

examples.sentence: Les enfants sont fatigués.
examples.translation: The children are tired.

examples.sentence: J'aime les petites rues de Lyon.
examples.translation: I like the small streets of Lyon.

examples.sentence: Ce sont des problèmes normaux.
examples.translation: These are normal problems.

examples.sentence: Mon frère et ma sœur sont blonds.
examples.translation: My brother and my sister are blond.

constructs.name: accord du participe passé avec être
constructs.description: Past participle agreeing with the subject in compound tenses with être.

card.formation: In compound tenses formed with être (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur and others), the past participle agrees with the subject in gender and number, like an adjective: -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural. The same rule applies in the passive voice.
card.use: It applies to the verbs of movement and change of state that take être (aller, venir, partir, naître, mourir and others) and to passive sentences. The agreement shows who the subject is, though it is often silent in speech.
pitfalls: Forgetting the -e or -s because it is not heard: elles sont parties.
Applying this rule to verbs with avoir: elle a mangé, not mangée.
With vous for one person, agreeing with that person, not with the plural: vous êtes arrivée, madame.
With on meaning nous, the participle may agree with the people meant: on est partis.
With pronominal verbs the être rule does not always apply; they have their own rules.

contrasts.note: With avoir the participle agrees only with a direct object placed before the verb, never with the subject.
Pronominal verbs also use être, but agreement depends on the role of the reflexive pronoun.
That entry covers which verbs take être and how the tense is built; this one covers the endings.
In the passive, être plus participle also agrees with the subject, but the meaning is passive.
A participle used as an adjective agrees with its noun, without forming a tense.

examples.sentence: Marie est arrivée hier soir.
examples.translation: Marie arrived last night.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes allés au cinéma.
examples.translation: We went to the cinema.

examples.sentence: Mes cousines sont nées à Lille.
examples.translation: My cousins were born in Lille.

examples.sentence: La lettre est écrite en anglais.
examples.translation: The letter is written in English.

constructs.name: accord du participe passé avec avoir
constructs.description: Past participle agreeing with a direct object placed before the verb in tenses with avoir.

card.formation: In compound tenses with avoir, the past participle normally does not change. It agrees in gender and number only with a direct object that comes before the verb: a pronoun (le, la, l', les, me, te, nous, vous), the relative pronoun que, or a noun fronted in a question with quel or combien de.
card.use: The agreement is mainly a matter of written French, because most participles sound the same; it is audible only for participles ending in a consonant, such as mise, prise, faite, écrite. It tells the reader which noun the object pronoun or que refers to.
pitfalls: Agreeing with the subject: elle a mangé, not elle a mangée.
Agreeing with a direct object that comes after the verb: j'ai acheté les pommes.
Agreeing with an indirect object: je leur ai parlé, not parlés.
Agreeing with en: des pommes, j'en ai mangé, without agreement.
Forgetting the agreement after que: la robe que j'ai achetée.

contrasts.note: With être the participle agrees with the subject; with avoir only with a preceding direct object.
Covers the exceptions: en, a following infinitive, verbs of measure and impersonal verbs.
Direct object pronouns placed before the verb are the most common trigger of this agreement.
Que as direct object of the relative clause triggers agreement with its antecedent.
That entry covers forming the tense; this one covers when its participle changes.

examples.sentence: Ta lettre ? Je l'ai lue hier.
examples.translation: Your letter? I read it yesterday.

examples.sentence: Voici les photos que j'ai prises.
examples.translation: Here are the photos I took.

examples.sentence: Où sont mes clés ? Je les ai perdues.
examples.translation: Where are my keys? I've lost them.

examples.sentence: Quelle robe as-tu choisie ?
examples.translation: Which dress did you choose?

constructs.name: accord du participe passé des verbes pronominaux
aliases: past participle agreement of reflexive verbs
constructs.description: Agreement of the past participle of pronominal verbs, depending on the role of the reflexive pronoun.

card.formation: Pronominal verbs form compound tenses with être, but the participle does not simply agree with the subject. If the reflexive pronoun is the direct object (se laver, se lever), the participle agrees with it; if it is an indirect object (se parler, se téléphoner, se dire, se laver les mains), there is no agreement. Verbs that exist only as pronominals (s'enfuir, se souvenir) and pronominals with idiomatic meaning agree with the subject.
card.use: To decide, rewrite the verb with avoir and ask what the pronoun stands for: elle a lavé qui? elle-même, so elle s'est lavée; ils ont parlé à qui? à eux, so ils se sont parlé. When a direct object follows the verb, there is no agreement, but a direct object placed before it triggers agreement as with avoir.
pitfalls: Always agreeing with the subject: elles se sont téléphoné, not téléphonées.
Agreeing when a direct object follows: elle s'est lavé les mains, not lavée.
Forgetting agreement with a preceding object: les mains qu'elle s'est lavées.
Missing the indirect construction of verbs such as se parler, se sourire, se ressembler, se succéder.
Forgetting that verbs like se souvenir and s'en aller agree with the subject.

contrasts.note: Ordinary être verbs always agree with the subject; pronominal verbs depend on the role of the pronoun.
The pronominal rule works like the avoir rule: agreement only with a direct object placed before.
That entry covers forming the compound tenses with être; this one covers the participle's ending.
Reciprocal verbs agree or not depending on whether the verb takes a direct or an indirect object (se voir vs se parler).
Passive pronominals agree with the subject: ces maisons se sont bien vendues.

examples.sentence: Elle s'est levée tôt ce matin.
examples.translation: She got up early this morning.

examples.sentence: Ils se sont parlé pendant une heure.
examples.translation: They talked to each other for an hour.

examples.sentence: Elle s'est lavé les mains.
examples.translation: She washed her hands.

examples.sentence: Nous nous sommes souvenus de son nom.
examples.translation: We remembered his name.

constructs.name: accords particuliers du participe passé
constructs.description: Special cases of past participle agreement, such as with en, before an infinitive or with verbs of measure.

card.formation: With en as the preceding direct object, the participle stays invariable, even when en stands for a feminine or plural noun. Before an infinitive, the participle agrees only if the preceding object performs the action of the infinitive, a rule that traditionally covers laissé too; fait before an infinitive never agrees, and the 1990 spelling reform allows laissé to stay invariable as well. Participles of verbs of measure (coûter, valoir, peser, durer, vivre, courir) and of impersonal verbs (il a fait, il y a eu) do not agree with an amount or an impersonal complement.
card.use: These rules concern careful written French and are tested at advanced levels; most of them make no difference in speech. They matter when reading formal texts and when writing with correct spelling.
pitfalls: Agreeing with en: des fraises, j'en ai mangé, not mangées.
Agreeing fait before an infinitive: la maison qu'il a fait construire.
Agreeing when the object is not the doer of the infinitive: la chanson que j'ai entendu chanter.
Agreeing coûté or duré with an amount: les vingt euros que ça m'a coûté.
Agreeing impersonal participles: les chaleurs qu'il a fait.

contrasts.note: The basic rule; these are its exceptions and harder cases.
The causative construction is why fait stays invariable before an infinitive.
With verbs of perception the participle agrees if the preceding object performs the infinitive: les enfants que j'ai entendus chanter.
En as an object pronoun is the main source of the no-agreement case.
Traditionally laissé agrees when the preceding object performs the infinitive (je les ai laissés partir); the 1990 reform also allows it to stay invariable, like fait.

examples.sentence: Des cerises ? J'en ai mangé beaucoup.
examples.translation: Cherries? I ate a lot of them.

examples.sentence: Voici la maison qu'il a fait construire.
examples.translation: Here is the house he had built.

examples.sentence: Ce sont les musiciens que j'ai entendus jouer.
examples.translation: Those are the musicians I heard playing.

examples.sentence: Je regrette les vingt euros que ce livre m'a coûté.
examples.translation: I regret the twenty euros this book cost me.

constructs.name: prépositions de lieu
constructs.description: Prepositions and prepositional phrases locating something in space.

card.formation: Simple prepositions (à, dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, entre, chez, vers) are placed before a noun. Compound ones end in de (près de, loin de, à côté de, en face de, au-dessus de, au milieu de), which contracts with le and les to du and des.
card.use: They say where something is or where it goes. Dans means inside an enclosed space, à marks a point or a place in general, sur and sous mean on and under, and chez means at someone's home or business.
pitfalls: Forgetting de in compound prepositions: près de la gare, not près la gare.
Not contracting de + le: à côté du cinéma, not à côté de le cinéma.
Using à for a person's home: je vais chez Paul, not à Paul.
Confusing devant (in front of) and en face de (opposite, facing).
Translating English in as dans everywhere: à Paris, à la maison, à l'école.

contrasts.note: Before towns, countries and regions the choice of à, en, au, aux follows special rules.
À and de merge with le and les (au, aux, du, des) after many place prepositions.
Y replaces a place phrase introduced by à, dans, sur and similar.
Several of the same words (à, dans, vers, entre) also locate events in time, with different rules.

examples.sentence: Le chat dort sous la table.
examples.translation: The cat is sleeping under the table.

examples.sentence: J'habite près de la gare.
examples.translation: I live near the station.

examples.sentence: Ce soir, on mange chez mes parents.
examples.translation: Tonight we're eating at my parents' place.

examples.sentence: La pharmacie est à côté du cinéma.
examples.translation: The pharmacy is next to the cinema.

constructs.name: prépositions devant les noms géographiques
constructs.description: Choice of preposition before names of cities, countries and regions.

card.formation: For location and destination, use à before cities, en before feminine countries and before masculine countries starting with a vowel, au before other masculine countries, and aux before plural countries. For origin, use de (d') before cities and feminine countries, du before masculine countries and des before plural ones.
card.use: These forms answer where someone is, where they go and where they come from, with the same preposition for being in and going to. Countries ending in -e are usually feminine (la France, l'Italie), with exceptions such as le Mexique and le Cambodge.
pitfalls: Using à before countries: en France, au Japon, not à France.
Using au before masculine countries starting with a vowel: en Iran, en Irak.
Forgetting that le Mexique and le Cambodge are masculine: au Mexique.
Forgetting the article of city names that have one: au Havre, au Caire.
Using de la before feminine countries for origin: je viens de France, not de la France.

contrasts.note: General place prepositions work with any noun; this entry is specific to proper names of places.
Au, aux, du and des here are contracted articles, since country names take an article.
Y replaces à Paris or en France: j'y vais.
Country names take a definite article as subjects or objects (j'aime la France), which disappears after en and de.

examples.sentence: J'habite à Lyon depuis deux ans.
examples.translation: I've been living in Lyon for two years.

examples.sentence: Cet été, nous allons en Italie.
examples.translation: This summer we are going to Italy.

examples.sentence: Mon collègue travaille au Canada.
examples.translation: My colleague works in Canada.

examples.sentence: Elle vient des États-Unis.
examples.translation: She comes from the United States.

constructs.name: prépositions de temps
constructs.description: Prepositions situating an event in time: hours, dates, months, years.

card.formation: Use à for clock times (à huit heures), en for months, years and most seasons (en mai or au mois de mai, en 2020, en hiver, but au printemps), and le with no preposition before a date (le 3 mai). Other common prepositions are vers (around), avant, après, jusqu'à (until) and dès (from, as early as).
card.use: They place an event at a point in time or relative to another time. Days of the week take no preposition: lundi means this coming or past Monday, and le lundi means every Monday.
pitfalls: Adding a preposition before a date or day: le 14 juillet, lundi, not en lundi or sur lundi.
Saying en printemps instead of au printemps.
Confusing lundi (one Monday) with le lundi (every Monday).
Forgetting à in jusqu'à: jusqu'à midi.
Translating in the morning as dans le matin; French says le matin.

contrasts.note: Duration words (depuis, pendant, dans, en, il y a) measure how long or how far away, not when.
Some prepositions (à, dans, vers) are shared with place, but their rules differ.
Connectors like d'abord and ensuite order events in a text rather than giving a time.
Time clauses with quand or après que use a whole clause instead of a preposition + noun.

examples.sentence: Le film commence à neuf heures.
examples.translation: The film starts at nine o'clock.

examples.sentence: Je suis né en 1995.
examples.translation: I was born in 1995.

examples.sentence: On part en vacances au printemps.
examples.translation: We go on holiday in spring.

examples.sentence: Je travaille jusqu'à six heures.
examples.translation: I work until six o'clock.

constructs.name: expression de la durée
aliases: depuis, il y a, pendant, dans
constructs.description: Prepositions and expressions for duration and the time elapsed since or until an event.

card.formation: Depuis + duration or date goes with the present for an action still going on; il y a + duration goes with a past tense to mean ago. Pendant + duration gives the length of an action, dans + duration a point in the future counted from now, en + duration the time needed to finish, and pour + duration a planned period after verbs like partir. Il y a ... que and ça fait ... que mean the same as depuis.
card.use: These expressions answer how long, since when and how long ago. The choice depends on whether the action is still going on, finished, or still to come.
pitfalls: Using a past tense with depuis for an ongoing action: j'habite ici depuis deux ans, not j'ai habité.
Translating for as depuis for a finished action: j'ai dormi pendant huit heures.
Confusing dans (in two days, from now) with en (in two days, time taken).
Confusing il y a (ago) with depuis (since or for).
Using pendant with partir for a planned stay; French prefers pour une semaine.

contrasts.note: Time prepositions name a point in time (à midi, en mai); these measure a length or distance in time.
Il y a also means there is or there are; followed by a duration with a past tense it means ago.
The present with depuis expresses an action begun in the past and still continuing.
The passé composé goes with il y a and pendant for completed actions.

examples.sentence: J'apprends le français depuis trois ans.
examples.translation: I have been learning French for three years.

examples.sentence: Je l'ai vu il y a une semaine.
examples.translation: I saw him a week ago.

examples.sentence: Nous avons marché pendant deux heures.
examples.translation: We walked for two hours.

examples.sentence: Le train part dans dix minutes.
examples.translation: The train leaves in ten minutes.

constructs.name: verbe + préposition + nom
constructs.description: Verbs whose complement is introduced by a preposition, mainly à or de.

card.formation: Some verbs take their complement through a preposition, usually à (parler à, penser à, téléphoner à, répondre à) or de (parler de, avoir besoin de, s'occuper de). The preposition contracts with le and les (au, aux, du, des).
card.use: The preposition belongs to the verb and must be learned with it; it often differs from English. Some verbs change meaning with the preposition, such as jouer à (a game or sport) and jouer de (an instrument).
pitfalls: Adding a preposition after verbs that are direct in French: écouter la radio, regarder la télé, chercher ses clés, attendre le bus.
Leaving out the preposition after verbs that need it: téléphoner à sa mère, répondre à une question.
Forgetting contraction: je pense au voyage, not à le voyage.
Confusing jouer au tennis and jouer du piano.
Using lui or leur for things: for things, y or en replaces the phrase.

contrasts.note: Many of the same verbs take à or de before an infinitive instead of a noun.
Verbs followed by de + infinitive; the noun construction does not always use the same preposition.
Lui and leur replace à + person after these verbs.
Y replaces à + thing and en replaces de + thing after these verbs.
Adjectives, not verbs, can also require a preposition before a noun (fier de).

examples.sentence: Je téléphone à ma mère tous les soirs.
examples.translation: I phone my mother every evening.

examples.sentence: J'ai besoin d'un stylo.
examples.translation: I need a pen.

examples.sentence: Elle joue du piano depuis l'enfance.
examples.translation: She has played the piano since childhood.

examples.sentence: Nous parlons de nos vacances.
examples.translation: We're talking about our holidays.

constructs.name: adjectif + préposition + nom
constructs.description: Adjectives followed by a preposition and a noun.

card.formation: Some adjectives take a complement introduced by a fixed preposition: de (content de, fier de, plein de, différent de, responsable de), à (fidèle à, prêt à, semblable à), en (fort en, bon en, nul en), or others (gentil avec, intéressé par). The preposition contracts with le and les.
card.use: The complement says what the quality relates to. The preposition depends on the adjective and must be learned with it.
pitfalls: Translating the English preposition: différent de, not différent que; fier de, not fier sur.
Using à for school subjects: bon en maths, not bon à maths.
Forgetting contraction: content du résultat.
Saying intéressé dans instead of intéressé par.
Forgetting that plein de is followed by a noun without article: plein d'eau.

contrasts.note: The same adjectives can be followed by à or de + infinitive instead of a noun (content de partir).
There a verb, not an adjective, requires the preposition.
En replaces de + thing after these adjectives too: j'en suis fier.
There de or à links two nouns, not an adjective and a noun.

examples.sentence: Je suis très content de mon travail.
examples.translation: I am very happy with my work.

examples.sentence: Ma fille est forte en maths.
examples.translation: My daughter is good at maths.

examples.sentence: Ce pays est différent du mien.
examples.translation: This country is different from mine.

examples.sentence: Elle est gentille avec les enfants.
examples.translation: She is kind to the children.

constructs.name: complément du nom
constructs.description: A noun followed by de or à and another noun to specify it.

card.formation: A noun is followed by de and a second noun that specifies it: owner, content, topic or type (la voiture de Paul, un livre de cuisine). À + noun gives purpose or a characteristic feature (une tasse à café, une glace à la vanille), and en or de gives material (une table en bois). The second noun often has no article when it names a type rather than a specific thing.
card.use: It is French's main way of combining nouns, where English uses 's or puts one noun before another. The main noun comes first and the specifying noun second.
pitfalls: Keeping the English word order: le livre de Paul, not Paul livre.
Confusing une tasse à café (a coffee cup) and une tasse de café (a cup of coffee).
Adding an article for a type: un professeur de français, not de le français.
Not contracting with a specific noun: la voiture du voisin.
Using a possessive 's construction, which does not exist in French.

contrasts.note: De + le becomes du when the second noun is specific (le bureau du directeur).
After a quantity word (un kilo de, beaucoup de), de measures an amount rather than specifying a noun.
There the preposition follows an adjective, not a noun.
Dont can replace de + noun in a relative clause (le livre dont la couverture est rouge).

examples.sentence: C'est la voiture de mon frère.
examples.translation: It's my brother's car.

examples.sentence: J'ai acheté un livre de cuisine.
examples.translation: I bought a cookbook.

examples.sentence: Je voudrais une glace à la fraise.
examples.translation: I would like a strawberry ice cream.

examples.sentence: Nous avons une table en bois.
examples.translation: We have a wooden table.

constructs.name: négation ne ... pas
constructs.description: Basic negation around the conjugated verb.

card.formation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and pas after it; ne becomes n' before a vowel or mute h. In compound tenses the two parts surround the auxiliary (je n'ai pas mangé), and object pronouns stay between ne and the verb (je ne le vois pas).
card.use: It is the basic way to make a verb negative. In everyday speech ne is very often dropped (je sais pas), but it is kept in writing and careful speech.
pitfalls: Putting pas after the participle: je n'ai pas vu, not je n'ai vu pas.
Putting ne after an object pronoun: je ne la connais pas, not je la ne connais pas.
Forgetting that un, une, des and partitives become de after pas: je n'ai pas de voiture.
Dropping ne in writing.
Forgetting the elision: il n'aime pas, not il ne aime pas.

contrasts.note: After ne ... pas, indefinite and partitive articles become de, except after être.
Before an infinitive, ne pas stay together in front of the verb.
Ne ... plus means no longer and is built the same way.
Ne ... jamais means never and is built the same way.
Pas or non can be used alone, without ne and without a verb.

examples.sentence: Je ne parle pas allemand.
examples.translation: I don't speak German.

examples.sentence: Il n'aime pas le poisson.
examples.translation: He doesn't like fish.

examples.sentence: Nous n'avons pas fini.
examples.translation: We haven't finished.

examples.sentence: Je ne le connais pas.
examples.translation: I don't know him.

constructs.name: négation sans verbe
constructs.description: Pas or non used alone or before a word, without a verb.

card.formation: Pas is placed before or after a word without a verb or ne (pas moi, pas encore, pas du tout, pas de problème). Non is used alone as an answer or before a phrase (non merci), and moi non plus answers a negative statement.
card.use: It gives short negative answers and comments, very common in speech. Non answers a question by itself, while pas negates one element instead of a whole clause.
pitfalls: Answering a negative statement with moi aussi instead of moi non plus.
Adding ne when there is no verb: pas moi, not ne pas moi.
Using non where pas is needed before a word: pas encore, not non encore.
Answering a negative question with oui instead of si to contradict it.

contrasts.note: The full negation needs a verb and both parts ne and pas.
Si is the positive counterpart of non when contradicting a negative question.
Verbless sentences in general; this entry is the negative short form.
Short negative answers often use a stressed pronoun: pas moi, lui non plus.

examples.sentence: Tu veux du café ? Non merci.
examples.translation: Do you want some coffee? No thanks.

examples.sentence: Qui veut sortir ? Pas moi !
examples.translation: Who wants to go out? Not me!

examples.sentence: Je n'aime pas le froid. Moi non plus.
examples.translation: I don't like the cold. Me neither.

examples.sentence: Tu as fini ? Pas encore.
examples.translation: Have you finished? Not yet.

constructs.name: ne ... jamais
constructs.description: Negation meaning never.

card.formation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and jamais after it, like ne ... pas; in compound tenses jamais comes before the participle (je n'ai jamais vu). Jamais can also stand alone as an answer or start the sentence for emphasis.
card.use: It means never or not ever. It replaces pas, and like pas it turns un, une, des and partitives into de.
pitfalls: Adding pas: je ne fume jamais, not je ne fume pas jamais.
Placing jamais after the participle: je n'ai jamais vu, not je n'ai vu jamais.
Keeping the article: je ne mange jamais de viande.
Forgetting that jamais without ne can mean ever in questions and after si (si jamais tu viens).
Translating never ... again as ne ... jamais; French says ne ... plus jamais.

contrasts.note: Ne ... plus means something has stopped; ne ... jamais means it never happens at all.
Same structure; jamais replaces pas and adds the meaning never.
Jamais can combine with plus, rien or personne in one clause.
Jamais, like pas, turns indefinite and partitive articles into de.

examples.sentence: Je ne bois jamais de café le soir.
examples.translation: I never drink coffee in the evening.

examples.sentence: Il n'a jamais vu la mer.
examples.translation: He has never seen the sea.

examples.sentence: Elle n'est jamais en retard.
examples.translation: She is never late.

constructs.name: ne ... plus
constructs.description: Negation meaning no longer.

card.formation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and plus after it, like ne ... pas; in compound tenses plus comes before the participle. In this negation the s of plus is not pronounced.
card.use: It says that something that used to be true has stopped: no longer, not anymore, no more. Like pas, it turns un, une, des and partitives into de.
pitfalls: Adding pas: je ne fume plus, not je ne fume pas plus.
Confusing ne ... plus (no longer) with non plus (neither).
Pronouncing the s, which makes it sound like the comparative plus.
Keeping the article: il n'y a plus de pain.
Dropping ne in writing, which makes plus ambiguous (j'en veux plus).

contrasts.note: Ne ... jamais means never at any time; ne ... plus means no longer, implying it was true before.
Plus without ne means more; with ne it is a negation, and its s is silent.
Moi non plus (me neither) is a separate short negative answer.
Plus combines with jamais, rien and personne: je ne vois plus personne.

examples.sentence: Je ne fume plus depuis un an.
examples.translation: I haven't smoked for a year.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a plus de lait.
examples.translation: There's no more milk.

examples.sentence: Elle n'habite plus à Paris.
examples.translation: She doesn't live in Paris anymore.

constructs.name: pronoms négatifs (rien, personne)
constructs.description: Negative pronouns meaning nothing and nobody, as object or as subject.

card.formation: As objects, rien and personne replace pas in the negation: je ne vois rien, je ne vois personne. In compound tenses rien goes before the participle (je n'ai rien vu) but personne goes after it (je n'ai vu personne). As subjects they come first and are followed by ne without pas: rien ne marche, personne n'est venu.
card.use: Rien means nothing or not anything, personne means nobody or not anyone. Both can stand alone as answers, and take de before an adjective (rien de grave, personne d'intéressant).
pitfalls: Adding pas: personne n'est venu, not personne n'est pas venu.
Putting personne before the participle: je n'ai vu personne, not je n'ai personne vu.
Forgetting ne as a subject: rien ne change.
Leaving out de before an adjective: rien de nouveau, not rien nouveau.
Confusing the pronoun personne (nobody, masculine) with the noun une personne (a person).

contrasts.note: Quelque chose and quelqu'un are the positive counterparts of rien and personne.
Aucun means not a single one of a known set and agrees with a noun; rien and personne are general.
Rien and personne take the place of pas; they are not added to it.
Rien and personne combine with plus and jamais: je ne dis plus rien.
Before an infinitive ne rien stays together, but personne follows the infinitive: ne voir personne.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai rien compris.
examples.translation: I didn't understand anything.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a personne dans la salle.
examples.translation: There's nobody in the room.

examples.sentence: Personne n'a répondu.
examples.translation: Nobody answered.

examples.sentence: Rien ne marche aujourd'hui !
examples.translation: Nothing works today!

constructs.name: négation de l'infinitif
constructs.description: Both parts of the negation placed together before an infinitive.

card.formation: Before an infinitive both parts of the negation stand together in front of it: ne pas, ne plus, ne jamais, ne rien + infinitive. Object pronouns come between the negation and the infinitive (ne pas le dire). Personne, aucun, nulle part and que still follow the infinitive (ne voir personne).
card.use: It negates an infinitive after verbs and prepositions (décider de ne pas partir, pour ne pas oublier) and in written instructions and signs (ne pas fumer).
pitfalls: Splitting the negation around the infinitive: de ne pas venir, not de ne venir pas.
Negating the conjugated verb when the infinitive is meant: il a décidé de ne pas venir differs from il n'a pas décidé de venir.
Placing the object pronoun before ne pas: pour ne pas le perdre, not pour le ne pas perdre.
Moving personne before the infinitive: ne voir personne, not ne personne voir.

contrasts.note: With a conjugated verb the negation surrounds the verb; with an infinitive it precedes it.
The negative imperative surrounds the verb (ne fume pas), while instructions in the infinitive group the negation before it (ne pas fumer).
Infinitives used as instructions are often negated this way.
After pour, afin de, sans the infinitive is often negated: pour ne pas rater le train.

examples.sentence: Ne pas fumer dans le train.
examples.translation: No smoking on the train.

examples.sentence: J'ai décidé de ne plus boire de café.
examples.translation: I've decided not to drink coffee anymore.

examples.sentence: Je pars tôt pour ne pas rater le bus.
examples.translation: I'm leaving early so as not to miss the bus.

examples.sentence: Il préfère ne rien dire.
examples.translation: He prefers not to say anything.

constructs.name: ne ... que (restriction)
constructs.description: Restriction meaning only, which is not a true negation.

card.formation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and que directly before the element it restricts, which can be an object, a time, a place or another complement. In compound tenses que usually comes after the participle (je n'ai bu que de l'eau).
card.use: It means only and has the same meaning as seulement. It is not a real negation, so articles stay unchanged: il ne mange que des légumes.
pitfalls: Changing the article to de: je ne bois que du thé, not que de thé.
Treating it as negative in meaning: il n'a que dix euros means he has only ten euros.
Placing que in the wrong spot, which changes what is restricted.
Adding pas: ne ... pas que means not only, a different meaning.

contrasts.note: Ne ... pas negates; ne ... que restricts and keeps the sentence positive.
Ne pas ... que means not only, the opposite of the restriction.
The article change to de applies after true negations, not after ne ... que.
Seulement expresses the same restriction as an adverb, without ne.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai que dix euros.
examples.translation: I only have ten euros.

examples.sentence: Il ne mange que des légumes.
examples.translation: He only eats vegetables.

examples.sentence: Le magasin n'ouvre que le matin.
examples.translation: The shop only opens in the morning.

constructs.name: ne ... aucun
constructs.description: Negative determiner or pronoun meaning not a single one.

card.formation: Aucun (aucune) is a determiner before a noun or a pronoun replacing one, used with ne and without pas. It agrees in gender with the noun and is almost always singular. As a subject it comes first (aucun élève n'est venu); as an object pronoun it goes with en (je n'en ai aucun).
card.use: It means not a single one, not any or none, and is stronger than pas de. It is often used for one member of a known group.
pitfalls: Adding pas: je n'ai aucune idée, not je n'ai pas aucune idée.
Using the plural: aucun problème, not aucuns problèmes.
Forgetting the agreement: aucune question.
Forgetting en with the pronoun: je n'en ai aucun.
Forgetting ne with aucun as subject: aucun train ne part.

contrasts.note: Pas de is the neutral negation of a noun; aucun stresses not even one.
Rien and personne are general pronouns; aucun refers to a noun and agrees with it.
Ni ... ni negates two named items; aucun negates every member of a set.
Other indefinite determiners such as chaque or plusieurs are positive.
Aucun as a pronoun object is used with en, like other quantity pronouns.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai aucune idée.
examples.translation: I have no idea.

examples.sentence: Aucun train ne part ce soir.
examples.translation: No trains are leaving tonight.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a aucun problème.
examples.translation: There's no problem at all.

examples.sentence: Des amis ? Il n'en a aucun.
examples.translation: Friends? He doesn't have any.

constructs.name: ne ... ni ... ni
constructs.description: Negation of two or more coordinated elements.

card.formation: Ne goes before the verb and ni before each negated element, without pas: je n'aime ni le thé ni le café. Indefinite and partitive articles are dropped after ni (je ne bois ni thé ni café), while definite articles stay. As a subject, ni ... ni comes first with ne before the verb, which is usually plural.
card.use: It negates two or more coordinated elements: neither ... nor. It is the negative counterpart of et or ou.
pitfalls: Adding pas: je n'ai ni frère ni sœur.
Keeping un or des: il n'a ni voiture ni vélo.
Forgetting ne: ni Paul ni Marie ne sont venus.
Translating or after a negative with ou: je ne parle ni anglais ni allemand.

contrasts.note: Et and ou join elements positively; ni joins them in a negative clause.
Aucun negates every member of a set; ni ... ni negates named elements one by one.
Ne ... pas negates the whole verb; ni ... ni negates selected elements and replaces pas.
Moi non plus or ni moi express a short negative answer without a full clause.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai ni frère ni sœur.
examples.translation: I have neither a brother nor a sister.

examples.sentence: Il n'aime ni le thé ni le café.
examples.form: n'aime ni le thé ni le café
examples.translation: He likes neither tea nor coffee.

examples.sentence: Ni Paul ni Léa ne sont venus.
examples.form: Ni Paul ni Léa ne sont venus
examples.translation: Neither Paul nor Léa came.

constructs.name: ne ... nulle part
constructs.description: Negation meaning nowhere.

card.formation: Ne goes before the conjugated verb and nulle part after the verb, without pas. In compound tenses and with infinitives nulle part comes after the participle or infinitive: je ne l'ai trouvé nulle part.
card.use: It means nowhere or not anywhere. It can also stand alone as an answer to où.
pitfalls: Placing nulle part before the participle: je ne l'ai vu nulle part, not je ne l'ai nulle part vu.
Adding pas: je ne vais nulle part.
Writing nul part; part is a feminine noun, so nulle.
Using pas quelque part for nowhere.

contrasts.note: Like personne, nulle part follows the participle; rien precedes it.
Place prepositions locate positively; nulle part denies any place.
Jamais negates time (never); nulle part negates place (nowhere).
Before an infinitive ne stays in front, but nulle part follows: n'aller nulle part.

examples.sentence: Je ne trouve mes lunettes nulle part.
examples.form: ne trouve mes lunettes nulle part
examples.translation: I can't find my glasses anywhere.

examples.sentence: Ce week-end, on ne va nulle part.
examples.translation: This weekend we're not going anywhere.

examples.sentence: Je ne l'ai vu nulle part.
examples.translation: I haven't seen him anywhere.

constructs.name: combinaison de négations
constructs.description: Combining several negative words in one clause, and the negative restriction ne pas ... que.

card.formation: Several negative words can share one ne, without pas: ne ... plus jamais, ne ... plus rien, ne ... jamais personne, ne ... plus que. Plus usually comes before jamais, and both come before rien or personne. Ne pas ... que is a separate pattern meaning not only.
card.use: Combined negations stack meanings (no longer anything, never again anyone) without cancelling each other. Ne pas ... que denies a restriction: il n'y a pas que le travail dans la vie.
pitfalls: Reading two negatives as a positive: je ne vois plus personne means I don't see anyone anymore.
Adding pas to the combination: je ne dis plus rien, not je ne dis pas plus rien.
Putting the words in the wrong order: plus jamais rien, not rien jamais plus.
Confusing ne ... que (only) and ne pas ... que (not only).
Translating never again as ne ... jamais instead of ne ... plus jamais.

contrasts.note: Ne ... que restricts (only); with pas added it means not only.
The single negation; combined with jamais or rien it adds meanings.
Rien and personne can be added after plus or jamais in the same clause.
Jamais alone means never; plus jamais means never again.

examples.sentence: Je ne dirai plus jamais rien.
examples.translation: I'll never say anything again.

examples.sentence: Il ne voit plus personne.
examples.translation: He doesn't see anyone anymore.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a pas que l'argent dans la vie.
examples.translation: There's more to life than money.

examples.sentence: On ne fait jamais rien le dimanche.
examples.translation: We never do anything on Sundays.

constructs.name: ne explétif
constructs.description: A ne without negative meaning in formal style after expressions of fear, some conjunctions and comparisons.

card.formation: A single ne, without pas or another negative word, is placed before the verb of a subordinate clause, mostly in the subjunctive. It appears after verbs of fear (avoir peur que, craindre que), after certain conjunctions (avant que, à moins que, de peur que, de crainte que) and after comparisons of inequality (plus ... que je ne pensais).
card.use: It adds no negative meaning; the clause is positive. It marks formal or written style and is optional, and is usually left out in everyday speech.
pitfalls: Reading it as a negation: j'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve means I'm afraid it will rain.
Adding pas when no negation is meant.
Using it after conjunctions that do not take it, such as bien que or pour que.
Thinking it is required; it is always optional.
Adding ne after sans que, which most grammars advise against.

contrasts.note: A real negation needs pas or another negative word; ne alone in these contexts negates nothing.
Clauses of fear are the most common setting for the expletive ne.
After avant que the subjunctive is required and the ne is optional.
After a comparison of inequality followed by a clause, formal French can add ne.
Both are formal, but guère and point are true negations.

examples.sentence: J'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve demain.
examples.translation: I'm afraid it will rain tomorrow.

examples.sentence: Partons avant qu'il ne soit trop tard.
examples.translation: Let's leave before it's too late.

examples.sentence: C'est plus difficile que je ne le pensais.
examples.translation: It's harder than I thought.

constructs.name: négations littéraires (ne ... guère, ne ... point)
constructs.description: Literary negations meaning hardly or not at all.

card.formation: Guère and point replace pas after the conjugated verb, with ne before it, exactly like ne ... pas. Like pas, they turn indefinite and partitive articles into de.
card.use: Ne ... guère means hardly, scarcely or not much; ne ... point is a literary or old-fashioned equivalent of ne ... pas, sometimes felt as stronger. Both are found mainly in literature and formal writing.
pitfalls: Reading guère as a full negation: il ne mange guère means he eats very little.
Adding pas: je ne le crois point.
Using them in everyday speech, where they sound old-fashioned or ironic.
Confusing point (not) with the noun le point (point, dot).

contrasts.note: Ne ... point means the same as ne ... pas in a literary register.
Peu (little) expresses the same idea as ne ... guère in neutral style.
The expletive ne is also formal but has no negative meaning.
Ne ... guère plus means hardly any more, combining both.

examples.sentence: Il ne mange guère le soir.
examples.translation: He hardly eats in the evening.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai guère de temps.
examples.translation: I have hardly any time.

examples.sentence: Je ne le crois point.
examples.translation: I do not believe it at all.

constructs.name: interrogation par intonation
constructs.description: Yes/no question formed with rising intonation and statement word order.

card.formation: The sentence keeps the word order of a statement, and the voice rises at the end; in writing it ends with a question mark. A question word can be added at the end in informal speech (tu vas où ?).
card.use: It is the most common way to ask yes/no questions in everyday spoken French. It is informal and less used in careful writing.
pitfalls: Not raising the voice, so the question sounds like a statement.
Using it in formal letters, where est-ce que or inversion fits better.
Placing que at the end: informal speech uses quoi (tu fais quoi ?), never que.
Mixing intonation with inversion: tu viens ? or viens-tu ?, not viens-tu tu ?.

contrasts.note: Est-ce que marks the question explicitly at the start and suits neutral style.
Inversion puts the verb before the pronoun and is formal.
Question words can be added to intonation questions, often at the end in speech.
Exclamations also use intonation, but falling or emphatic, not rising.

examples.sentence: Tu viens avec nous ?
examples.translation: Are you coming with us?

examples.sentence: Vous avez des enfants ?
examples.translation: Do you have children?

examples.sentence: Il fait beau aujourd'hui ?
examples.translation: Is the weather nice today?

constructs.name: interrogation avec est-ce que
constructs.description: Questions formed with est-ce que, alone or after a question word.

card.formation: Est-ce que is placed at the start of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question; it becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel. After a question word it gives open questions (où est-ce que tu habites ?). The subject and verb keep statement order.
card.use: It is the neutral way of asking questions, suitable in speech and writing. It makes the question clear from the first words without inverting.
pitfalls: Inverting after est-ce que: est-ce que tu viens ?, not est-ce que viens-tu ?.
Forgetting the elision: est-ce qu'il pleut ?.
Using que instead of qu'est-ce que for what: qu'est-ce que tu fais ?.
Thinking est-ce que has a meaning of its own; it only marks the question.

contrasts.note: Intonation marks the question only with the voice; est-ce que marks it with words.
Inversion is the formal alternative; est-ce que avoids changing word order.
Qu'est-ce que, qui est-ce qui and others combine a pronoun with est-ce que or est-ce qui.
In indirect questions est-ce que disappears and si is used: je me demande s'il vient.

examples.sentence: Est-ce que tu as faim ?
examples.translation: Are you hungry?

examples.sentence: Est-ce qu'il pleut encore ?
examples.translation: Is it still raining?

examples.sentence: Où est-ce que vous habitez ?
examples.translation: Where do you live?

examples.sentence: Quand est-ce que le train part ?
examples.translation: When does the train leave?

constructs.name: mots interrogatifs
aliases: qui, où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien
constructs.description: Question words for person, place, time, manner, reason and quantity, placed first or last.

card.formation: Question words are qui (who), que or quoi (what), où (where), quand (when), comment (how), pourquoi (why) and combien (de) (how much, how many). They usually come first, followed by est-ce que or inversion, or last in informal speech with statement order (tu pars quand ?).
card.use: They ask open questions about a person, thing, place, time, manner, reason or quantity. The question style (final position, est-ce que, inversion) shows the register.
pitfalls: Using que at the end or without inversion: tu fais quoi ? or que fais-tu ?, not tu fais que ?.
Forgetting de after combien before a noun: combien de temps.
Answering pourquoi with pour que instead of parce que.
Confusing qui (who) with que (what).
Placing comment at the start without est-ce que or inversion in writing.

contrasts.note: Quel goes with a noun (quel livre ?); mots interrogatifs stand alone.
Long forms such as qu'est-ce qui distinguish subject and object explicitly.
Question words can be preceded by a preposition: d'où, avec qui, à quoi.
Question words also introduce indirect questions, without inversion: je ne sais pas où il habite.
Qui and où also work as relative pronouns linking clauses, not asking.

examples.sentence: Où habites-tu ?
examples.translation: Where do you live?

examples.sentence: Pourquoi est-ce que tu ris ?
examples.translation: Why are you laughing?

examples.sentence: Tu pars quand ?
examples.translation: When are you leaving?

examples.sentence: Combien de frères as-tu ?
examples.translation: How many brothers do you have?

constructs.name: déterminant interrogatif quel
constructs.description: Quel agreeing with the noun to ask which or what.

card.formation: Quel agrees in gender and number with its noun: quel, quelle, quels, quelles, all pronounced the same. It stands directly before the noun (quel livre ?) or before être followed by the noun (quelle est ton adresse ?).
card.use: It asks which or what about a noun, choosing from possibilities or asking for information such as a name, time or age. The same forms also introduce exclamations (quelle belle journée !).
pitfalls: Forgetting the agreement in writing: quelle heure, quels films.
Saying qu'est-ce que est ton nom ? instead of quel est ton nom ?.
Using quel alone as a pronoun: which one is lequel, not quel.
Forgetting the preposition before it: à quelle heure, not quelle heure tu pars.

contrasts.note: Lequel replaces the noun (lequel veux-tu ?); quel needs it.
Que, qui and other question words stand alone, without a noun.
Quel + noun can also be an exclamation, with no question.
Quel often follows a preposition: à quelle heure, dans quel quartier.

examples.sentence: Quelle heure est-il ?
examples.translation: What time is it?

examples.sentence: Quel est ton numéro de téléphone ?
examples.translation: What is your phone number?

examples.sentence: Quels films aimes-tu ?
examples.translation: Which films do you like?

examples.sentence: Tu prends quelle couleur ?
examples.translation: Which colour are you taking?

constructs.name: qui est-ce et qu'est-ce que c'est
aliases: who is it, what is it
constructs.description: Fixed questions to identify a person or a thing.

card.formation: Qui est-ce ? asks about a person and qu'est-ce que c'est ? about a thing; both are fixed forms. The usual answer is c'est + noun or name. Informal speech uses c'est qui ? and c'est quoi ?.
card.use: These questions identify someone or something that is seen, heard or mentioned. They are among the first questions learners meet.
pitfalls: Using qu'est-ce que c'est for a person: qui est-ce ? for people.
Answering with il est + noun instead of c'est: c'est mon frère.
Writing qu'est-ce que c'est without hyphen or apostrophe.
Using c'est quoi ? in formal contexts.

contrasts.note: C'est and voici present or identify; these questions ask for that identification.
Qu'est-ce que and qui est-ce que are general question pronouns; these two are fixed identification questions.
Quel est ...? asks for specific information (name, address), not for identification.
Qui and quoi alone are the basic question words behind these forms.

examples.sentence: Qui est-ce ? C'est ma voisine.
examples.translation: Who is it? It's my neighbour.

examples.sentence: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? C'est un cadeau.
examples.translation: What is it? It's a present.

examples.sentence: C'est qui, sur la photo ?
examples.translation: Who is that in the photo?

constructs.name: interrogation par inversion
constructs.description: Question formed by inverting subject pronoun and verb, typical of formal style.

card.formation: The subject pronoun is placed after the verb and joined to it by a hyphen (parlez-vous ?); in compound tenses the auxiliary is inverted (as-tu mangé ?). A -t- is inserted between a verb ending in a vowel and il, elle or on (a-t-il, parle-t-elle). Question words come first (où habitez-vous ?).
card.use: It is used in formal speech, writing and some fixed questions (quelle heure est-il ?). With je it is avoided except for a few verbs (puis-je, suis-je, ai-je).
pitfalls: Forgetting the -t-: a-t-il, not a-il.
Inverting the participle instead of the auxiliary: avez-vous fini ?, not finissez-vous ?.
Inverting with a noun subject directly: Paul vient-il ?, not vient Paul ? for yes/no questions.
Inverting with je for most verbs: est-ce que je peux is usual, puis-je is formal.
Forgetting the hyphen in writing.

contrasts.note: With a noun subject the noun stays first and a pronoun is inverted (Marie vient-elle ?).
Est-ce que is the neutral alternative without changing word order.
Intonation questions keep statement order and are informal.
After peut-être, ainsi and similar, inversion appears in statements, not questions.

examples.sentence: Parlez-vous anglais ?
examples.translation: Do you speak English?

examples.sentence: Où habite-t-elle ?
examples.translation: Where does she live?

examples.sentence: As-tu bien dormi ?
examples.translation: Did you sleep well?

examples.sentence: Quelle heure est-il ?
examples.translation: What time is it?

constructs.name: interrogation par inversion complexe
constructs.description: Question with a noun subject kept first and taken up by a subject pronoun inverted after the verb.

card.formation: The noun subject stays before the verb, and a subject pronoun of the same gender and number is added after the verb with a hyphen: Marie vient-elle ? The rules of simple inversion apply, including -t- and inversion of the auxiliary in compound tenses (tes parents sont-ils partis ?).
card.use: It is the formal way to invert when the subject is a noun or a name, mainly in writing. It is required in yes/no questions and after pourquoi; after other short question words a simple inversion of the noun is also possible (où travaille ton frère ?).
pitfalls: Inverting the noun itself in yes/no questions: Paul est-il là ?, not est Paul là ?.
Choosing a pronoun that does not match the noun: les filles sont-elles là ?.
Forgetting -t-: ton frère arrive-t-il ?.
Using it with que; que requires simple inversion (que veut ton frère ?).

contrasts.note: Simple inversion swaps the verb and a pronoun subject; complex inversion keeps the noun and repeats it as a pronoun.
Dislocation repeats a noun with a pronoun for emphasis in speech; complex inversion is a formal question pattern.
Est-ce que avoids inversion altogether: est-ce que Marie vient ?
The added pronoun copies the noun's gender and number.

examples.sentence: Marie vient-elle ce soir ?
examples.translation: Is Marie coming tonight?

examples.sentence: Pourquoi ton frère est-il en retard ?
examples.translation: Why is your brother late?

examples.sentence: Tes parents ont-ils aimé le film ?
examples.translation: Did your parents like the film?

constructs.name: interrogation avec préposition
constructs.description: Questions where a preposition comes before the question word.

card.formation: When the question is about a prepositional phrase, the preposition comes before the question word at the start: à qui, de quoi, pour qui, chez qui, d'où, à quelle heure. After a preposition, what is quoi, not que.
card.use: It asks about the person, thing, place or time linked to the verb by a preposition. French never leaves the preposition at the end as English does.
pitfalls: Leaving the preposition at the end: à qui tu parles ?, not qui tu parles à ?.
Using que after a preposition: de quoi parles-tu ?, not de que.
Forgetting the preposition the verb requires: à quoi tu penses ?.
Writing de où instead of d'où.

contrasts.note: Simple question words without a preposition: qui, que, où.
Lequel merges with à and de (auquel, duquel) when choosing among known items.
The verb's preposition decides which one appears in the question.
Preposition + qui or lequel also introduce relative clauses (la personne à qui je parle).

examples.sentence: À qui tu écris ?
examples.translation: Who are you writing to?

examples.sentence: De quoi parlez-vous ?
examples.translation: What are you talking about?

examples.sentence: À quelle heure commence le cours ?
examples.translation: What time does the class start?

examples.sentence: Avec qui tu pars en vacances ?
examples.translation: Who are you going on holiday with?

constructs.name: pronoms interrogatifs avec est-ce
constructs.description: Interrogative pronouns reinforced with est-ce qui or est-ce que, distinguishing subject and object.

card.formation: The first part says person or thing (qui for a person, que for a thing), the last part says subject or object (qui for subject, que for object): qui est-ce qui (who, subject), qui est-ce que (whom), qu'est-ce qui (what, subject), qu'est-ce que (what, object).
card.use: These long forms ask about a person or thing while keeping statement word order. Qu'est-ce qui is the usual form for what as the subject (qu'est-ce qui se passe ?).
pitfalls: Using qu'est-ce que for a subject: qu'est-ce qui se passe ?, not qu'est-ce que se passe ?.
Using qu'est-ce que for a person: qui est-ce que tu as vu ?.
Inverting after the long form: qu'est-ce que tu fais ?, not qu'est-ce que fais-tu ?.
Using qu'est-ce que in indirect questions instead of ce que: je sais ce que tu veux.

contrasts.note: The short forms qui and que (with inversion) ask the same questions in fewer words.
Est-ce que alone forms yes/no questions; here it is fused with a question pronoun.
Ce qui and ce que replace qu'est-ce qui and qu'est-ce que in indirect questions.
Qui est-ce ? and qu'est-ce que c'est ? are fixed identification questions.
Indirect questions drop est-ce: dis-moi ce qui se passe.

examples.sentence: Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?
examples.translation: What's happening?

examples.sentence: Qu'est-ce que tu veux manger ?
examples.translation: What do you want to eat?

examples.sentence: Qui est-ce que tu attends ?
examples.translation: Who are you waiting for?

examples.sentence: Qui est-ce qui a pris mon stylo ?
examples.translation: Who took my pen?

constructs.name: réponse si à une question négative
constructs.description: Si used instead of oui to contradict a negative question or statement.

card.formation: Si replaces oui in an answer to a negative question or statement, alone or followed by the positive statement (si, je viens). It can be strengthened as mais si or si si.
card.use: It contradicts a negative question or claim, meaning yes, on the contrary. To agree with the negative, the answer is non.
pitfalls: Answering oui to a negative question: tu ne viens pas ? si, je viens.
Using non to mean yes I am, as in English No, I'm coming.
Using si to answer a positive question, where oui is correct.
Confusing this si with si meaning if or so.

contrasts.note: Non and pas are short negative answers; si is the short positive answer to a negative.
Si also means if and introduces conditions, a different word in use.
Si before an adjective means so (si gentil), unrelated to answering.

examples.sentence: Tu n'as pas faim ? Si, un peu.
examples.translation: Aren't you hungry? Yes, a little.

examples.sentence: Il ne vient pas ce soir ? Mais si !
examples.translation: He's not coming tonight? Yes, he is!

examples.sentence: Tu n'aimes pas le fromage ? Si, beaucoup.
examples.translation: You don't like cheese? Yes, I do, a lot.

constructs.name: pronom interrogatif lequel
constructs.description: Lequel and its forms asking which one among several.

card.formation: Lequel agrees with the noun it stands for: lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles. After à and de the masculine and plural forms contract: auquel, auxquels, auxquelles, duquel, desquels, desquelles (but à laquelle, de laquelle).
card.use: It asks which one or which ones among people or things already mentioned or known. It replaces quel + noun.
pitfalls: Using quel without a noun: lequel préfères-tu ?, not quel préfères-tu ?.
Forgetting the agreement: laquelle for a feminine noun.
Forgetting the contraction: auquel penses-tu ?, not à lequel.
Using lequel when nothing has been mentioned to choose from.

contrasts.note: Quel stands before a noun; lequel replaces the noun.
The same forms serve as relative pronouns after prepositions (la table sur laquelle).
Celui-ci and celle-là are typical answers to lequel questions.
Preposition + lequel merges into auquel or duquel.

examples.sentence: J'ai deux robes. Laquelle préfères-tu ?
examples.translation: I have two dresses. Which one do you prefer?

examples.sentence: Lequel de ces livres est à toi ?
examples.translation: Which of these books is yours?

examples.sentence: Il y a trois cafés. Duquel tu parles ?
examples.translation: There are three cafés. Which one are you talking about?

constructs.name: conjonctions de coordination
constructs.description: Joining words, phrases or clauses with coordinating conjunctions.

card.formation: A coordinating conjunction (et, ou, mais, donc, or, ni, car) is placed between two words, phrases or clauses of the same kind. It does not change the mood or word order of either part.
card.use: Et adds, ou offers a choice, mais contrasts, donc draws a consequence, car gives a reason, ni joins negated elements, and or introduces a new fact in an argument (formal).
pitfalls: Writing ou (or) when où (where) is meant, or the reverse.
Starting a sentence with car; it always follows the clause it explains.
Using ni without ne before the verb.
Putting a comma before et in a simple list, as in English.
Reading or as the noun 'gold' when it links two statements.

contrasts.note: Car coordinates and cannot answer pourquoi or open a sentence; parce que subordinates and can do both.
Donc can also act as an adverb inside the clause (il est donc parti), like the other consequence connectors.
Ni as a conjunction needs ne before the verb and usually repeats before each element.
Mais simply links two contrasting parts; en revanche or par contre set two facts side by side, often across sentences.

examples.sentence: J'aime le thé, mais je préfère le café.
examples.translation: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.

examples.sentence: Tu veux du pain ou des croissants ?
examples.translation: Do you want bread or croissants?

examples.sentence: Je reste à la maison, car il pleut.
examples.translation: I'm staying home, for it's raining.

examples.sentence: Il est malade, donc il ne vient pas.
examples.translation: He is ill, so he isn't coming.

constructs.name: cause (conjonction + indicatif)
constructs.description: Expressing cause with conjunctions followed by the indicative.
