card.formation: A conjunction of cause (parce que, comme, puisque, étant donné que, vu que) introduces a clause with a conjugated verb in the indicative. Que becomes qu' before a vowel.
card.use: Parce que gives a new reason and answers pourquoi; puisque gives a reason the listener already knows or accepts; comme gives the cause first, at the start of the sentence. Étant donné que and vu que present the cause as an established fact, like puisque.
pitfalls: Putting a comme clause of cause after the main clause; it opens the sentence.
Answering pourquoi with puisque or car instead of parce que.
Forgetting the elision: parce qu'il, puisqu'elle.
Using the subjunctive after these conjunctions; they always take the indicative.
Following parce que with a noun instead of a clause; use à cause de + noun.

contrasts.note: À cause de or grâce à are followed by a noun, not by a clause with a verb.
Car also gives a reason but coordinates: it cannot start a sentence or answer a question.
D'autant plus que adds a reason that reinforces one already given.
Non que or ce n'est pas que reject a cause and take the subjunctive.
Donc and alors introduce the result, not the reason.

examples.sentence: Je suis en retard parce que le bus n'est pas venu.
examples.translation: I'm late because the bus didn't come.

examples.sentence: Comme il fait beau, on mange dehors.
examples.translation: As the weather is nice, we're eating outside.

examples.sentence: Puisque tu es là, aide-moi un peu.
examples.translation: Since you're here, help me a bit.

constructs.name: conséquence (connecteurs)
constructs.description: Expressing consequence with adverbs and connectors.

card.formation: An adverb or connector of consequence (donc, alors, c'est pourquoi, par conséquent, du coup) links a result to what was said before. Donc and par conséquent can also sit after the conjugated verb.
card.use: It presents the second fact as the result of the first. Alors and du coup are frequent in speech, par conséquent and c'est pourquoi in writing.
pitfalls: Using du coup in formal writing; it is informal.
Placing donc only at the start; inside the clause it often follows the verb (il est donc parti).
Reading alors as 'then' in time when it means 'so'.
Confusing c'est pourquoi (that's why) with parce que (because).

contrasts.note: Si bien que and de sorte que join the result as a subordinate clause in the same sentence.
Tellement ... que links the result to a degree or quantity in the main clause.
Parce que introduces the cause, the opposite direction.
Bref or en somme sum up an argument rather than stating a direct result.

examples.sentence: Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
examples.translation: It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.

examples.sentence: Le magasin était fermé, alors je suis rentré.
examples.translation: The shop was closed, so I went home.

examples.sentence: Il était malade. C'est pourquoi il n'est pas venu.
examples.translation: He was ill. That's why he didn't come.

examples.sentence: J'ai raté le train, du coup je suis en retard.
examples.translation: I missed the train, so I'm late.

constructs.name: but (préposition + nom ou infinitif)
constructs.description: Expressing purpose with a preposition followed by a noun or an infinitive.

card.formation: Pour, afin de, dans le but de or en vue de is followed by an infinitive; pour and en vue de can also take a noun. The infinitive has the same subject as the main verb.
card.use: It states the purpose or goal of an action. Pour is the everyday choice; afin de and dans le but de are more formal.
pitfalls: Using pour + infinitive when the two subjects differ; then use pour que + subjunctive.
Using à or de alone instead of pour to express purpose.
Translating 'for + -ing' as pour + present participle; French uses the infinitive.
Forgetting de after afin: afin de partir.

contrasts.note: Pour que or afin que + subjunctive are needed when the purpose has a different subject.
Other prepositions (sans, avant de) can also take an infinitive but do not express purpose.
Pour + noun can also mean cause (puni pour son retard); purpose looks forward, cause backward.
The general rule behind the choice: same subject gives an infinitive, different subjects a que + subjunctive clause.

examples.sentence: Je travaille pour gagner ma vie.
examples.translation: I work to earn my living.

examples.sentence: Elle se lève tôt afin de ne pas rater le bus.
examples.translation: She gets up early so as not to miss the bus.

examples.sentence: Il économise pour un nouveau vélo.
examples.translation: He is saving for a new bike.

constructs.name: cause (préposition + nom)
constructs.description: Expressing cause with a preposition followed by a noun.

card.formation: A prepositional phrase of cause (à cause de, grâce à, en raison de, faute de, à force de, par) is followed by a noun or pronoun. De and à contract with le and les: à cause du, grâce aux.
card.use: It names the cause without a full clause. À cause de is neutral or negative, grâce à gives a positive cause, en raison de is formal, faute de means 'for lack of', and à force de stresses repetition.
pitfalls: Using à cause de for a good outcome where grâce à is expected.
Following these prepositions with a clause; use parce que + verb instead.
Forgetting the contraction: à cause du bruit, grâce au soleil.
Adding an article after faute de: faute de temps, not faute du temps.

contrasts.note: Parce que and puisque introduce a clause with a conjugated verb, not a noun.
Malgré + noun gives an obstacle that did not prevent the result, the opposite of a cause.
À cause de + le and grâce à + le contract to du and au.
Pour + noun can express purpose (pour un vélo) as well as cause.

examples.sentence: Le match est annulé à cause de la pluie.
examples.translation: The match is cancelled because of the rain.

examples.sentence: J'ai réussi grâce à ton aide.
examples.translation: I succeeded thanks to your help.

examples.sentence: Le magasin est fermé en raison des travaux.
examples.translation: The shop is closed due to the building work.

constructs.name: proposition complétive à l'indicatif
constructs.description: A que-clause in the indicative as the object of a verb of saying, thinking or knowing.

card.formation: A verb of saying, thinking, knowing or perceiving (dire, penser, croire, savoir, espérer, voir) is followed by que and a clause in the indicative. Que becomes qu' before a vowel and can never be left out.
card.use: It reports a statement, belief or piece of knowledge as a fact. The indicative is used because the speaker presents the content as real.
pitfalls: Leaving out que, as English often leaves out 'that'.
Using the subjunctive after espérer; in the affirmative it takes the indicative.
Keeping the indicative after a negative opinion verb (je ne pense pas que), where the subjunctive is usual.
Writing que il instead of qu'il.

contrasts.note: Verbs of wanting (vouloir que) take the subjunctive, not the indicative.
Penser and croire switch to the subjunctive when negated or inverted in a question.
Covers the full choice of mood after opinion verbs.
Relative que refers back to a noun; completive que follows a verb and introduces its whole object.
Reported speech uses this structure for statements, with changes of pronouns.

examples.sentence: Je pense que tu as raison.
examples.translation: I think you're right.

examples.sentence: Elle dit qu'elle est fatiguée.
examples.translation: She says she is tired.

examples.sentence: J'espère que vous allez bien.
examples.translation: I hope you are well.

constructs.name: hypothèse sur le futur (si + présent)
constructs.description: A si-clause in the present with a main clause in the present, future or imperative.

card.formation: Si + present tense in the condition clause, and the present, future or imperative in the main clause. Si becomes s' only before il and ils.
card.use: It states a real, likely condition and its result, now or in the future.
pitfalls: Putting the future after si: si il fera beau is wrong, use s'il fait beau.
Writing si il instead of s'il; but si elle is never elided.
Confusing conditional si with si meaning 'whether', which can take the future.

contrasts.note: Si + imparfait with the conditional presents the condition as unlikely or imagined.
Si meaning 'whether' after demander or savoir can be followed by the future.
Quand with a future main clause takes the future itself, unlike si.
Même si keeps the same tenses but says the result happens despite the condition.

examples.sentence: S'il fait beau demain, on ira à la plage.
examples.form: S'il fait beau demain, on ira
examples.translation: If the weather is nice tomorrow, we'll go to the beach.

examples.sentence: Si tu as faim, mange une pomme.
examples.translation: If you're hungry, eat an apple.

examples.sentence: Si tu veux, je peux t'aider.
examples.translation: If you want, I can help you.

constructs.name: connecteurs chronologiques
constructs.description: Connectors ordering the steps of a story or a list.

card.formation: Adverbs and phrases such as d'abord, premièrement, ensuite, puis, après, enfin and finalement are placed at the start of each step, usually followed by a comma (except puis).
card.use: They put the events of a story or the steps of a list or instructions in order.
pitfalls: Using enfin only as 'at last'; in a sequence it marks the final step.
Using finalement for the last item of a list when it often means 'in the end, after all'.
Overusing après in writing where ensuite or puis is more natural.
Confusing d'abord (first) with au début (at the beginning).

contrasts.note: Bref, en somme and pour conclure close an argument rather than ordering steps.
De plus and en outre add arguments without implying any order in time.
Quand or dès que link two events within one sentence through a subordinate clause.

examples.sentence: D'abord, on achète les billets. Ensuite, on mange.
examples.translation: First, we buy the tickets. Then we eat.

examples.sentence: Il a pris une douche, puis il est sorti.
examples.translation: He took a shower, then he went out.

examples.sentence: Enfin, ajoutez le sel.
examples.translation: Finally, add the salt.

constructs.name: connecteurs d'addition
aliases: en plus, de plus, en outre
constructs.description: Connectors adding an element or an argument.

card.formation: Connectors such as aussi, en plus, de plus, en outre, par ailleurs and non seulement ... mais aussi link a new element to the previous one. Aussi meaning 'also' comes after the verb, not at the start.
card.use: They add an extra fact or argument, often to strengthen a point. En plus is spoken; de plus, en outre and par ailleurs are written.
pitfalls: Starting a sentence with aussi to mean 'also'; at the start it means 'therefore'.
Using en plus in formal writing.
Using aussi in a negative sentence where non plus is needed (moi non plus).
Reading par ailleurs only as 'moreover'; it also means 'in other respects'.

contrasts.note: Aussi at the head of a clause, followed by inversion, means 'therefore', not 'also'.
Et simply joins two elements; addition connectors usually start a new clause or sentence.
Ensuite orders steps in time; de plus adds arguments without a time order.
En revanche introduces a contrast, not an extra point in the same direction.

examples.sentence: L'hôtel est calme. En plus, il n'est pas cher.
examples.translation: The hotel is quiet. Plus, it's cheap.

examples.sentence: Cette voiture est rapide. De plus, elle consomme peu.
examples.translation: This car is fast. Moreover, it uses little fuel.

examples.sentence: Il parle anglais et aussi un peu d'allemand.
examples.translation: He speaks English and also a little German.

constructs.name: connecteurs de reformulation
constructs.description: Connectors introducing a rewording or explanation of what was said.

card.formation: A connector such as c'est-à-dire, autrement dit, en d'autres termes, à savoir or plutôt is placed before the rewording, usually after a comma.
card.use: It introduces a clearer or more precise way of saying what was just said, or a correction of it.
pitfalls: Forgetting the hyphens in c'est-à-dire.
Using à savoir to rephrase; it introduces a list or detail, not a new wording.
Using plutôt as a reformulation without signalling the correction (ou plutôt).

contrasts.note: Bref and en somme sum up the whole argument instead of rewording one point.
De plus brings a new element; reformulation repeats the same idea in other words.
Donc draws a result, while c'est-à-dire explains the same thing again.

examples.sentence: Il est végétarien, c'est-à-dire qu'il ne mange pas de viande.
examples.translation: He's vegetarian, that is, he doesn't eat meat.

examples.sentence: Il n'a pas répondu. Autrement dit, il refuse.
examples.translation: He didn't answer. In other words, he refuses.

examples.sentence: Je viens lundi, ou plutôt mardi.
examples.translation: I'm coming on Monday, or rather Tuesday.

constructs.name: hypothèse sur le présent (si + imparfait)
constructs.description: A si-clause in the imperfect with a main clause in the present conditional, for unlikely or imagined situations.

card.formation: Si + imparfait in the condition clause, and the present conditional in the main clause. The clauses can come in either order.
card.use: It imagines a situation that is contrary to present reality or unlikely in the future, and its consequence.
pitfalls: Putting the conditional after si: si j'aurais is wrong, use si j'avais.
Using the imparfait in both clauses instead of the conditional in the main clause.
Reading the imparfait here as past time; it refers to the present or future.
Writing si il instead of s'il.

contrasts.note: Si + présent presents the condition as real and likely.
Si + plus-que-parfait imagines a different past.
Si + imparfait without a main clause makes a suggestion, not a hypothesis.
Gives the forms used in the main clause.
In a narrative, si + imparfait can also mean 'whenever' (habit), with the imparfait in both clauses.

examples.sentence: Si j'avais le temps, je lirais plus.
examples.form: Si j'avais le temps, je lirais
examples.translation: If I had time, I would read more.

examples.sentence: Si elle était là, elle saurait quoi faire.
examples.form: Si elle était là, elle saurait
examples.translation: If she were here, she would know what to do.

examples.sentence: On partirait demain si on gagnait au loto.
examples.translation: We would leave tomorrow if we won the lottery.

constructs.name: si + imparfait (suggestion)
constructs.description: An independent si-clause in the imperfect used to make a suggestion.

card.formation: Si (often et si) + subject + imparfait, used alone as a question, with no main clause.
card.use: It suggests or proposes something to do, often with on. It sounds friendly and informal.
pitfalls: Adding a conditional main clause; the si-clause stands alone.
Reading the imparfait as past time; the suggestion is about now or later.
Using the present (et si on va) where the imparfait is the normal form.

contrasts.note: The same si + imparfait with a conditional main clause expresses an imagined situation.
Tu pourrais or on pourrait also suggest, through the conditional of a full sentence.
The nous imperative (allons) is a more direct way to propose.

examples.sentence: Et si on allait au cinéma ce soir ?
examples.translation: How about going to the cinema tonight?

examples.sentence: Si on prenait un café ?
examples.translation: Shall we get a coffee?

examples.sentence: Et si tu l'appelais ?
examples.translation: What if you called him?

constructs.name: proposition subordonnée de temps (indicatif)
constructs.description: Time clauses in the indicative for simultaneity or succession.

card.formation: A time conjunction (quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, pendant que, depuis que, chaque fois que, tant que) introduces a clause in the indicative. When the main clause is in the future, the time clause is in the future or future perfect too.
card.use: It places the main action relative to another one: at the same moment (quand, pendant que), just after it (dès que), since it began (depuis que) or as long as it lasts (tant que).
pitfalls: Using the present after quand for a future event, as in English: say quand je serai, not quand je suis.
Using the simple future instead of the future perfect for an earlier completed action (dès que j'aurai fini).
Putting avant que in this group; it takes the subjunctive.
Confusing pendant que (while, time) with alors que (whereas, contrast).

contrasts.note: Avant que, jusqu'à ce que and en attendant que take the subjunctive.
Après que also takes the indicative in standard French, though the subjunctive is common in speech.
Si never takes the future, while quand does when the main clause is future.
Used after dès que or quand for an action finished before a future one.
En + present participle can express simultaneity without a conjunction when the subject is the same.

examples.sentence: Quand je serai grand, je serai pilote.
examples.translation: When I grow up, I'll be a pilot.

examples.sentence: Appelle-moi dès que tu arrives.
examples.translation: Call me as soon as you arrive.

examples.sentence: Il lit pendant que les enfants dorment.
examples.translation: He reads while the children are sleeping.

examples.sentence: Je n'ai pas fumé depuis que j'ai arrêté.
examples.translation: I haven't smoked since I quit.

constructs.name: discours indirect au présent
constructs.description: Reporting statements, questions and orders with a reporting verb in the present.

card.formation: A reporting verb in the present (dit, demande, explique) is followed by que + clause for statements, si or a question word for questions, and de + infinitive for orders. Pronouns and possessives change to fit the new speaker, but tenses stay the same.
card.use: It reports what someone says, asks or orders, when the act of saying is in the present.
pitfalls: Changing the tenses; with a present reporting verb they stay as in the original.
Forgetting to change je, tu, mon, ton to match the new point of view.
Keeping est-ce que or inversion in a reported question.
Reporting an order with que + imperative instead of de + infinitive.

contrasts.note: With a past reporting verb, tenses and time words shift.
Covers reported questions in detail: si, ce que, ce qui and question words.
Reported statements use the same verb + que + indicative pattern.
Reported orders use dire de or demander de + infinitive.

examples.sentence: Il dit qu'il arrive dans dix minutes.
examples.translation: He says he's arriving in ten minutes.

examples.sentence: Elle demande si tu viens ce soir.
examples.translation: She is asking whether you're coming tonight.

examples.sentence: Le médecin me dit de rester au lit.
examples.translation: The doctor tells me to stay in bed.

constructs.name: interrogation indirecte
aliases: si, ce que, ce qui + discours indirect
constructs.description: Questions embedded after a verb, with statement word order.

card.formation: After a verb such as demander, savoir or se demander, a yes/no question is introduced by si, and a question word (où, quand, comment, pourquoi, qui, combien) is kept. Qu'est-ce que becomes ce que and qu'est-ce qui becomes ce qui; word order is that of a statement, with no question mark.
card.use: It embeds a question inside a sentence, to report it or to ask politely and indirectly.
pitfalls: Keeping est-ce que or inversion inside the embedded question.
Using qu'est-ce que instead of ce que (je ne sais pas ce que tu veux).
Writing si il instead of s'il.
Ending a statement containing an indirect question with a question mark.

contrasts.note: Direct questions may invert subject and verb; indirect ones never do.
Ce qui and ce que also start free relative clauses; in indirect questions they replace qu'est-ce qui/que.
Si meaning 'whether' can take the future or conditional, unlike conditional si.
With a past reporting verb, the tense of the embedded question also shifts.

examples.sentence: Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.
examples.translation: I don't know what you want.

examples.sentence: Il me demande si j'ai faim.
examples.translation: He asks me whether I'm hungry.

examples.sentence: Dis-moi où tu habites.
examples.translation: Tell me where you live.

constructs.name: opposition (conjonction + indicatif)
constructs.description: Contrasting two facts with conjunctions followed by the indicative.

card.formation: Alors que or tandis que joins two clauses, and the verb after it is in the indicative.
card.use: It sets two facts side by side to show that they differ or contrast. Both conjunctions can also mean 'while' in time; context decides.
pitfalls: Using the subjunctive after alors que by analogy with bien que.
Using pendant que for contrast in writing; it is mainly about time.
Confusing contrast (alors que) with concession (bien que): concession states that something did not prevent something else.

contrasts.note: Bien que and quoique express concession and take the subjunctive.
En revanche and par contre contrast two facts across separate clauses or sentences.
Pendant que expresses simultaneity, not contrast.
Même si presents a condition that does not change the result, not a simple difference.

examples.sentence: Il aime la mer, alors que sa femme préfère la montagne.
examples.translation: He loves the sea, whereas his wife prefers the mountains.

examples.sentence: Paul travaille tandis que son frère joue.
examples.translation: Paul works while his brother plays.

constructs.name: concession (connecteurs)
constructs.description: Expressing concession with adverbs and connectors.

card.formation: An adverb or connector of concession (pourtant, cependant, toutefois, néanmoins, quand même, tout de même, malgré tout) introduces the second clause or is placed inside it. Quand même usually follows the verb.
card.use: It shows that a fact holds even though the previous one could have prevented it. Quand même is spoken; cependant, toutefois and néanmoins are formal.
pitfalls: Starting a clause with quand même meaning 'anyway'; it normally comes after the verb.
Using pourtant for a simple difference where en revanche is meant.
Using néanmoins or toutefois in casual speech, where they sound stiff.

contrasts.note: En revanche simply compares two facts; pourtant says the second is unexpected given the first.
Bien que puts the concession in a subordinate clause with the subjunctive.
Malgré + noun expresses the concession inside one clause.
Même si states the obstacle as a condition in a subordinate clause.
Mais can also mark concession but is weaker and more general.

examples.sentence: Il est riche. Pourtant, il n'est pas heureux.
examples.translation: He is rich. And yet he isn't happy.

examples.sentence: Il pleuvait, mais on est sortis quand même.
examples.translation: It was raining, but we went out anyway.

examples.sentence: Le projet est bon. Il est cependant trop cher.
examples.translation: The project is good. It is, however, too expensive.

constructs.name: concession (préposition + nom)
constructs.description: Expressing concession with a preposition followed by a noun.

card.formation: Malgré or en dépit de is followed by a noun or pronoun. De contracts with le and les: en dépit du, en dépit des.
card.use: It names an obstacle that did not prevent the action. En dépit de is more formal than malgré.
pitfalls: Following malgré with a clause; use bien que + subjunctive instead.
Writing malgré que, which the norm rejects in careful writing.
Using à cause de where an obstacle, not a cause, is meant.

contrasts.note: À cause de + noun gives the reason for something, not an obstacle overcome.
Bien que + subjunctive expresses the same idea with a full clause.
Pourtant or malgré tout link two separate clauses.
Même si presents the obstacle as a condition with a verb.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes sortis malgré la pluie.
examples.translation: We went out despite the rain.

examples.sentence: Il est venu malgré sa fatigue.
examples.translation: He came in spite of being tired.

examples.sentence: En dépit des critiques, le film a du succès.
examples.translation: Despite the criticism, the film is a success.

constructs.name: concession avec même si
constructs.description: Même si followed by the indicative to express concession.

card.formation: Même si is followed by the indicative, with the same tense pattern as conditional si: present, imparfait or plus-que-parfait after même si, and the matching tense or conditional in the main clause.
card.use: It states a condition or fact that does not change the result: the main clause is true anyway.
pitfalls: Using the subjunctive after même si by analogy with bien que.
Putting the conditional or future right after même si.
Writing même s'elle; only il and ils cause the elision (même s'il).

contrasts.note: Bien que states a real fact and takes the subjunctive; même si can also be hypothetical.
Si gives a condition that leads to the result; même si one that does not stop it.
Pourtant and quand même mark the concession in the main clause instead.
Malgré + noun expresses the obstacle without a verb.

examples.sentence: Je sors même s'il pleut.
examples.translation: I'm going out even if it rains.

examples.sentence: Même si j'étais riche, je travaillerais.
examples.translation: Even if I were rich, I would work.

examples.sentence: Elle a souri, même si elle était triste.
examples.translation: She smiled, even though she was sad.

constructs.name: connecteurs de conclusion
constructs.description: Connectors closing an argument or a story.

card.formation: A connector such as finalement, enfin, bref, en somme, en résumé, pour conclure or en définitive opens the final sentence, followed by a comma.
card.use: It closes a story or an argument by giving the outcome or summing up. Bref is spoken; en somme, en définitive and pour conclure are written.
pitfalls: Using finalement to mean only 'lastly'; it often means 'in the end, after all', implying a change of plan.
Using enfin only as 'at last'; it can also mean 'in short' or 'well'.
Using bref in a formal essay.

contrasts.note: Enfin in a sequence marks the last step, not a summary.
C'est-à-dire rewords one point instead of summing up.
Donc gives a direct result of the previous fact, not a closing summary.

examples.sentence: Finalement, on est restés à la maison.
examples.translation: In the end, we stayed home.

examples.sentence: Bref, la soirée était ratée.
examples.translation: In short, the evening was a failure.

examples.sentence: En somme, le projet est une réussite.
examples.translation: All in all, the project is a success.

constructs.name: opposition (connecteurs)
aliases: en revanche, par contre, au contraire
constructs.description: Contrasting two facts with adverbs and connectors.

card.formation: An adverb or connector of contrast (en revanche, par contre, au contraire, d'un côté ... de l'autre) introduces the second fact, at the start of the clause or after the verb.
card.use: It contrasts two facts that differ. Au contraire says the second is the reverse of the first; par contre is spoken, en revanche is preferred in writing.
pitfalls: Using au contraire for a mere difference; it means the exact opposite.
Using par contre in formal writing, where en revanche is safer.
Using pourtant where there is a contrast but nothing unexpected.

contrasts.note: Alors que and tandis que put the contrast in a subordinate clause of the same sentence.
Pourtant marks an unexpected fact; en revanche only compares.
Mais is the basic, neutral contrast word.

examples.sentence: Le quartier est bruyant. En revanche, l'appartement est grand.
examples.translation: The area is noisy. On the other hand, the flat is big.

examples.sentence: Je n'aime pas le thé. Par contre, j'adore le café.
examples.translation: I don't like tea. But I love coffee.

examples.sentence: Il n'est pas timide, au contraire.
examples.translation: He isn't shy, quite the opposite.

constructs.name: hypothèse sur le passé (si + plus-que-parfait)
constructs.description: A si-clause in the pluperfect with a past or present conditional for unreal past situations.

card.formation: Si + plus-que-parfait in the condition clause, and the past conditional in the main clause. If the result is in the present, the main clause uses the present conditional.
card.use: It imagines a different past from what actually happened, often to express a regret or a reproach.
pitfalls: Putting the conditional after si: si j'aurais su is a common error for si j'avais su.
Using the passé composé after si instead of the plus-que-parfait.
Forgetting the present conditional when the result is in the present (je serais riche maintenant).
Choosing the wrong auxiliary in both clauses (si elle était venue).

contrasts.note: Si + imparfait imagines a different present, not past.
The past conditional alone (j'aurais dû) expresses regret without a si-clause.
Gives the forms used after si; here it does not mean 'earlier in the past' but 'unreal'.
Gives the forms used in the main clause.

examples.sentence: Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
examples.form: Si j'avais su, je serais venu
examples.translation: If I had known, I would have come.

examples.sentence: Si tu avais pris un parapluie, tu ne serais pas mouillé.
examples.form: Si tu avais pris un parapluie, tu ne serais pas mouillé
examples.translation: If you had taken an umbrella, you wouldn't be wet.

examples.sentence: On aurait gagné si elle avait joué.
examples.form: aurait gagné si elle avait joué
examples.translation: We would have won if she had played.

constructs.name: hypothèse sans si
constructs.description: Expressing a condition or hypothesis with prepositions, au cas où, a gerund or other means than si.

card.formation: A condition can be expressed by au cas où + conditional, en cas de + noun, à condition de + infinitive, avec or sans + noun followed by a conditional main clause, a gerund, or two juxtaposed clauses in the conditional.
card.use: It gives a condition or a possibility without si, to vary style, to stress a precaution (au cas où) or to keep the sentence short. Sans + noun often means 'if it weren't for'.
pitfalls: Putting the indicative after au cas où (au cas où il pleut) instead of the conditional (au cas où il pleuvrait).
Following à condition que with the indicative instead of the subjunctive.
Using à condition de + infinitive when the two subjects differ; then à condition que is needed.
Keeping the main clause in the indicative after sans or avec + noun when the situation is imagined (sans toi, je serais perdu).
Adding an article after en cas de in general instructions (en cas de la pluie instead of en cas de pluie).

contrasts.note: À condition que, pourvu que and à moins que take the subjunctive.
The standard si-structure for an imagined condition.
A gerund can carry a condition (en partant tôt), but it also expresses manner or time.
The conditional after au cas où expresses a possibility, not unconfirmed news.

examples.sentence: Prends un pull au cas où il ferait froid.
examples.form: au cas où il ferait froid
examples.translation: Take a jumper in case it gets cold.

examples.sentence: En cas d'urgence, appelez le 112.
examples.translation: In case of emergency, call 112.

examples.sentence: En partant maintenant, tu arriveras à l'heure.
examples.translation: If you leave now, you'll arrive on time.

examples.sentence: Sans ton aide, je n'aurais pas réussi.
examples.form: Sans ton aide, je n'aurais pas réussi
examples.translation: Without your help, I wouldn't have succeeded.

constructs.name: discours indirect au passé (concordance des temps)
constructs.description: Shifting tenses and time expressions when the reporting verb is in the past.

card.formation: When the reporting verb is in a past tense, the present becomes imparfait, the passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait, the future becomes present conditional and the future perfect becomes past conditional. Imparfait, plus-que-parfait and conditional stay; time and place words shift (demain → le lendemain, hier → la veille, ici → là).
card.use: It reports what someone said, asked or ordered at a past moment, from the point of view of the present.
pitfalls: Leaving the present unchanged after il a dit que when the statement is no longer current.
Changing an imparfait in the original; it stays imparfait.
Keeping demain or hier when they no longer fit the moment of reporting.
Using the future instead of the conditional for a future seen from the past.

contrasts.note: With a present reporting verb, tenses do not shift.
The present conditional here expresses a future seen from the past, not a hypothesis.
Replaces the passé composé of the original statement.
Reported questions follow the same tense shifts, with si or a question word.

examples.sentence: Il m'a dit qu'il était fatigué.
examples.translation: He told me he was tired.

examples.sentence: Elle a dit qu'elle viendrait le lendemain.
examples.form: a dit qu'elle viendrait le lendemain
examples.translation: She said she would come the next day.

examples.sentence: Il a expliqué qu'il avait perdu ses clés.
examples.translation: He explained that he had lost his keys.

constructs.name: conséquence (conjonction + indicatif)
aliases: si bien que, de sorte que
constructs.description: Expressing consequence with conjunctions followed by the indicative.

card.formation: A conjunction of consequence (si bien que, de sorte que, de façon que, de manière que, au point que) introduces a clause in the indicative, usually after a comma.
card.use: It presents the second clause as the result of the first within one sentence. It is more formal than donc or alors.
pitfalls: Using the subjunctive after de sorte que when a real result is meant; the subjunctive turns it into a purpose.
Confusing si bien que (so that, result) with bien que (although).
Putting the result clause before the cause; it always comes second.

contrasts.note: De sorte que or de façon que + subjunctive express an intended goal, not a result.
Donc and alors link the result more loosely, often in a new clause or sentence.
Tellement ... que ties the result to a degree expressed in the main clause.
Bien que, unlike si bien que, means 'although' and takes the subjunctive.

examples.sentence: Il a beaucoup plu, si bien que la route est fermée.
examples.form: si bien que la route est fermée
examples.translation: It rained a lot, so the road is closed.

examples.sentence: J'ai oublié mes clés, de sorte que je suis resté dehors.
examples.form: de sorte que je suis resté
examples.translation: I forgot my keys, so I stayed outside.

constructs.name: conséquence liée à l'intensité
aliases: si ... que, tant ... que, tellement ... que
constructs.description: Consequence linked to an intensity or quantity: an adverb in the main clause and que.

card.formation: An intensifier in the main clause is answered by que + indicative: si or tellement + adjective or adverb, tant or tellement + verb, tant de or tellement de + noun, un tel or une telle + noun. À tel point que and au point que also work after a whole clause.
card.use: It says that something is so strong or so frequent that a result follows.
pitfalls: Using si with a verb: il a si mangé is wrong, use tant or tellement.
Saying tellement beaucoup; tellement already means 'so much'.
Forgetting de before a noun: tellement de travail, not tellement du travail.
Forgetting to make tel agree: une telle peur.

contrasts.note: Si bien que gives a result without an intensifier in the main clause.
Si, tant and tellement alone are simple intensifiers; here they need a que-clause.
Aussi ... que compares two things; si ... que announces a result.
Donc gives a result without tying it to a degree.

examples.sentence: Il était si fatigué qu'il s'est endormi.
examples.translation: He was so tired that he fell asleep.

examples.sentence: J'ai tellement mangé que j'ai mal au ventre.
examples.translation: I ate so much that I have a stomach ache.

examples.sentence: Il y avait tant de monde qu'on est partis.
examples.form: tant de monde qu'on est partis
examples.translation: There were so many people that we left.

constructs.name: proposition participiale
constructs.description: A participle clause with its own subject, expressing cause or time in formal writing.

card.formation: A participle (present, past or compound) with its own subject, different from the subject of the main clause, forms a clause set off by a comma. A past participle agrees with that subject.
card.use: In formal writing it expresses the cause or the time of the main action compactly, without a conjunction.
pitfalls: Using the same subject in both parts; then it is an ordinary participle phrase.
Forgetting to make the past participle agree with its own subject (la nuit tombée).
Using it in casual speech, where a clause with comme or quand sounds natural.

contrasts.note: A plain participle phrase shares the subject of the main clause.
En + present participle must have the same subject as the main verb.
Comme + clause expresses the same cause with a conjugated verb.
Ayant fini or étant parti often appears in participle clauses for an earlier action.

examples.sentence: La nuit tombée, nous sommes rentrés.
examples.translation: Once night had fallen, we went home.

examples.sentence: Le professeur étant malade, le cours est annulé.
examples.translation: The teacher being ill, the class is cancelled.

examples.sentence: Le repas terminé, chacun est parti.
examples.translation: The meal over, everyone left.

constructs.name: après que + indicatif
constructs.description: Après que followed by the indicative for an action completed before the main one.

card.formation: Après que is followed by the indicative, usually a compound tense that marks the earlier action: passé composé, plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur for a future sequence, or the literary passé antérieur.
card.use: It says that the main action happens after another one is completed. The rule is standard; in speech the subjunctive is very common.
pitfalls: Using the subjunctive, by analogy with avant que; the norm requires the indicative.
Choosing a simple tense where a compound one shows the earlier action.
Using après que when the subject is the same; après + past infinitive is lighter.

contrasts.note: Avant que takes the subjunctive, après que the indicative.
Après avoir mangé is used when both actions share a subject.
Quand and dès que also take the indicative in time clauses.
Used after après que for an action completed before a future one.

examples.sentence: Nous partirons après que vous aurez mangé.
examples.translation: We'll leave after you've eaten.

examples.sentence: Il est arrivé après que le film avait commencé.
examples.form: après que le film avait commencé
examples.translation: He arrived after the film had started.

constructs.name: cause (conjonctions de justification)
constructs.description: Conjunctions that add or stress a justifying cause.

card.formation: A conjunction such as d'autant (plus) que, surtout que, dans la mesure où, considérant que or sous prétexte que introduces a clause in the indicative.
card.use: It adds, stresses or frames a reason: d'autant plus que gives an extra reason that strengthens the claim, dans la mesure où limits it, sous prétexte que presents a reason the speaker doubts, and considérant que belongs to legal and formal texts.
pitfalls: Splitting d'autant plus ... que wrongly; the adjective goes between plus and que (d'autant plus content que).
Using surtout que in formal writing; it is informal.
Reading sous prétexte que as a neutral cause; it suggests the reason is false.
Using the subjunctive after these conjunctions.

contrasts.note: Parce que and puisque give a plain cause without extra emphasis.
Non que rejects a cause and takes the subjunctive.
De plus adds an argument in a new sentence rather than in a subordinate clause.

examples.sentence: Prends un taxi, d'autant qu'il pleut.
examples.translation: Take a taxi, especially as it's raining.

examples.sentence: Il est resté chez lui sous prétexte qu'il était malade.
examples.translation: He stayed home, claiming he was ill.

examples.sentence: Je suis d'autant plus content que tu es là.
examples.translation: I'm all the happier because you're here.

constructs.name: comparatif de l'adjectif et de l'adverbe
aliases: plus ... que, moins ... que, aussi ... que
constructs.description: Comparing qualities with plus, moins or aussi before an adjective or adverb and que.

card.formation: Plus (more), moins (less) or aussi (as) is placed before the adjective or adverb, and que before the second term: plus grand que, aussi vite que. The adjective agrees with its noun, and a pronoun after que takes the stressed form (plus âgé que moi).
card.use: It compares a quality or manner between two people, things or situations, expressing superiority, inferiority or equality. The second term can be left out when it is clear.
pitfalls: Using comme for equality: aussi grand que, not aussi grand comme.
Using a subject pronoun after que: plus grand que moi, not que je.
Saying plus bon or plus bien instead of meilleur and mieux.
Forgetting agreement: elle est plus grande que lui.
Using aussi with nouns or verbs, where autant is needed.

contrasts.note: With nouns and verbs, equality uses autant (de) instead of aussi.
Bon and bien have special forms (meilleur, mieux).
The superlative adds an article (le plus grand) and compares with a whole group.
Comme and le même que express similarity, not degree.
After que, pronouns take the stressed form (moi, toi, lui).

examples.sentence: Mon frère est plus grand que moi.
examples.translation: My brother is taller than me.

examples.sentence: Ce film est moins intéressant que le livre.
examples.translation: This film is less interesting than the book.

examples.sentence: Elle court aussi vite que sa sœur.
examples.translation: She runs as fast as her sister.

constructs.name: comparatif du nom et du verbe
aliases: plus de ... que, autant de ... que
constructs.description: Comparing quantities and actions with plus (de), moins (de), autant (de) and que.

card.formation: With nouns use plus de, moins de or autant de before the noun and que before the second term: plus de livres que moi. With verbs put plus, moins or autant after the verb, followed by que: il travaille plus que moi.
card.use: It compares quantities of things or how much an action is done. Before a number, plus de and moins de mean more than and less than (plus de vingt personnes).
pitfalls: Using aussi with a noun or verb: autant de temps que, il mange autant que moi.
Leaving out de before the noun: plus de temps, not plus temps.
Using an article after de: plus d'argent, not plus de l'argent.
Using que before a number: plus de dix euros, not plus que dix euros.
Pronouncing plus without its s after a verb: il travaille plus, with a final s sound.

contrasts.note: Adjectives and adverbs use aussi for equality, nouns and verbs autant.
Plus de and autant de work like other quantity expressions, with de and no article.
Le plus de and le plus after a verb give the superlative of quantity.
Mieux compares how well an action is done (il chante mieux que moi).
With ne, plus is a negation meaning no longer, not a comparison.

examples.sentence: J'ai moins de temps que toi.
examples.translation: I have less time than you.

examples.sentence: Il y a autant de filles que de garçons.
examples.translation: There are as many girls as boys.

examples.sentence: Mon fils dort plus que moi.
examples.translation: My son sleeps more than me.

examples.sentence: Elle travaille autant que son mari.
examples.translation: She works as much as her husband.

constructs.name: comparatifs et superlatifs irréguliers
constructs.description: Irregular comparative and superlative forms of good and well.

card.formation: Bon becomes meilleur in the comparative and le meilleur in the superlative, agreeing like an adjective. Bien becomes mieux and le mieux, which do not change. Mauvais becomes plus mauvais or pire (le pire), while mal becomes plus mal.
card.use: These forms compare quality (meilleur, adjective, with nouns) and manner (mieux, adverb, with verbs). Pire is often used for things that are bad in an abstract or moral sense.
pitfalls: Saying plus bon or plus bien: meilleur, mieux.
Confusing meilleur (adjective) and mieux (adverb): il chante mieux, son meilleur ami.
Forgetting agreement of meilleur: les meilleures places.
Saying le plus bien instead of le mieux: c'est elle qui danse le mieux.
Saying plus pire, which is wrong because pire is already comparative.

contrasts.note: Regular adjectives and adverbs use plus + adjective; bon and bien have one-word forms.
Le meilleur and le mieux are superlatives built from these irregular forms.
Bien and mal are adverbs, like adverbs in -ment, so they compare with mieux and plus mal.
Plus after a verb measures quantity; mieux after a verb measures quality.

examples.sentence: Ce gâteau est meilleur que l'autre.
examples.translation: This cake is better than the other one.

examples.sentence: Elle parle mieux anglais que moi.
examples.translation: She speaks English better than me.

examples.sentence: C'est mon meilleur ami.
examples.translation: He's my best friend.

examples.sentence: La situation est pire qu'avant.
examples.translation: The situation is worse than before.

constructs.name: superlatif
constructs.description: Article plus plus or moins to express the highest or lowest degree.

card.formation: The definite article (le, la, les) is placed before plus or moins and the adjective, and it agrees with the noun. An adjective that normally follows the noun keeps that position and repeats the article (le film le plus drôle). The group compared with is introduced by de (de la classe, du monde); with adverbs and verbs the article is always le (c'est elle qui court le plus vite).
card.use: It expresses the highest or lowest degree of a quality within a group. A possessive can replace the article (mon plus beau souvenir).
pitfalls: Forgetting the second article after the noun: la ville la plus belle, not la ville plus belle.
Using dans instead of de for the group: le plus grand du monde.
Making the article agree with an adverb: elle court le plus vite, not la plus vite.
Saying le plus bon instead of le meilleur.
Using que instead of de: la plus jeune de la famille.

contrasts.note: The comparative compares two terms with que, without an article.
Bon and bien give le meilleur and le mieux.
The adjective's usual position decides whether the superlative stands before or after the noun.
A relative clause after a superlative often takes the subjunctive (le meilleur film que je connaisse).
Très expresses a high degree without comparing; the superlative compares within a group.

examples.sentence: C'est la plus belle ville du pays.
examples.translation: It's the most beautiful city in the country.

examples.sentence: C'est le film le plus drôle de l'année.
examples.translation: It's the funniest film of the year.

examples.sentence: Paul est l'élève le moins bavard de la classe.
examples.translation: Paul is the least talkative pupil in the class.

examples.sentence: C'est Léa qui court le plus vite.
examples.translation: Léa is the one who runs fastest.

constructs.name: comparaison progressive
aliases: de plus en plus, de moins en moins
constructs.description: Expressing a gradual increase or decrease.

card.formation: The fixed patterns de plus en plus and de moins en moins are placed before an adjective or adverb, after a verb, or before de + noun (de plus en plus de monde). Irregular forms give de mieux en mieux and de pire en pire.
card.use: They express a gradual increase or decrease over time: more and more, less and less, better and better.
pitfalls: Translating word by word: de plus en plus cher, not plus et plus cher.
Leaving out de before a noun: de plus en plus de touristes.
Saying de plus en plus bien instead of de mieux en mieux.
Leaving out the first de: de moins en moins, not moins en moins.

contrasts.note: Plus ... plus links two clauses that change together; de plus en plus describes one change over time.
The comparative compares two terms at one moment, not a change over time.
Mieux and pire also appear in the progressive form (de mieux en mieux).
With nouns, de plus en plus de follows the same de rule as plus de.

examples.sentence: Il fait de plus en plus froid.
examples.translation: It's getting colder and colder.

examples.sentence: Je comprends de mieux en mieux.
examples.translation: I understand better and better.

examples.sentence: Il y a de moins en moins d'oiseaux.
examples.translation: There are fewer and fewer birds.

constructs.name: comparaison de ressemblance
constructs.description: Expressing sameness or similarity with comme, le même ... que and similar words.

card.formation: Comme compares one thing with another directly (il chante comme un oiseau). Le même, la même, les mêmes + noun + que express sameness, and pareil (à), semblable à, comparable à, ainsi que and tel que express similarity.
card.use: It says that two people or things are alike or identical, rather than comparing a degree. Comme can also introduce a manner (fais comme moi).
pitfalls: Using comme after même: le même que, not le même comme.
Using aussi ... que for similarity of kind instead of degree.
Forgetting agreement of même: les mêmes chaussures.
Using pareil que in formal writing, where pareil à or le même que is preferred.

contrasts.note: Aussi ... que compares the degree of a quality; comme compares the whole thing or manner.
Autant que compares quantities; le même que says it is the same item or kind.
Comme at the start of a sentence can also mean since or as, giving a cause.
Comme also starts exclamations (comme c'est beau !).

examples.sentence: Il mange comme un ogre.
examples.translation: He eats like an ogre.

examples.sentence: J'ai le même téléphone que toi.
examples.translation: I have the same phone as you.

examples.sentence: Ta veste est pareille à la mienne.
examples.translation: Your jacket is the same as mine.

examples.sentence: Fais comme moi.
examples.translation: Do as I do.

constructs.name: comparaison proportionnelle
constructs.description: Two parallel clauses expressing proportion.

card.formation: Two clauses each start with plus, moins, autant or mieux, without an article and without que: plus on travaille, plus on réussit. The second clause may also start with et (plus il pleut, et plus il fait froid). Before a noun, plus de and moins de are used.
card.use: It expresses that two things change together, in the same or opposite direction: the more ..., the more ..., the less ..., the more ...
pitfalls: Adding an article as in English: plus on lit, not le plus on lit.
Adding que: plus tu manges, plus tu grossis, not plus que tu manges.
Inverting the subject as in a question: plus il parle, not plus parle-t-il.
Forgetting de before a noun: plus j'ai d'argent, plus je dépense.

contrasts.note: De plus en plus describes one gradual change; plus ... plus links two changes.
A verb comparison compares two people or things with que; here two clauses vary together.
Le plus marks the top of a group, while plus ... plus has no article.
Si ... que and tellement ... que express a consequence of intensity, not a proportion.

examples.sentence: Plus on lit, plus on apprend.
examples.form: Plus on lit, plus on apprend
examples.translation: The more you read, the more you learn.

examples.sentence: Moins je dors, plus je suis fatigué.
examples.form: Moins je dors, plus je suis
examples.translation: The less I sleep, the more tired I am.

examples.sentence: Plus il pleut, et plus il fait froid.
examples.form: Plus il pleut, et plus il fait froid
examples.translation: The more it rains, the colder it gets.

constructs.name: place de l'adjectif
aliases: adjectif avant ou après le nom
constructs.description: Most adjectives follow the noun; a small group of short frequent adjectives comes before it.

card.formation: Most adjectives come after the noun, especially those of colour, shape, nationality, religion, and participles. A small group of short, frequent adjectives (beau, bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, joli, mauvais, nouveau, gros, premier) usually comes before it.
card.use: The position is mostly fixed by the adjective. Long adjectives and those that classify the noun follow it; the short common ones that evaluate it precede it.
pitfalls: Putting colour or nationality adjectives before the noun, as in English.
Forgetting the special forms bel, nouvel, vieil before a masculine noun starting with a vowel.
Keeping des before a plural adjective in writing, where de is expected (de beaux jours).
Placing two adjectives on the same side when one goes before and one after (une jolie robe rouge).

contrasts.note: Some adjectives can go on either side, with a different meaning.
Agreement is needed wherever the adjective stands.
Plural agreement applies whether the adjective comes before or after.
Participles used as adjectives always follow the noun.

examples.sentence: J'ai acheté une voiture rouge.
examples.translation: I bought a red car.

examples.sentence: C'est un petit village.
examples.translation: It's a small village.

examples.sentence: Elle a un bel appartement.
examples.translation: She has a lovely flat.

examples.sentence: J'aime la cuisine italienne.
examples.translation: I like Italian food.

constructs.name: place des pronoms compléments
constructs.description: Object pronouns placed before the conjugated verb, or before the infinitive they depend on.

card.formation: Object pronouns (me, te, le, la, lui, nous, vous, leur, y, en) go before the conjugated verb, or before the auxiliary in compound tenses. When the verb is followed by an infinitive, they go before the infinitive they belong to.
card.use: This order is used in all statements, questions and negative sentences except the affirmative imperative. In a negation, ne comes before the pronoun and pas after the verb or auxiliary.
pitfalls: Putting the pronoun after the verb, as in English (je vois le instead of je le vois).
Putting it before the first verb in verb + infinitive (je le vais voir instead of je vais le voir).
Placing pas between the pronoun and the verb instead of after the verb.
Putting the pronoun before the infinitive after faire, laisser or verbs of perception; it goes before the conjugated verb (je le fais venir).

contrasts.note: In the affirmative imperative, pronouns follow the verb with a hyphen.
Gives the order when two pronouns are combined (je le lui donne).
Tonic pronouns (moi, lui) follow prepositions and are not placed before the verb.
With faire + infinitive, pronouns go before faire, not before the infinitive.
Gives the forms; this entry gives their position.

examples.sentence: Je le vois tous les jours.
examples.translation: I see him every day.

examples.sentence: Je vais lui téléphoner ce soir.
examples.translation: I'm going to phone her tonight.

examples.sentence: Je ne les ai pas trouvés.
examples.translation: I didn't find them.

constructs.name: place des pronoms à l'impératif
constructs.description: Object pronouns after the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative imperative, before it in the negative.

card.formation: In the affirmative imperative, object pronouns follow the verb and are joined by hyphens; me and te become moi and toi, and the direct object comes before the indirect one (donne-le-moi). In the negative imperative, pronouns go back before the verb in the usual order.
card.use: It is used to give orders, advice or instructions that involve a pronoun object.
pitfalls: Writing donne-me instead of donne-moi.
Leaving out the hyphens.
Keeping the pronoun after the verb in the negative (ne donne-le pas instead of ne le donne pas).
Forgetting the s added to the tu form of -er verbs before en and y (vas-y, manges-en).
Putting the indirect pronoun first (donne-moi-le instead of donne-le-moi).

contrasts.note: Elsewhere, pronouns go before the verb.
The negative imperative uses the normal pronoun order before the verb.
The order of two pronouns differs between the imperative and other forms.
Moi and toi after the imperative look tonic but are object pronouns.

examples.sentence: Regarde-moi !
examples.translation: Look at me!

examples.sentence: Donne-le-lui, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Give it to him, please.

examples.sentence: Ne le dis pas à ta sœur.
examples.translation: Don't tell your sister.

examples.sentence: Tu as du pain ? Achètes-en.
examples.translation: Do you have bread? Buy some.

constructs.name: dislocation
constructs.description: Placing an element at the start or end of the sentence and taking it up with a pronoun, for emphasis.

card.formation: A noun, pronoun or phrase is moved to the start or the end of the sentence, separated by a comma, and taken up inside the clause by a pronoun (le, la, les, lui, en, y, ça, or a subject pronoun).
card.use: It puts the topic up front or adds it as an afterthought, to make it prominent. It is very common in speech and informal writing.
pitfalls: Leaving out the pronoun that takes up the moved element.
Using a subject pronoun (je, tu) instead of a tonic one (moi, toi) as the detached element.
Forgetting en or y when the detached element needs one (du café, j'en veux).
Using it heavily in formal writing, where it sounds conversational.

contrasts.note: C'est ... qui/que singles out one element as the right answer; dislocation only sets the topic.
Ce que je veux, c'est ... builds emphasis with a relative clause rather than a pronoun.
Tonic pronouns (moi, toi, lui) are used for detached persons.
Ça often takes up a detached infinitive or idea (le sport, j'aime ça).

examples.sentence: Ce film, je l'ai déjà vu.
examples.translation: That film, I've already seen it.

examples.sentence: Il est beau, ton pull.
examples.translation: Your jumper is nice.

examples.sentence: Moi, je préfère la mer.
examples.translation: Me, I prefer the sea.

constructs.name: mise en relief (c'est ... qui, c'est ... que)
constructs.description: Highlighting one element of the sentence by framing it with c'est and a relative pronoun.

card.formation: C'est + the highlighted element + qui (if it is the subject) or que (for any other element) + the rest of the clause. A preposition stays with the highlighted element (c'est à toi que), and persons are given as tonic pronouns.
card.use: It singles out one element, often to correct or contrast it: this one and not another.
pitfalls: Making the verb after qui agree with c'est instead of the highlighted word: c'est moi qui suis, not qui est.
Using qui or dont after a preposition phrase: c'est à lui que je parle, not à qui.
Using subject pronouns instead of tonic ones (c'est je qui instead of c'est moi qui).
Choosing qui or que by the person instead of by grammatical role.

contrasts.note: The pseudo-cleft puts the relative clause first and the highlighted element after c'est.
Dislocation sets a topic with a pronoun; the cleft selects one element against others.
Qui here follows c'est + element, not an ordinary noun antecedent.
Plain c'est presents or identifies without a following relative clause.

examples.sentence: C'est Paul qui a gagné.
examples.translation: It's Paul who won.

examples.sentence: C'est ce livre que je cherche.
examples.translation: It's this book I'm looking for.

examples.sentence: C'est moi qui paie.
examples.translation: I'm the one paying.

examples.sentence: C'est à toi que je parle.
examples.translation: It's you I'm talking to.

constructs.name: mise en relief (ce qui ..., c'est)
constructs.description: Highlighting with a ce qui/ce que/ce dont clause taken up by c'est.

card.formation: Ce qui, ce que or ce dont + clause, then a comma and c'est + the highlighted element. Ce qui is used when ce is the subject, ce que when it is the object, and ce dont with verbs taking de, whose de is repeated after c'est.
card.use: It builds suspense and puts strong emphasis on what comes after c'est, often an opinion, a wish or a need.
pitfalls: Mixing up ce qui and ce que: ce qui me plaît (subject), ce que j'aime (object).
Using ce que with verbs that take de: ce dont j'ai besoin, not ce que j'ai besoin.
Dropping de after c'est when ce dont is used (c'est d'un café).
Leaving out the comma or c'est, which leaves the sentence incomplete.

contrasts.note: The cleft starts with c'est; the pseudo-cleft ends with it.
Gives the choice between ce qui, ce que and ce dont in general.
Dislocation takes up a noun with a pronoun rather than with c'est.
Ce que after savoir or demander introduces a question, not emphasis.

examples.sentence: Ce qui me plaît, c'est le calme.
examples.translation: What I like is the quiet.

examples.sentence: Ce que je veux, c'est dormir.
examples.translation: What I want is to sleep.

examples.sentence: Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'un café.
examples.translation: What I need is a coffee.

constructs.name: place de l'adverbe
constructs.description: Position of adverbs after the conjugated verb, and between auxiliary and participle in compound tenses.

card.formation: In simple tenses the adverb follows the conjugated verb. In compound tenses short common adverbs (bien, mal, déjà, encore, souvent, toujours, beaucoup, trop) go between auxiliary and participle, while adverbs of time and place (hier, demain, ici, là-bas) go after the participle.
card.use: The position depends on the kind of adverb and on the tense; it never sits between the subject and the verb as it often does in English.
pitfalls: Putting the adverb between subject and verb (je souvent mange instead of je mange souvent).
Putting hier between auxiliary and participle (j'ai hier mangé).
Putting bien or déjà after the participle (j'ai dormi bien instead of j'ai bien dormi).
With an infinitive, short adverbs usually come before it (pour bien comprendre).

contrasts.note: Long adverbs in -ment more often follow the participle or start the sentence.
Très or trop before an adjective sit before that adjective, not after the verb.
Pas also goes between auxiliary and participle, like short adverbs.
Some adverbs placed first in formal writing trigger inversion.

examples.sentence: Il mange souvent au restaurant.
examples.translation: He often eats at the restaurant.

examples.sentence: J'ai bien dormi.
examples.translation: I slept well.

examples.sentence: Nous sommes arrivés hier.
examples.translation: We arrived yesterday.

examples.sentence: Tu as déjà mangé ?
examples.translation: Have you already eaten?

constructs.name: adjectifs à sens variable selon la place
aliases: un grand homme, un homme grand
constructs.description: Adjectives whose meaning changes depending on whether they come before or after the noun.

card.formation: A small set of adjectives (ancien, grand, cher, pauvre, propre, seul, dernier, prochain, même, certain, brave, curieux, simple) can go before or after the noun. Before the noun the meaning is usually figurative or subjective; after it, literal or objective.
card.use: The position changes the meaning: un ancien collègue is a former colleague, un meuble ancien an old piece of furniture.
pitfalls: Translating pauvre always as 'poor in money'; before the noun it means 'unfortunate'.
Saying la dernière semaine for 'last week'; it means 'the final week', while last week is la semaine dernière.
Reading un grand homme as 'a tall man'; it means 'a great man'.
Confusing ma propre chambre (my own room) with ma chambre propre (my clean room).

contrasts.note: For most adjectives the position is fixed and does not change the meaning.
Certains as a pronoun means 'some people', unlike certain as an adjective.
Certain before a noun works like a determiner (some), after it as an adjective (sure).

examples.sentence: C'est mon ancien professeur.
examples.translation: He's my former teacher.

examples.sentence: Ils habitent une maison ancienne.
examples.translation: They live in an old house.

examples.sentence: Ce pauvre homme a perdu son chien.
examples.translation: This unfortunate man lost his dog.

examples.sentence: Je l'ai vu la semaine dernière.
examples.translation: I saw him last week.

constructs.name: inversion du sujet après certains adverbes
constructs.description: Subject-verb inversion in formal writing after some adverbs placed first in the clause.

card.formation: When an adverb such as aussi (therefore), ainsi, peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du moins or encore opens the clause, the subject pronoun is placed after the verb with a hyphen. A noun subject stays before the verb and is repeated by a pronoun after it (peut-être Marie viendra-t-elle).
card.use: It is a feature of careful written French, where it is the expected order after these adverbs; after aussi and ainsi the plain order also occurs. After peut-être and sans doute, the alternative is to add que and keep the normal order (peut-être qu'il viendra), which is usual in speech.
pitfalls: Reading aussi at the head of a clause as 'also'; with inversion it means 'therefore'.
Inverting after peut-être que; que blocks the inversion.
Forgetting the t between vowels (peut-être viendra-t-il).
Putting a noun subject after the verb instead of repeating it with a pronoun.

contrasts.note: The same word order here makes a statement, not a question.
A noun subject is repeated by a pronoun in both, so they look alike.
Aussi meaning 'also' comes after the verb and causes no inversion.
Elsewhere adverbs follow the verb and do not change the word order.

examples.sentence: Il était tard, aussi sommes-nous rentrés.
examples.translation: It was late, so we went home.

examples.sentence: Peut-être viendra-t-il demain.
examples.translation: Perhaps he will come tomorrow.

examples.sentence: À peine était-elle arrivée qu'il est parti.
examples.translation: She had hardly arrived when he left.

constructs.name: présentatifs (c'est, voici, voilà)
constructs.description: Expressions used to present or identify a person or thing.

card.formation: C'est + singular noun or pronoun, ce sont + plural noun (c'est is also common with plurals in speech). Voici and voilà are followed by a noun, or preceded by an object pronoun (le voilà).
card.use: C'est identifies or describes a person or thing; voici and voilà point something out or hand it over. Voilà is the everyday form; voici is formal or points to what comes next.
pitfalls: Saying il est un médecin; use c'est un médecin or il est médecin without the article.
Using voilà with a subject pronoun (voilà il) instead of the object pronoun (le voilà).
Using ce sont in casual speech, where c'est is normal.
Using c'est when describing a specific person with an adjective (elle est gentille, not c'est gentille).

contrasts.note: Il y a states that something exists or is present; c'est identifies it.
C'est followed by qui or que highlights one element of a sentence.
Ce, ça and cela as pronouns, of which c'est is one use.
Il est / elle est + adjective or profession without article describe a known person.

examples.sentence: C'est mon frère.
examples.translation: This is my brother.

examples.sentence: Ce sont mes amis.
examples.translation: These are my friends.

examples.sentence: Voilà ton café.
examples.translation: Here's your coffee.

examples.sentence: Le voilà enfin !
examples.translation: There he is at last!

constructs.name: il y a
constructs.description: Impersonal il y a stating that something exists or is present.

card.formation: Impersonal il + y + avoir, always in the third person singular, even before a plural noun. It changes tense (il y avait, il y aura), takes ne ... pas de in the negative, and becomes y a-t-il in an inverted question.
card.use: It says that something exists or is present somewhere. Followed by a length of time, il y a means 'ago'.
pitfalls: Making it plural (il y ont) before a plural noun.
Keeping un, une or des after the negative: il n'y a pas de pain.
Using est instead of il y a to say something exists (in the box there is ...).
Forgetting the t in the inverted question: y a-t-il.

contrasts.note: C'est identifies something; il y a says it exists.
Il y a + time means 'ago', a different use of the same words.
Il n'y a pas de follows the general rule un/des → de after negation.
Y here is part of the fixed expression, not a pronoun replacing a place.
Other verbs with impersonal il (il reste, il manque) work similarly.

examples.sentence: Il y a un chat dans le jardin.
examples.translation: There's a cat in the garden.

examples.sentence: Il n'y a pas de lait.
examples.translation: There's no milk.

examples.sentence: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
examples.translation: There were a lot of people.

constructs.name: adverbes d'intensité et de quantité
constructs.description: Adverbs modifying the degree of an adjective, adverb or verb.

card.formation: Très, si, assez, trop, plutôt and peu go before an adjective or adverb; beaucoup, trop, assez, peu and un peu go after a conjugated verb. Before a noun these quantity words take de (beaucoup de, trop de), never très.
card.use: They raise or lower the degree of a quality or the amount of an action: très beau, trop cher, il travaille beaucoup.
pitfalls: Saying très beaucoup; beaucoup cannot be modified by très.
Using très with a verb (je très aime) instead of beaucoup after the verb.
Confusing peu (little, not much) with un peu (a little, some).
Adding an article after beaucoup: beaucoup de gens, not beaucoup des gens.

contrasts.note: Beaucoup de or trop de + noun belong to quantity expressions with de.
Si, tant or tellement followed by que announce a result.
Plus, moins and aussi compare two things instead of stating a degree.
In compound tenses beaucoup and trop go between auxiliary and participle.
Que or comme also express high degree, but as an exclamation.

examples.sentence: Ce gâteau est très bon.
examples.translation: This cake is very good.

examples.sentence: Il travaille beaucoup.
examples.translation: He works a lot.

examples.sentence: C'est trop cher pour moi.
examples.translation: It's too expensive for me.

examples.sentence: Je suis un peu fatigué.
examples.translation: I'm a bit tired.

constructs.name: phrase exclamative
constructs.description: Exclamatory sentences with an exclamative word or intonation.

card.formation: An exclamation is built with quel (agreeing with the noun) + noun, with que or comme + a full clause, with ce que + clause in speech, or with exclamatory intonation alone. The word order is that of a statement.
card.use: It expresses surprise, admiration, indignation or another strong feeling about a degree or a quality.
pitfalls: Forgetting to make quel agree: quelle belle journée.
Using comme or que with an adjective alone (comme beau !); they need a clause (comme c'est beau !).
Inverting subject and verb as in a question.
Using combien as in English 'how' with an adjective.

contrasts.note: Quel has the same forms in questions; the exclamation has no question meaning.
Très states a high degree plainly; the exclamation adds emotion.
Both rely on intonation, but exclamations do not ask anything.

examples.sentence: Quelle belle journée !
examples.translation: What a beautiful day!

examples.sentence: Comme c'est beau !
examples.translation: How beautiful it is!

examples.sentence: Qu'il fait chaud aujourd'hui !
examples.translation: It's so hot today!

constructs.name: phrase nominale
constructs.description: Sentences without a conjugated verb, typical of signs, titles and headlines.

card.formation: A sentence built around a noun, adjective or other word without a conjugated verb, often with a noun derived from a verb (arrivée, fermeture) and its complement introduced by de.
card.use: It is used in headlines, titles, signs, notices, notes and lists, where brevity matters more than a full sentence.
pitfalls: Reading a headline noun as a subject and looking for a missing verb.
Missing that a noun like fermeture stands for an action (closing).
Using verbless sentences in a regular essay, where they look like notes.

contrasts.note: Nominalisation is the process of turning verbs into nouns; the verbless sentence often uses its results.
Pas de or non without a verb is a short negative reply, not a title or sign.
Signs and instructions can also use an infinitive (ne pas fumer).

examples.sentence: Fermeture du magasin le lundi.
examples.translation: Shop closed on Mondays.

examples.sentence: Défense de fumer.
examples.translation: No smoking.

examples.sentence: Grève des trains ce week-end.
examples.translation: Train strike this weekend.

constructs.name: adverbes en -ment
constructs.description: Forming adverbs of manner from the feminine of the adjective plus -ment, with the -amment/-emment forms.

card.formation: Add -ment to the feminine of the adjective (lente → lentement), or to the masculine if it ends in a vowel (vrai → vraiment). Adjectives in -ant and -ent give -amment and -emment (constant → constamment, prudent → prudemment), both pronounced with [a].
card.use: These adverbs mostly say how something is done; some also comment on the whole sentence (heureusement, malheureusement).
pitfalls: Adding -ment to a masculine ending in a consonant (lentment instead of lentement).
Writing -ament instead of -amment, or pronouncing -emment with [e].
Forgetting the irregular forms: gentil → gentiment, bref → brièvement, and some with -ément (précisément, énormément).
Forming bonnement or mauvaisement for 'well' and 'badly'; use bien and mal.
Treating lent like prudent: the adverb is lentement, not lemment.

contrasts.note: Gives where these adverbs go in simple and compound tenses.
The feminine form is the base for most -ment adverbs.
En + present participle can also describe the manner of an action.
Bien and mal have irregular comparatives (mieux, pire).

examples.sentence: Parle lentement, s'il te plaît.
examples.translation: Speak slowly, please.

examples.sentence: Heureusement, il n'a pas plu.
examples.translation: Fortunately, it didn't rain.

examples.sentence: Il conduit prudemment.
examples.translation: He drives carefully.

examples.sentence: C'est vraiment délicieux.
examples.translation: It's really delicious.

constructs.name: nominalisation
constructs.description: Turning a verb or adjective into a noun, often to make writing more compact.

card.formation: A noun is formed from a verb with suffixes such as -tion, -ment, -age, -ure or -ée (construire → construction, lancer → lancement) or without suffix (départ), and from an adjective with -té, -eur, -esse or -ise (beau → beauté). The verb's subject or object becomes a complement introduced by de.
card.use: It makes writing more compact and impersonal, typical of reports, headlines, summaries and academic texts.
pitfalls: Getting the gender wrong: nouns in -tion and -té are feminine, those in -ment and -age mostly masculine.
Inventing a suffix where French uses another (la décision, not la décidement).
Keeping the verb's construction instead of using de (la construction du pont).
Making a text too heavy by nominalising every verb.

contrasts.note: Verbless headlines and notices are a frequent use of nominalised forms.
The suffix of a nominalised noun usually decides its gender.
The complement of a nominalised verb is introduced by de, like other noun complements.
Some nouns come from participles (l'arrivée), which can also be used as adjectives.

examples.sentence: La construction du pont a duré deux ans.
examples.translation: The building of the bridge took two years.

examples.sentence: Le départ du train est prévu à midi.
examples.translation: The train's departure is scheduled for noon.

examples.sentence: La beauté du paysage m'a frappé.
examples.translation: The beauty of the landscape struck me.

constructs.name: apposition
constructs.description: A noun phrase placed beside a noun, usually between commas, to identify or describe it, often without an article.

card.formation: A noun phrase is placed right next to a noun that refers to the same person or thing, usually after it and between commas (or after a single comma at the end of the sentence). A noun giving a role or profession usually has no article; a definite article is used when it identifies a known or unique referent.
card.use: It adds information about someone or something without a relative clause, typically a profession, role or identifying description. It is very common in newspapers, biographies and other written texts.
pitfalls: Adding un or une before a profession, as in English 'a doctor' (Paul, un médecin), where French usually has no article.
Forgetting the second comma when the apposition sits in the middle of the sentence.
Taking the apposition for the subject and making the verb agree with it instead of with the main noun.
Using un where a known, unique referent needs le or la (Victor Hugo, l'auteur des Misérables).
Adding qui est in every case, which makes the sentence heavy where a plain apposition is natural.

contrasts.note: A relative clause between commas (Paul, qui est médecin, ...) adds the same kind of information with a verb.
In la ville de Paris, de + noun names the same thing as the head noun; an ordinary noun complement names something different (la gare de Paris).
The missing article before a profession in apposition follows the same rule as il est médecin.
An adjective or participle can also be set off by commas, but it must agree with the noun, while an apposed noun keeps its own gender.
A detached element at the start taken up by a pronoun sets the topic; an apposition only describes a noun already present.

examples.sentence: Marie, professeure de maths, habite à Lyon.
examples.translation: Marie, a maths teacher, lives in Lyon.

examples.sentence: Victor Hugo, l'auteur des Misérables, est né en 1802.
examples.translation: Victor Hugo, the author of Les Misérables, was born in 1802.

examples.sentence: Je te présente Paul, mon voisin.
examples.translation: This is Paul, my neighbour.
